And the loan forgiveness portion of this only applies to the down payment assistance, not the first lien mortgages? Correct. Okay. Thank you, Mr. Mayor. Chairman, five minutes. Thank you. And that includes 150 loans for individuals earning less than $60,000. To create an enhanced visual environment for our residents. To commemorate the City's rich cultural and ethnic diversity. Third, to integrate the design work of artists into the development of our infrastructure. And finally, to promote tourism and economic vitality through the design of our public spaces. 2001 was a year in which the Council established the program by enacting the Public Art Ordinance, which is now part of the City Code. The Council subsequently, in 2002, appointed the Fort Worth Art Commission. And through the process of issuing a request for proposal, selected the Arts Council to manage that program. They've been managing the program ever since. In 2003, you adopted the Public Art Master Plan, which outlined many of the fundamental policies governing the Public Art Program. And you authorized the very first artwork contracts for the Fort Worth Convention Center. You see on the lower left the depiction of the hat made of the star made of hats, which is located in the Convention Center. 2004, you approved the first bond program that included 2% for public art. And you adopted, in 2005, the public art plan corresponding to that bond program. For each debt program, you've adopted a corresponding public art plan outlining how those funds would be expended for public art projects. Similarly, in 2006, you adopted a public art plan for the Water Fund. In 2008, you launched the Community ID Program, Public Art in Neighborhoods. In 2010, anti-graffiti murals. I think it's fair to say that Fort Worth Public Art has received broad recognition throughout the state of Texas and even at the national scale. The Art Commission advises the City Council on all issues involving public art and the public art program. It's comprised of nine at-large members appointed by the City Council, five of which are art professionals, and the other four are representatives of the community. They serve, as do members of most boards and commissions, two-year terms, and may be reappointed for up to an additional two terms, so maximum of six years of service on the Fort Worth Art Commission. Let's talk about the funding levels for public art. And we can begin by comparing Fort Worth to the five other major cities in Texas. And I think it's fair to say, not only in Texas but nationally, cities that have established public art programs tend to allocate anywhere between 1% and 2% of their capital funds for public art, anywhere from 1% to 2%. In Texas, you can see that three of the largest cities, Fort Worth, Austin, and El Paso, are at the 2% level. San Antonio is at 1%, Houston 1.75%, Dallas at 1.5%. So we see that range from 1% to 2%, with three of the six being at the 2% level. If we look nationally at the cities that allocate 2% of their capital funds for public art, I think we can discern a couple of trends. First and perhaps most obvious, California, a very large concentration of cities allocating 2% public art. Texas happens to be number two in the number of cities at the 2% level. More subtly, perhaps, if you look at some of the other cities, Portland, Santa Fe, Austin, what do they have in common? I think you can say that most of these other 2% cities have in common some degree of success in attracting, retaining, educated professionals who are driving the economy of the future. What author Richard Florida describes as the creative class. And just a few weeks ago at the Visional Texas Regional Summit, I think some of you were there. I know Mayor Price spoke. I know Councilman Skarth is present. Dr. Florida, at the invitation of UT Arlington, spoke about the preliminary results of an economic study he's conducted about the North Texas region. And he concluded not only by highlighting some of the strengths of the region, how Fort Worth complements Dallas more so than competes with Dallas. He also suggested three strategies we might use to attract and retain that creative class in North Texas. Suggested that we facilitate greater regional cooperation, that we develop a network of nationally competitive research universities. And third, of specific relevance to public art, is that we promote broader participation in arts and culture. Obviously, public art is only one component of participatory arts and culture, but it can be an important one. Looking at how we've actually generated funds for public art, you can look at the various debt programs, the 2004, 2007, 2008. These are the same programs that Dr. Wersig discussed a few minutes ago in connection with our street projects. Also, water and sewer and other sources total over $21 million over a 10-year period. So a little more than $2 million per year on the average during the 10-year life of the public art program. Other sources are outlined at the bottom of the screen on the footnote. In the year 2014, right now this same time frame, I had 287 individuals signed up to say I want to be a lifeguard. About 50 to 60% of those individuals actually passed the lifeguarding test, and so I would get an extra 140 or an extra 125 individuals. Right now at this time, I have 106 individuals signed up right now who say that they want to be a lifeguard. If the statistics stay the same, that would mean that 50% of them, or 53, would pass the lifeguarding, which would mean that would bring my total of lifeguards for the season to approximately 300. In order for me to effectively open all of the swimming pools this year, I need a minimum of 500. Ideally, I'd love to have 700. And so the reason that we're asking to pay lifeguards, individuals who have to earn that lifeguarding certification, a minimum of 1303, regardless of their age, is because they're asked to do the exact same duties and responsibilities that lifeguards are asked to do, whether they're 18, 21, or 15, and we're feeling as though that this is a recruitment tool because I'm in a position right now where I'm in jeopardy of not having enough staff to be able to serve the public appropriately. And I certainly understand that, and it's not just the age, it's the lack of experience as well. And so it seems like there should be a career kind of ladder, so we start them at 11. Maybe we could move, because my concern is that we're dipping into our reserve funds. And so if we could start some people at that lower level and maybe work up from 8 to 10, then 11, then to 13, and then you could start your more experienced people regardless of their age, but they've had experience, they've done a good job, they've worked for three seasons or whatever it is, then maybe it's the impact of the cost initially would not be so much. Because the next year we're going to ask for a budget amendment to try to get everybody up to that 13 level. I'm just trying to help us think through with the limited budget. Can we kind of phase people in rather than going with all 300 or 600, or if you're lucky, 700 people at 1303 an hour? And I would say that our history says that in our tiered experience that we have right now, albeit we're not paying everyone $11, but in our tiered experience right now, I'm in the position that I'm in because I'm hearing from our individuals. And this was something that we talked about last year, but I'm hearing from individuals that I can go to Amy's Ice Cream and make $15 an hour. I can go to Home Depot and make $14 an hour. I can go to Dairy Queen and make $12 an hour. What's the incentive for me to come to the City of Austin Parks and Recreation Department and be a lifeguard where you're requiring me to be trained, you're requiring me to have the responsibility of saving people's lives, yet you're paying me a wage that's less than I could make at other retail locations. And while I have not, frankly, I have not called Amy's Ice Cream or I haven't called the Home Depot or other entities, you know, we did do research last year that's similar, telling us the similar thing, that our wage is not competitive enough to attract folks to want to come and work for us seasonally, which then puts the safety and our service in jeopardy. Last thing, Mayor, is that I'm glad to know Amy's pays $15 an hour. That's more than I get. So I'm going to go start working for Amy's. Ms. Poole. I think it's specifically at the airport. I'm not sure. Ms. Poole. Thanks. I think part of the 1303 is that that was the direction that this council moved in as far as our employees, that our minimum wage would be $13.03. Is that where that number is coming from? So that's a policy that this council had decided. Yes. As I understand it, the policy was that individuals would make 1303 who were temporary employees. Right. Transcript:
And it carries unanimously. Thank you. And we also, it's another example that we would like to provide to other homeowners, historic preservation neighborhood associations, and people who are working within the district that get together, because this is another example of excellent cooperation between the two, which makes life easier for them and easier for us to really be on board. Thank you both. Thank you. Next case. Next case is COA 11-99, 2319 West Rosedale Street South. Applicant requests a certificate of appropriateness to modify the detached two-car garage, including a reconfiguration of two one-car openings into one two-car opening, and a waiver from the Mistletoe Heights Historic District Standards and Guidelines to replace wood siding with hardy board siding, and have a two-car metal garage door. Staff report, please. The 1926 Sanborn map shows a one-car garage in approximately the same location as the current structure. This structure was enlarged by 1951, as indicated on that same year's Sanborn map. As proposed, the applicant would like to convert the two single-width openings to a one double-width opening. Because the structure was built with two-car openings, the center's support between the doors is most likely structural. This must be taken into consideration if the openings are changed. The applicant has also requested a waiver for the use of hardy board siding and a metal garage door to fit the proposed double-width opening. Staff recommends approval for the certificate of appropriateness, including the requested waivers.

You know, buses are more about moving people around, and they're less about influencing and supporting land uses. So, you know, that's been the objective of the community, I think, really, is to add more rail, to have that permanence, which, you know, enables it, a transportation mode, to really support and work with land use, unlike many other modes. Garages were almost always detached from the main structure. This mostly had to do with the fear of exploding gasoline as it was kept in the garage and not at the filling station. As a result of the fear, most detached garages were built of brick, concrete, block, or hollow clay tile rather than wood, even if the house was wood-framed and had wood siding. By the 1920s, people were more comfortable with cars and filling stations opened up. Garages were sometimes built in the style and with like materials of the main structure, but it wasn't uncommon for it to have a different type of cladding and typically had rolled roofing or metal roofing regardless of what was on the main structure. In dense urban areas, these structures were often built on the property line. If alleys were used, the garage door would typically face the alley or would be at a right angle to the alley. And then on the regulation side, Jacob's team is really focused on the licensure process itself and overall monitoring with the companies. Jason, do you want to add any more? No, not at this time, no. All right. First speaker is Ray Nadler-Alinek, Water Fluoridation. Good afternoon, Mayor and Council Members. Next Wednesday morning, May 18th, the Council's Committee on Public Health and Human Services will meet here in City Hall with representatives of both sides – on both sides of the fluoridation debate for a work session. That event could prove a historic turning point if only you are willing to think outside the box and carefully consider the scientific information our experts will provide. I urge you to place scientific evidence above cut-and-paste dogma. When you hear safe and effective, ask yourselves how that can be in the light of today's evidence. When you hear CDC best practices, remember that those are the same best practices that have resulted in fluorosis-disfigured teeth for approaching half of our young people today. They call this mild. True endorsement by the CDC sounds impressive at first. When we think of CDC, we picture its grandiose Atlanta headquarters and army of 15,000 employees. We'll scratch that. The CDC's Division of Oral Health comprises 28 dentist bureaucrats without medical or toxological training paid to promote community fluoridation. They're PR people, basically. That's it. And there's strong resistance brewing in Atlanta, the CDC's backyard. Atlanta is a city of over half a million, 58% of it black. There, the African-American community is mobilizing against what was sold as a social entitlement but is now recognized as environmental racism. Last month, Andrew Young, iconic MLK-era civil rights leader, former Atlanta mayor, former U.N. ambassador, three-time member of the U.S. House of Representatives, and a dentist's son, came out forcefully against fluoridation. Noting that cavities are rampant in inner cities that have been fluoridated for decades and that both cavity and fluorosis rates are higher among blacks, he said, quote, I am most deeply concerned for poor families who have babies. If they cannot afford unfluoridated water for their baby's milk formula, do their babies not count? This is an issue of fairness, civil rights, and compassion, unquote. Two days ago, Martin Luther King's daughter, Bernice, issued an equally forthright statement calling for an end to the practice and for fluoride gate investigations into the deception which has always surrounded it. The cat's out of the bag on this one, Consul. People are waking up to the fact that fluoride is bad for you. It needs to be ended and soon. Thank you. Thank you. Next speaker is Pat Balstrales. Welcome, Pat. Your topic is Animal Adoption Center. You have three minutes. Thank you, Mayor Pro Tem, and thank you, Council members. Thank you for all you've done in the last three years for the animals. I think you've been a great council, and I really appreciate that. Before I talk about the Adoption Center, I would like to briefly state that I understand that the city's new social services selection process leaves no funding for legal services, and I would like to ask you what my usual mantra is, that you have a lot of public comment and a lot of public input on that decision before you finalize that. I support legal services, and I have not followed that very carefully, but I think that with a lot of public comment, you'll make a good decision. Similarly, along those lines about the Adoption Center, I would like to also ask for a very open and collaborative process for what to do after the six months that I understand you've directed, and I understand there's some discussion about those six months, but I'm not here to talk about that. I fully support the directive you already made that the two facilities stay open for six months. My concern is what happens after the six months, and here's what I would like to request of you. One, that you put it on a council agenda where you discuss a directive to staff to work with all groups that might be interested in contributing to running that facility as an animal facility after the six months. I understand there have been some private conversations taking place, and what usually happens with private conversations is the big groups are part of it, and the little groups don't even really know what's going on. And I'm here to speak for the little groups that I hope get a chance to give their input and maybe be part of that process. At that open meeting that I hope can occur pretty soon, you would give a directive to staff to work with everybody to solicit ideas, to have open forums where all of us could talk about some of our ideas. One idea I have is to reach out to Texas A&M to see if they'd like to have some of their vet students come and help with the spay-neuter for animals of the small rescue groups that can't afford spay-neuter. I mean, or that it hits them really hard to pay that fee. That's just one idea. I'm sure other people can come up with great ideas. I think we have a great community, and if we work together, we'll keep doing great things that you've already started us down the path. Thanks again, and let me know if you have any questions. Thank you, Pat. On the social service item you brought up about the legal services, right now it's simply a proposal. The Parks Department has announced that it intends to close the Norwood Dog Park and replace it with an unspecified project, such as a parking lot for the extended hike and bike trail, a parking lot for a light rail stop, or as a garden for the restored Norwood house. The director of the parks department has said that the dog droppings at the dog park pollute town lake. However, almost nothing pollutes waterways as much as parking lots. Users of the dog park are especially concerned because the parks department has not yet followed through on a previous commitment to provide a replacement for the disc golf area that was in Peace Park. Communiques from the parks department have stated that they would probably replace the Norwood Dog Park with another off-leash area, showing little understanding of the need many dogs and their owners have for a secure place to bring their dogs and their small children. Many types of dogs are bred to run and cover large areas. They cannot be exercised in an off-leash area, which is not fenced. One recent letter from the director of the parks department to a member of our group, I think I have the wrong page, talked about using a four to six foot fence, and many of our dogs can jump over a four foot fence. This park is used by training groups who are training and socializing puppies to visit jails and nursing homes. It's used by disabled people, disabled seniors who have trouble walking their dogs. It's used by people in apartments and condos downtown and in the dense Riverside apartment area. It's visible from Interstate 35 and accessible, and people travel from as far away as Kyle and Pflugerville, people who are not necessarily in residence of the city of Austin. We've gathered letters and names of people who support the dog park, and I have a packet for each of you that I'll take to be passed out today. We're asking you to please do whatever is necessary to save the dog park in its current location. Thank you very much. Next speaker is Linda Green from Fluorosilic Acid. Thank you, Mayor. The exact title of my speech is Fluorosilic Acid is Not the Same as Fluoride. Why won't City Council stop adding hazardous waste to our water? There are many sources of fluoride. There's calcium fluoride, which one of our speakers showed you last week. It's a pretty green rock. It comes abundantly from China and West Texas, and if you suck on it, you'll probably get sick. There's sodium fluoride, which is put in our toothpaste, which is largely a waste product from, or I should say, byproduct from the aluminum industry. Transcript:
Well, I seem to remember a state law that specifically excludes highest and best-use tax valuation for use other than residential for residential homes. Does legal know? I'm familiar with the law that you're referring to. It was passed. It wasn't this session. It was the previous session. But I don't know the specifics that we, I haven't had, I don't have experience in property taxes, and it's fair to the city because it's not something that we traditionally do internally. So I could not answer that question. Commissioner Shockey. I have a question as well in terms of the density that's going to occur with the rezoning. Am I reading this correctly, that the maximum dwelling units in this area can only be 19? I mean, are the lot sizes going to change? I mean, this looks like a rural residential area. So I applaud all the conditions in the overlay district because you wouldn't want that area to change. But now, will the lot size change and increase the density in the proposed zoning? No. What I was trying to show here in this slide is that, first of all, all of the properties within that subdivision were not annexed. It is to consider making a recommendation to the City Council regarding applying an initial zoning designation of Rural Commercial with an overlay district to approximately 37 acres of land located within the Milam Creek Ranch Subdivision. And our planner is Ms. Matthews. Thank you, Mr. Chairman, members of the Commission. The Milam Creek Ranch Subdivision is located on the south side of Milam Road and on the east and west sides of Milam Ridge Road. In the northern portion of town, east of I-35. The subdivision was included in an area identified as PAA-4 during last year's annexation proceedings. And just to recap, PAA-4 included approximately 1,558 acres. It was located on the south side of Milam Road north of Loop 288 and east of I-35. Approximately 454 of the total 1,558 acres was annexed. Approximately 37 of the total 79 acres within the Milam Creek Ranch Subdivision was annexed. And the subdivision is circled here in yellow. And again, the remaining properties return non-annexation agreements. This subdivision was platted through the city of Denton and was approved by the Planning and Zoning Commission in 1996. At that time, it was still in our ATJ. For newly annexed land, it is not annexed. Newly annexed land is not annexed. However, it is subject to the list of permitted uses, intensities, dimensions of the R-D-5 zoning district. So for lack of a better word, the properties that were annexed have a default zoning of R-D-5. And approximately 12 lots of the 23 lots were annexed. Remaining, again, highlighted or shown here in white are still in the ETJ. Due to the previously mentioned stipulations in the R-D-5 designation, the Milam Creek Ranch Subdivision is considered non-conforming due to the maximum density requirements of 0.2 dwelling units per acre allowed in the R-D-5. This would equate to for the entire subdivision because we are looking at this holistically because we do anticipate that the entire subdivision will be in the city at some point. So looking at the subdivision as a whole, only 16 dwelling units would be allowed within that subdivision. Right now, 16 currently exist and there are several lots that are undeveloped. So the RC zoning district allows 0.5 dwelling units per acre. So that would equate to approximately 40 dwelling units for the entire subdivision and 19 for those that were annexed already. Again, the proposed zoning district is rural commercial with an overlay district, and I'll get into the overlay district in the next few slides. The future land use designation for this area is rural areas, so a comprehensive plan amendment is not required. We held a neighborhood meeting at the Civic Center on September 22nd. Several property owners were in attendance at that meeting, and they did not object to the RC zoning district. However, they did object to some of the uses that are or would be permitted by right or with a specific use permit or limitation in the RC zoning district. And so the next few slides I've highlighted in yellow what the neighborhood would like to see prohibited via this overlay district. So as it relates to residential, they would like to see dwellings above businesses be prohibited. Community homes for the disabled, group homes, multifamily dwellings, and manufactured housing developments they would like to see prohibited. However, after consulting with our legal department regarding the community homes for the disabled, I learned that section 123.003 of the Texas Human Resources Code prohibits a city from zoning out community homes for the disabled. So we cannot zone out that use, so we're proposing that it remain. In terms of the commercial uses, the neighborhood would like to see a bed and breakfast, restaurant, or private club prohibits it. Professional services and offices, vehicle repair, outdoor recreation, major event entertainment, the neighborhood would like to see prohibited. Administrative research facilities, broadcasting, sexually oriented businesses, temporary uses, the neighborhood would like to see prohibited. In terms of the industrial land use category, in terms of the industrial land use category, bakeries, light manufacturing, and wholesale nurseries are all permitted in the proposed zoning district. Either by right or with limitations or an SUP, the neighborhood would like to see those uses prohibited. Kennels, veterinary clinics as well. Community service, churches, semi-public halls, clubs and lodges, adult or child daycare facilities, kindergarten or elementary schools. The neighborhood would like to see prohibited. As well as community service, churches. Oh, is that a... And that was a repeat, I'm sorry. And so these are the remaining uses, and there is no difference there, and they will remain the same. The next few slides are photos taken on site. This is as you enter into the Milam Creek Ranch subdivision at the corner of Milam Creek. I'm sorry, Milam Road and Milam Ridge. Just looking at our sign, one of the homes within the subdivision. Another home on the east side, west side of Milam Ridge Road. And this is one of the undeveloped lots on the east side of Milam Ridge Road. Staff sent notices, certified notices to the property owners, 26 within 200 feet of the area, 500 feet. We sent four notices. We received two notices in opposition, which represents less than 20%. We received two notices neutral to the request. One is not shown on this map because it is in your backup, but it's not shown here because I can't find that address. The property owner did not include an address on that notice or a property ID number, and I could not find that person's name in my address list. So the Development Review Committee recommends approval of applying an official zoning district of RC with an overlay district to properties within the Milam Creek Ranch subdivision that are currently located within the boundaries of the city of Denton. And I can stand for questions at this time. Thank you. We have a question from Commissioner Bentley. I have one question. This is being done so we can go ahead and develop those undeveloped lots. And there's, I believe, 29 lots within that subdivision. But the RC would allow 40 units in there. Do you know if there's any kind of deed restriction or anything that stops the subdividing of the existing lots? At the neighborhood meeting they did mention there are deed restrictions as it relates to the size of the lots and the size of the homes. You may want to ask someone that's here representing that community, though. But, yes, there are deed restrictions from what I understand. Thank you. Commissioner Taylor. I have two questions. First, the uses, that there are a lot of uses in that overlay district. It appears that those uses match NR1. Is there a reason that NR1 wasn't proposed? Like, so RC is somewhat misleading because it's a commercial use zoning. And this is obviously a residential area. Is there a reason that NR1 wasn't proposed instead? We looked at NR1 initially, and when we submitted the application to the city, that's what we were proposing. But in looking at the maximum density allowed in the NR1, which is one dwelling unit per acre, that would allow 79, 80 additional dwelling units. And so we wanted to kind of, we just don't have a zoning district that fits every particular scenario. But we felt like this was the best one with the use, with an overlay district. If I may elaborate on that a little bit more. As John has said, we did look initially at the NR1 zoning district. But again, the density is such that it would allow for potential subdivisions of those lots. I think there's a deed restriction that you can't have a lot less and smaller than two acres. The problem or the challenge is that the city cannot enforce deed restrictions. So one could potentially come to us under the NR1 zoning district with a subdivision application. And we would be able to deny, per se. But then they would still have to abide by the deed restriction. So we were trying to avoid those types of conflicts where we're issuing a permit for something that can't be done. Now, that being said, I believe that there are some lots out there that are larger than the deed restricted lots. That they could potentially be subdivided. But it was the closest district we could find in the DDC that would meet what was already out there to allow for the lot sizes, to allow for the residential uses, and not to create ambiguity between the DDC and the deed restrictions. Okay, I'll set that issue aside for just a moment. I have another question. There are a lot of public comment cards regarding increased taxes, worried about increased taxes due to a commercial zoning. I just want to clarify, I would like somebody to clarify to me, can a single-family home that's in something like an RC or potential multi-use zoning be taxed at higher than single-family tax rates? That is not something that we can address in the city that we don't do tax assessment. It's done at the property appraisal Denton Central Appraisal District. That's right. So we don't, I can't speak. Well, I seem to remember a state law that specifically excludes highest and best-use tax valuation for use other than residential for residential homes. Does legal know? I'm familiar with the law that you're referring to. It was passed. It wasn't this session. It was the previous session.

Colonel Fitzgerald was a native of South Carolina. He was a very prominent newspaper man and had worked at newspapers in Dallas, Fort Worth, and Wichita Falls before coming to Austin in 1921 to become the political and chief editorial writer for both the American and the Statesman, because they were separate newspapers at that time. He was very active in political circles, both in Austin and throughout the state, and in fact, in 1931, the Texas State Senate hung his portrait on the walls of the Senate chambers in recognition of his contributions to Texas journalism and politics. He died in 1936, and the next year, his widow sold the property to Fred and Alice Gray Upchurch. Fred Upchurch was a native of Corsicana, Texas. He was a lawyer and the city attorney in Corsicana, and then moved to Austin with his job as an assistant state attorney general, purchased this house. He personally handled all of the oil, gas, and public utility litigation for the Railroad Commission, and then became a federal attorney after World War II. Then he went back into private practice. In the 1960s, he moved back to Corsicana, where he became the city attorney up there once again. His wife, however, had a very different impact on Texas history. She was a very prominent author of county histories. Two of her most famous are histories of San Sava County and Nueces County. When the Upchurches moved back to Corsicana, they sold the house to Louis Scott Wilkerson and Florence Wilkerson. Mr. Wilkerson was a native of Beaumont. He went to Harvard Law School and worked as an assistant secretary of state in the 1950s. Then he went into private practice. His wife, Florence, was the daughter of Walter Benson, who was the brother of Madison Benson, who had the car company. Walter Benson got involved in school textbook publishing. And after her father's death, Florence basically took the company over, became the proofreader, very influential in determining the content of school textbooks in Texas. Can we share funding sources to provide a more integrated project and coordination? So this slide shows the Transportation Department's approach. What you'll see here is where public works is focused on the condition of existing assets and when we need to use capital dollars to improve those assets or keep them in quality working condition. ATD has a bit of a new mobility focus in terms of identifying projects that will either render better mobility on existing facilities where we team with public works and, as James said, find that sort of Venn diagram connection between the two, or actually new corridors or new assets and on a more regional basis. And so that's why you see a little bit different prioritization process here. We use a five-step project selection process. This prioritization process actually was developed prior to Imagine Austin, but we were obviously talking to the same people because the values that we were using in our prioritization process are verbatim identical to those from Imagine Austin. We do an initial project scoring. That gives us a set of candidate projects, as you can imagine, when we're talking about mobility needs in this region. That's multimodal capacity needs or improvement needs, and it certainly exceeds the capacity of any bond we might contemplate going forward. So we have to winnow those down. We analyze those projects. And that was a good thing that came out of this development of this bond proposition. The first slide talks specifically about the programs. The other important column on here is showing you what's actually going to be delivered at the end of that project. So we thought that was important. So you could see some will be construction, some will be design, or preliminary engineering reports, and sometimes a combination of both. The next slide shows the specific programs that were sponsored by ATD on this. And again, as you can see, there is coordination. Most of these projects do have a design and construction component. And as you can see, it also shows the allocation. As I mentioned before, there are seven name projects and are listed here. As you can see, there's mixed sponsorships and also some mixed stakeholders. Chapter: 5. Report of Arts Funding Task Force - Robert D. Benda, Arts Funding Task Force
Transcript:
How long do I have? Sorry. Annette. We'll give you the hot hook, dear Jungus. I, too, want to thank you and the committee. I've watched many of your meetings, and it is a very prestigious group, and we have concrete recommendations, and it's very astute and great. You know, I often say we live in the greatest city and the greatest state and the greatest nation on earth. And Cowboys in Culture and both the private and public partnerships have made us that way, and we want to keep us that way for our children and grandchildren. So I very much commend you. A couple of questions, and one really is for Horatio. But did you address the public art capital improvement program at all? And you probably know that we've had some discussion about the 2 percent, and we're getting ready for a bond package. Is that addressed in your report? It was addressed to the extent that we looked at whether or not we could get our hands on any of that. But as we understood the structure of it, we dismissed that as an option for our charter, and I'm aware of that other dialogue, but we relimited our study to whether or not it could be transferred. It was our understanding. To maintenance and operations and performing arts primarily. Next, we have Bob Benda from the Arts Task Force. Bob, welcome. Let's see. Thanks, Karen. Well, thank you for having me today. Our briefing is about the arts funding task force that I chaired that's been working since the beginning of January to bring you some recommendations relative to the arts funding challenges that y'all have faced. And based on the resolution that y'all passed, we've been working diligently on that for the last couple of months here. Let me see if I've got this right. So as you all know, all of the budget is under siege, and arts funding has been impacted by that as well as many others. During last year's budget process, many of the arts supporters lobbied you about the fact that this funding had dipped to critically low levels and really asked you to consider ways that you might be able to restore some of that funding. The arts funding task force that y'all appointed was asked to look at the feasibility and desirability of city funding for local arts. So can we do it and do we want to do it, as well as cultural exchange programs, being the sister cities program. And to identify alternatives to the general fund as potential sources of funding so that we're no longer competing with essential city services for our cultural support. Assessing the legal basis, appropriateness, capacity, stability, and relative merits of those funding sources. And I want to comment here on the excellent support that we had from your staff in assessing all these technical, governmentally oriented things that people aren't familiar with. I can't say enough about their cooperation, their diligence, their willingness to chase rabbits for us whenever we dreamed one up that needed to be chased. And we're very grateful to all your staff, Tom, for the service. Oh, sorry. Closer to the mic. They say they can't hear you, and we're being broadcast live. Yes, okay. Thank you. And then you asked us to conduct one or more public meetings to receive public comment. We did not create any public hearings, per se. All of the meetings were posted per the public meeting guidelines, and we had great community participation, a number of people that came and testified before us relative to a lot of the different things that we were trying to educate ourselves on. So we did that. This is your task force. All of these folks are very engaged, motivated, people passionate about our community, conversant on the needs of the various arts, as well as understanding the challenges that the city has. My task was easy. It was to moderate the input of these talented folks and come to a consensus recommendation for you, and I'm proud to say that I was able to do that. As with any recommendation from a group of this stature, there's some compromise involved, and we think what we're recommending to you is a compromise that's appropriate for the community to consider, given our budget challenges, our needs to underscore, underwrite our arts community, and hopefully be something that will make sense to you all. We organized, after our first couple of briefing meetings, where we asked a lot of questions about the various options that we might have to consider, organized into four committees that we felt would be a more efficient way to pursue some of the questions that were raised through that briefing process. And those four committees focused on the following four elements, the economic impact of the arts, in other words, what's the return on investment for the community in having a vibrant and healthy arts culture, arts funding in other Texas communities. We don't necessarily do what others in Texas do, but we want to understand what the standards are in that regard, and if we're competitive, and if someone else has thought of a better way to manage this challenge than us. So we tried to look at a contextual status of how we're doing things. A third committee based on those findings was to suggest in-kind opportunities perhaps for the city to help support our arts communities that may not have direct financial budgetary requirements. And finally, a committee to recommend art funding levels and sources based on all of this data collected by the group. We've provided, for your review, a fairly extensive appendix of data that were the basis of our final recommendations. In 2002, there was a cultural plan that was commissioned that the city participated in that commented on the value of the arts and recommended levels of the arts, and we included that because we think oftentimes studies that you all commission tend as there's turnover in the city leadership to go by the wayside, and we don't want to lose that past wisdom. And so we share that with you, again, if you're not already familiar with it, to reflect on as you look at the budget support in the coming year for the arts. Arts is an industry, talks about the financial impact and the fact that there's a real tangible economic value to our community and all its citizens from underwriting the arts. The leadership, Fort Worth, Class of 2013, has made some recommendations relative to the arts. Arts Council grant guidelines, we felt it was important for you to understand, if you're not already conversant in that area, what happens with the dollars that you allocate to the Arts Council for grants. And so this talks very clearly about the rigor of the guidelines that any applicant for arts funding have to meet to be recipients. This is a very formal and structured process that you've delegated to the Arts Council, and you can follow there those tangible guidelines, the application process. It's very rigorous. And a summary of the Arts Council grants, just to reaffirm for you where those funds go, how they're allocated out from the Arts Council. And finally, the makeup of Arts Council grant panels, which include, in each case, a city staffer, so that there's a very good alignment between city priorities, you're seeing where those funds are going. So our first committee, Economic Impact Committee, looked at a number of data points, and there was a study done in 2010 that was a collaboration of all the local arts communities and a national arts consultant that's able to help quantify the economic impact of arts activity within a community. And the finding was, and this is in 2010 dollars, so obviously there's been an escalator in those numbers over the time that's transpired since, but the total economic impact, including both goods and services acquired by the arts organizations and their payroll impact was $84.4 million from non-profit arts and culture organizations and audiences in Fort Worth. There were some notable organizations that did not participate, but of those that did, this is the number. So it's a conservative number from any perspective. In 2012, the Arts Council was good enough to provide us with a cumulative data about some of the impact on the community of their constituency, almost 3,000 performances, almost 3,000 performances, almost 2 million attendees, almost 3,000 employees, and nearing $44 million in purchasing of goods and services. Fort Worth's sister cities, of course, manages contracts for eight sister cities and results in impact on education, culture, economic relations, technology, et cetera. As you can see, unfortunately, given the realities of the picture that, as we understood it during our analysis, we're not able to bring you a recommendation for funding of Fort Worth's sister cities under your arts and culture allocations. However, we're strongly recommending that you consider its economic impact and its economic significance to us on an international basis, and perhaps with staff's assistance, we might be able to find some other way to continue some level of financial endorsement for that institution. So our committee that looked not only at arts funding in other Texas communities, but really looking at what the information that they gathered about benchmarking other Texas communities, what that suggested for Fort Worth as an aspirational goal about where ideally we might want to be if we want to be at the upper echelons of Texas communities in terms of our arts support. And so that committee and the detail of how we got to that analysis is in part of your package, but has recommended restoring historical levels of funding as soon as feasible. I might clarify at this point in time that because of the variability over the last years, we looked at numbers since 2003, basically. And there have been a number of organizations that one might or might not equate as being arts organizations. For instance, the Museum of Science and History, who you have supported at various significant levels in the past, are not included in our final recommendation. However, when we looked at the data provided by city staff, and we looked at historically where we've been and talk about levels going back to 2003, that does include the broader distribution of funds that have been in the past. Our recommendation today will only be about Arts Council, but I want to clarify when I talk about historical funding, it's a little bit apples and oranges, and that's something that we can certainly expand on for you during the Q&A period, if you like.

Council's direction on May 2nd fell into four subject matter areas. Housing capacity, missing middle housing, compatibility, and parking. Today's briefing will focus specifically on zoning as it relates to housing capacity. So, I'm going to hand the presentation over to Senior Planner, Lindy Garwood, who's going to brief the committee specifically on zoning categories, how we're handling residential uses along corridors, the preservation incentive, information on how we're handling accessory dwelling units and duplexes, how we're handling single family and multi-family zones, and then the co-lead, Brent Lloyd, will talk about changes to non-conforming regulations specific to single-family uses. So, with that, I'm going to hand it over to Lindy to go through our specifics. Thank you, Anique. Good morning, City Council members. My name is Lindy Garwood, and I am a member of the Planning and Zoning staff. I'm here to present a few of our recommendations for the LDC revision related to zoning. In your May 2nd directive, you instructed that the new LDC should focus on the size and scale of the built environment and regulate uses through context-sensitive policies that are clearly identified in the code and applied equitably throughout the city instead of through by-law zoning regulations. In the current code, zone categories are based on separating uses, residential here, commercial here, office over here, and then overlays were added over time that allowed mixed use, such as VMU. In our previous effort, we created zone categories that promoted mixed use and context-sensitive development, things like Main Street and mixed use. And in our effort today, we plan to carry forward those draft three categories, but simplify them with fewer zones within the zone categories themselves. The effect of this change is it will be more intuitive and simplified with context-sensitive, with a context-sensitivity that allows us to provide the code more consistently across the city and have less reliance on by-law zoning regulations. So, as a refresher, in reference for the future slides, here are the zoning categories that were developed in the previous effort that we're carrying forward today. Residential house scale, which allows house scale buildings with varying amounts of residential units. Residential multi-unit, which provides a transition between the low-density residential house scale and the higher-density corridors, which have mixed use in Main Street. Mixed use, which, by its name, allows a mix of uses, including office, housing, employment, services, and amenities. And then Main Street, which is really centered on transit centers and walkable areas, offering connected housing with jobs and amenities. There's also commercial and industrial zone category, and other, which includes things like public, park, agriculture, aviation, things like that. You directed that the new code should prioritize all types of homes for all kinds of people in all parts of town in a development pattern that supports 50-50 transportation mode share by 2039, as well as we should propose options for prohibiting uses along corridors that displace potential housing opportunities, such as self-storage facilities, and other uses that do not contribute to the overall policy goals. As previously mentioned, our current regulations separate our uses so that many of our base zoning districts don't allow residential on our corridors, which are primarily zoned commercial. Therefore, the commercial zones do not promote housing or walkability, as they are often auto-oriented and separate in their use. In our previous effort, we analyzed over 4,000 conditional overlays to find patterns and themes of where things were permitted and where things were not, and then created zoning districts that harmonize these to restrict commonly prohibited uses from the conditional overlays into context-sensitive districts. In today's code, we're continuing the effort that we had previously done, but also prioritizing the uses that support complete communities and everyday services to promote residential on our corridors. You also directed that the preservation incentive should be expanded citywide so that an additional unit beyond what would otherwise be allowed is allowed with the preservation of an existing structure. And if an existing affordable home is preserved, the balance of the lots entitlements can be used to add dwelling units. You also asked that we identify and implement opportunities throughout the code to encourage preservation of existing housing, especially market-rate affordable. In our current code, this incentive does not exist. This was a brainchild of the previous effort, and where if you had a house that was 10 years old and you preserved that, you could add an accessory dwelling unit, and it wouldn't count against your FAR. In today's effort, we're continuing the preservation incentive and expanding it to more zones, including multifamily zones, where you can exceed the FAR limit to achieve additional units. We are currently working to implement council's direction related to allowing additional units beyond what's permitted within your base zone. The effect of this change is that the preservation incentive is expanded to preserve existing structures while also providing more housing capacity and diversity across the city. So tonight we want to talk to you a little bit about Draft 3, Code Next. The staff recommendation came out on February 12th. It's the policy recommendation made by staff. We'll probably have an addendum and a RATA that would be coming out, a RATA that's going to be really addressing some section numbers that may have been in error or a typo. And then the addendum, because it's still going through a legal review right now of the policy draft recommendations that come out, and there have been brought to our attention a couple of errors that I have acknowledged publicly to various groups, and those will probably also be addressed in that addendum. But just to kind of give you a little bit of history, Code Next has been going on since 2013. We've gone through various directions of city council to listening to the community, looking at the character of our neighborhoods. With the change of council, we did something called prescription papers. And then we eventually got to the first draft that came out in January 2017, which we called Draft 1. And that draft, as it was presented, had more form-based elements to that ordinance, and it had something called transect zones. And so as we move forward with that, and we've had considerable public meetings, both by district and at large, on map and on text, we've had many, many meetings before, planning commissions, app, and council at different work sessions. The public, boards and commissions, we pretty much unanimously heard that no one really liked the transect approach, labeled it as a second code, that it only applied to certain parts of the city and not the entirety of the city. So for the most of 2017, we went back with our consultants on the zoning pieces and came forward with Draft 2. It removed the transect zones that went to a single spectrum of zones that theoretically could be applied citywide. It still had in there provisions that dealt with some of the design standards that you might find for McMansion or commercial design standards. Those are still very much part of that document. It actually addressed some of the concerns, I think, of the dual codes, but still had the original elements that we had in Draft 1 of going back. It is a code rewrite of the entire code and would still have a rezoning of the entire city of Austin. In Draft 3, the difference between Draft 2 and Draft 3, we still had more intensive zones that reflected residential areas. Right now in the ordinance, and you have a handout that I presented you, which is a little cheat sheet that might be helpful for you to look at, but we have our 1 zones, our 2 zones, our 3 zones, and our 4 zones. We took a look at comments that had been made by the public. We're always mindful of Imagine Austin because a lot of what Code Next, the reason why it's coming forward, it was designated as one of the eight priority programs that was set out in Imagine Austin. But we went back and looked at the R1, R2, and R3, and R4 zones and applied them in a manner that is probably more conservative. It's probably closer to what you might find in your current zoning as far as reflective of those residential districts. R1 is a district that allows pretty much a single unit on the property. R2 allows two units on a property, and R2 you might find similar to what you have as SF3 today. The Family Residence District allows duplexes and ADUs. R3 would be three units, and R4 would be four units. You see less of R3 and R4 in this current draft, but the units that have been provided, the capacity of what could be built, not a forecast, but what a capacity could be built, the total number of units has increased across the city. The number of affordable units has also increased. We've worked with our consultants in neighborhood housing, and there was an emphasis that was placed on the Imagine Austin corridors, also those centers, but mainly along the corridors, to allow for additional number of units to be constructed. And if affordable units are constructed, there are bonuses that are provided to a property owner to get a greater height or greater number of units, a greater bulk of building along these corridors in exchange for affordable housing. Another big change that we made in this ordinance was that if you had a commercial property today, basically a non-residential property that wasn't allowed any residential units, our current code is stratified in that manner, that we made them mixed use. They could either be something called a Main Street District or a mixed-use district that would allow residences. And if you had that situation, you could add the residential units to those properties, but it required you as building the residential units. You didn't need to seek a zoning change, but you had to have a set-aside for affordable units, or you must pay a fee in Lua. So that is very different than what we have today and what was in the previous drafts. So if you were building an apartment project, you had to do a set-aside. It still carried forward those elements of affordable units. The affordable unit would have a characteristic of 60% medium family income for rental. Today it's 80% under smart housing. This goes to 60. We carried over the 80 for ownership units, but the terms are much different under Code Next than they are today in smart housing. Smart housing today, it's five years for ownership and one year for rental. That would bump up to 40 years for rental and 99 years for ownership. So there's a big difference. We also dealt with accessory dwelling units. And accessory dwelling units are treated differently under this draft. There are provisions that reduce the parking requirement to zero for an accessory dwelling unit. We still maintain the one for regular residential unit. But they went to zero for an accessory dwelling unit. Today, if you're within a quarter mile of a transit zone, there's no parking requirement for an ADU today, but that's been carried forward. Parking in general is still relaxed, recognizing that our transportation demands that we have and how we get a move throughout the city are different. This code emphasizes not the automobile, but automobile plus bicycle plus pedestrian plus transit. So that's recognized in here. There are reductions for parking. If you're within a quarter mile or an eighth of a mile, it gets reduced 20% or 10% to different transit corridors. Going back to ADUs, the accessory dwelling units, this code where the previous code only allowed them behind, they could be behind, in front, attached. So that has changed drastically. There was an area that would be 80 feet from the front property line that we limit the height of buildings. That's been removed because we heard a lot of folks would like to build taller buildings at the rear property, two-story buildings, for instance, for an ADU. ADUs also, we heard loud and clear that they were difficult to determine what the square footage allowed would be. And so now you'll see in draft three, there are ranges that you can have an ADU of various sizes based on the size of your lawn. One thing I think that I know we heard from Preservation Austin, I'm not sure, I wasn't at the last meeting where code next came up, but I know that there was a desire to have some incentives to preserve the home in the front and to allow a homeowner to do certain things on their property. There's about a little over $400,000 to do that portion of the project alone. And that would simply be re-striping. There would be no overlay. There would be no ADA improvements. Nothing like that. It would simply be to re-strike the roadway. This allows you to gather more information about the improvements on Midway and Addison Road. You'll remember you approved a contract a few months ago with Garver to begin the engineering on Addison Road. So we can make spot improvements to that, but then also that starts to give us some more information about what are we going to need to do with that road in order to sell bonds. We are now in the process of finalizing the scope on Midway for Tignall and Perkins, and we will bring that to you for approval for them to get started on the design of Midway. By that time, then you have more information about these other roads, and then we could prepare a bond package for street improvements in general. And so that would give you more information at that point and buy you some time in order to do that. The upkeep for, if we went that route, if you instructed us to do that, what we would have to do is we would have to increase our budget for the upkeep of Beltline. If you have driven on Beltline recently, you've probably noticed there were a lot of potholes on Beltline. There is a lot of edge rattling that was happening on Beltline. That is because Beltline is a concrete street with an asphalt cap. And so with the winter that we just had, we have a lot of freeze and thaw, and that asphalt is beginning to pop up. That overlay is ten years old now. That is, it has reached the end of its life. And so in order to keep that roadway in any type of condition, we're going to need to do a crack sealing program this next year, fiscal year 15. We estimate that to be about $85,000. Spot repairs, about $40,000, just to be able to hold that road. That is fiscal year 15. The upkeep in 16, we'd have to continue a crack seal program. We wouldn't, we may not have to do the, we wouldn't have to do a full $85,000, probably $60,000 because as that roadway ages and that overlay becomes more and more brittle, more and more cracks are going to show up. And so we'll need to continue that crack seal program.

And, two, you know, even at other events, the Palmer still sometimes charges, and it's up to, like, $8 a car. So for people who want to walk a little more, if that's not a lot we're utilizing on the weekend, that seems like a real reasonable suggestion. So I'm going to – I would have to really think about it if we are charging over the weekend, whether that's – at least it should be – it would be my hope that our transportation department could monitor what kinds of events are going on. And when it's an event, a ticketed event at the Long Center, that is a different animal for me than, you know, a free event where we're trying to provide resources for Austin families. So when DSD split apart from Planning and Zoning, we still maintain the support for Planning and Zoning, human resources, finance, technology, et cetera. We have pegged that total support at three FTEs, and so for fiscal year 16-17, we would transfer over three FTEs to Planning and Zoning, and they would transfer over to us the Neighborhood Assistance Center, thereby relieving Planning and Zoning with having to come up for the additional funding for those three FTEs, or for those full three FTEs. The benefit, of course, is that the cost of the Neighborhood Assistance Center then gets rolled into our fee schedule because the work that they do is a direct result of the work that we do. And we feel that the relationship can be strengthened between the Neighborhood Assistance Center and our plan review and inspection staff to ultimately help our residents out. But that's it in a nutshell is that we actually want to make that transfer this year. And so next year, of course, we'd have to request, in 17-18, we'd have to request those positions to make us whole, if you will, in particular the two Neighborhood Assistance Center positions. So it's not in, you're going to give me more detail, but it's not in this budget, those two positions? It is, it is. We want to make the transfer now. Right. And we want to make up for it, of course, in the 17-18 proposed budget. Okay. And the support services that are being undertaken by Planning and Zoning include what kinds of things? So the three positions that would come from DSD, we would look at HR services, IT support, assisting with Amanda, public information records management, the customer assistance requests that we receive, handling those items that may come on the council agenda. I have one person that processes just for zoning and also takes care of the boards and commissions. But those other items that you might see, I actually go to Rodney's department to launch RCAs for code amendments. And so that might be coming for the assistance of that person back to my department. No, so this would eliminate any type of cross-funding scenario. So the two positions would go this year, the three positions would go to Greg this year, complete with the funding. The Neighborhood Assistance Center would come our way, and we would take on that funding ourselves, and we would have a clear distinction with regard to funding. There would not be any swap of funding. There would not be positions in Greg's shop that we financially support, and there would not be positions in our shop that Greg financially supports. So I understood that you said that the Neighborhood Assistance Center would then be coming out of fees. Would the three positions that are now going to be in Planning and Zoning be covered by fees or by the general fund? They would be covered by a general fund in my department. Okay, so that's an additional three positions in Planning and Zoning? Well, it might be a net of one, because if two are going to Rodney and three are coming to me, then there would be only one additional position within my department. Because Greg is already covering the cost for two. Okay. And so it would be a third one that he would have, that net of one that he'd have to cover the cost for. And currently the Neighborhood Assistance Center doesn't charge fees. Okay. So the benefit is that the Neighborhood Assistance Center is going to be able to charge fees through that. But I'm still trying to wrap my head around, and maybe this is in the detail and I can wait. But those three that are now coming out of the general fund, they were already being paid by the general fund within development services? Or were they being paid by fees within development services? So those three that are coming from the general fund, the vacant positions that we're using, because we're transferring vacant positions, two of them are vacant because they're the second team of the expedited building plan review position or program. And so we don't need to hire those positions. And so we can transfer those and make up for it in 17-18. The third position is an accounting position that recently became vacant. And so we're transferring that PC and that position over to Grim's shop as well. But in practice they were doing work for planning and zoning, but they were within development services. I'm trying to understand if this is additional. That's correct. These are additional positions that we are thereby authorizing within planning and zoning to do additional work, or is this just a transfer of where they're located? So right now the development service department provides planning and zoning department services that relate to public information for accounting, for records management, for IT services. I did want to just speak briefly about the relationship between land use and transit. So just transit-oriented design at a high level needs to be walkable and connected, dense and have diverse uses, and then be context-sensitive. So really looking at the placemaking and designing it to fit the scale of the area. We know that people within a five-mile radius are five times more likely to walk to a major transit stop than anyone else. So what does a successful TOD result in? Reduce greenhouse emissions, increase land property value, creates jobs, decreases infrastructure costs, enhances public health because of the walking component to it and the biking, changes travel patterns, and reduces household expenses because you don't have the cost of vehicle maintenance and fuel. But making a successful TOD can be a challenge. It requires development density, great street design, destination accessibility. It has to connect you to other places as well. That distance to transit, again, that half-mile radius, and then parking management. An example of this is a case study that was done in 2020 by the University Transportation Center, funded by USDOT, that looked at the Mockingbird TRD. Now, this is the development that was done on private property many years ago. Although it's a great project, highly utilized, it still has 79% of trips that are made by vehicle, not by rail. And only 55% of the parking there is utilized. So although a great development, it hasn't translated into increased ridership or a change in travel patterns.

And Caitlin has been working on that. My hope is that the board, at the board level, we can help expedite some of these processes, as well as working with the city, because ultimately, you know, it's the city that has the legal right to entitle land and what we end up doing with it. And then I'll give some comments afterwards. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Kennedy. As Mr. Kennedy said, my name is Caitlin Holland, Vice President of Real Estate and Economic Development. So in my role, I lead our real estate, economic development, railroad management, and environmental compliance sections for DART. Just give us one second for the slide deck to show up on our screen. Thank you. All right. Now that you can see what I'm talking about, UNT has been performing studies for DART for the last 25 years. So UNT has been studying the quarter-mile radius around our light rail stations, excluding CBD, because there's too much density there for meaningful results. But this study has revealed that over those 25 years, the DART light rail stations have resulted in an $18.1 billion economic impact to the area. This latest iteration that looked at 2022 to 2024 showed that there were 37 transit-oriented development projects, so within that quarter-mile radius of a station, that resulted in a $1.2 billion direct economic impact and a nearly $2 billion total economic impact. That translates to almost 10,000 new jobs, $724.2 million in wages, $51.5 million in state and local funds, and almost $200 million in total tax revenue. This particular study also looked at what developers could expect from rentals for these transit-oriented developments that resulted in a 10% rent premium for residential and 12.6% for commercial properties of rent premiums for those transit-oriented development projects. This shows our current transit-oriented development projects on DART-owned property. So, of course, there's been a lot of transit-oriented development that has occurred over the years on third-party-owned property that is reflected in those UNT numbers. But now we've embarked on a new era where we are really focused on trying to transform our empty parking lots into thriving development to support our system. Right now we have three projects under construction, and I'll get into more details on those three, but at Buckner Station, which you should all be familiar with, SMU Mockingbird as well, and then Trinity Mills. We have one project that's in pre-development at Addison, and one in the RFP process at Arapahoe in Richardson, and then we're looking at a future RFP at Westmoreland in southern Dallas. So, getting into Trinity Mills Station, which has been recognized by D Magazine as a finalist for the 2026 Commercial Projects of the Year, you'll notice a theme. I have this designated on all of our active projects under construction, and as well as Addison, all four of our projects have been recognized by D Magazine as finalists for the Commercial Real Estate Award. Trinity Mills is a 26-acre total TOD site. It's a project that we are performing in partnership with the City of Carrollton. City of Carrollton has some property involved in this as well as DART, so it's a joint effort. You'll see the apartment complexes that have already been constructed. We just had the ribbon cutting on that recently. 436 residential units and 10,000 square feet of retail space on the ground floor. The yellow highlighted is the portion of the site that will be developed. Working in partnership with the shared outcome of a robust arts and cultural scene, he proved to be a tremendous asset and collaborator in the discussion on how to best support local arts and cultural organizations and individual artists. We will continue to work with Paul to broaden our travel industry partners as Austin continues to enrich its cultural tourism and visibility of arts and culture. Secondly, we'd like to honor and recognize Ms. Gloria Pennington. Ms. Pennington served on the Austin Arts Commission for 10 years and served as chair for many of those years. We are forever grateful for her dedicated service to the citizens of Austin, and in particular, the arts community. She is an avid supporter of the many diverse forms of arts and culture, and often serves as master of ceremonies at many of the public art dedications in her role as department historian with the Parks and Recreation Department. She's been a fierce champion of all the arts, but particularly those of the Latino culture. In addition to her tireless work stateside, she's been an invaluable leader and liaison with our sister city, Saltillo, in the state of Coahuila, Mexico, bringing annual international artist exchanges between Austin and Saltillo. She currently serves as vice president for Austin Friends of Folk Art and continues to be a friend and advocate for arts, culture, and creativity in Austin. We thank you, Gloria Pennington.

Arts and Humanities Month is a coast-to-coast collective recognition of the importance of culture in America, and is designed to encourage all Americans to explore new facets of the arts and humanities in their lives, and to begin a lifelong habit of active participation in arts and humanities. So if you allow me this time, I'd like to read off those six individual, uh, individuals or organizations that we are honoring this year. First is Paul Boudreau. He is the general manager of Holiday Inn at Lady Bird Lake and served as the first hotelier representative to the Austin Arts Commission's Guidelines Working Group. Working in partnership with the shared outcome of a robust arts and cultural scene, he proved to be a tremendous asset and collaborator in the discussion on how to best support local arts and cultural organizations and individual artists. We will continue to work with Paul to broaden our travel industry partners as Austin continues to enrich its cultural tourism and visibility of arts and culture. Secondly, we'd like to honor and recognize Ms. Gloria Pennington. Ms. Pennington served on the Austin Arts Commission for 10 years and served as chair for many of those years. We are forever grateful for her dedicated service to the citizens of Austin, and in particular, the arts community. She is an avid supporter of the many diverse forms of arts and culture, and often serves as master of ceremonies at many of the public art dedications in her role as department historian with the Parks and Recreation Department. She's been a fierce champion of all the arts, but particularly those of the Latino culture. In addition to her tireless work stateside, she's been an invaluable leader and liaison with our sister city, Saltillo, in the state of Coahuila, Mexico, bringing annual international artist exchanges between Austin and Saltillo. She currently serves as vice president for Austin Friends of Folk Art and continues to be a friend and advocate for arts, culture, and creativity in Austin. We thank you, Gloria Pennington. Thirdly, we'd like to recognize Joe Leyva. Joe Leyva of the City of Austin Building Services has provided invaluable input into the success of the Cultural Arts Division's People's Gallery Exhibition since its inception in 2005, which is located here at City Hall. He designed the permanent hanging systems that are used to install artwork along the limestone walls and which are often sought out by others as examples to emulate. During the past seven years, he has repeatedly contributed creative solutions for hanging all sorts of unique artworks within the very particular constraints of City Hall. We cannot thank Joe enough for his partnership, and though he has been promoted to a different department, we hope that he will be able to continue his participation with People's Gallery. Fourthly, we'd like to recognize Jared Neese and Claudette Godfrey. They are both with South by Southwest Film, and they donated their time and effort to partner with the City of Austin to include Faces of Austin's short film program's 2012 premiere into South by Southwest's community screening programs. The partnership will continue for 2013 premiere in March. This generous donation helps promote Austin film and filmmakers to the Austin community and beyond. Lynn Osgood. She has served with various panels, boards, and work groups, including the Art in Public Places panel, the Waller Creek Citizens Advisory Committee, the Create Austin Task Force, and most recently was appointed to the Austin Parks and Recreation Board. Her thoughtful and insightful comments as a member of the Art in Public Places panel consistently reflected her desire to see high-quality artwork that provided a meaningful contribution to both the city at large and citizens individually. It's our pleasure to have been able to work so closely with her to shape the future of Austin's public art collection, and we look forward to tapping into her extensive body of knowledge in the future. And lastly, we'd like to thank the African-American Resource Advisory Commission. This commission volunteered their time and expertise to broaden community participation in the development of artwork for the new African-American Cultural and Heritage Facility. Through their guidance and leadership, artist Reginald Adams was able to connect with a large constituency of the African-American population in East Austin, where the new facility is located, and throughout the city. Participants in the project were able to engage with the artwork in a variety of ways, including the development of the mural design, the collection of portraits of significant community leaders, and the actual making of the mural. The mural will be installed later this year, and will be welcome additions to the Art in Public Places collection. So we thank all of our organizations and individual artists for their time and talent and contribution to the arts community. Thank you. Thank you. It's very exciting, and we will be recognizing them at a luncheon on this Friday. Thank you. We'll move on to item number F, new business.

This site was developed in the 1960s with two buildings on the site, one with 58 units and the other building with 20 units. The 20-unit building burned in 2011. This request is to allow the reconstruction of the 20-unit building, as well as the current zoning, because the current zoning will not allow the rebuilding, as well as rezoning the entire lot. And we've provided a photo of the site of the former 20-unit structure, which is proposed to be the site of the rebuilt 20-unit structure. I've provided a chart with some deficiencies from the current zoning ordinance. Currently, the most dense zoning for multifamily is MF 22, which is 22 dwelling units per acre. And as noted in this chart, the proposed use for Tanglewood apartments would be a maximum of 42 dwelling units per acre, as well as a couple other items I'd like to note. The parking, which is provided, is 87 spaces, and the zoning ordinance requires 149 spaces. Also of note is the unit size for a one-bedroom apartment. The zoning ordinance requires a minimum of 750 square feet for a one-bedroom apartment unit. And the applicant is proposing 394 square feet for the existing and proposed apartment building. In their request, the applicant is proposing to add a dumpster enclosure, as well as cover 14 existing parking spaces. They are proposing a seven-foot masonry wall along the properties adjacent to the residential properties to the west, as well as the reconstructed 20-unit building will be proposed 100 percent masonry, and the existing building is 80 percent masonry. Some items to consider, in this case, is that the development is not in compliance with the city's comprehensive plan and that the density is higher than it is allowed per zoning ordinance. The design standards of the current zoning ordinance for multifamily development are not met, and parking is not provided adequate for the development. The building was, however, previously existing prior to the fire in 2011. I do have one letter of opposition from AISD that should be noted. The owners of the property are George and Danita Terzian, and they are represented by Hugo Monsanto. And staff is available for any questions. Thank you. Do we have any questions from the commission?
