They could not be here tonight, so they asked me to speak in their behalf. You know that we are here because an application to rebuild the 20-unit structure was given back to us with a mandate that rezoning would be necessary before the building permit would be considered. This isn't the venue to make an issue of that. We're here tonight in a very strenuous effort to try to rezone the property. You know this arises out of a tragic fire. You know that this owner is passionate about rebuilding, recommitting to Arlington. Since the time of the fire, they've invested $75,000 in upgrades. They've installed better security cameras. They have a 97.5% rating by the code compliance people. Mission Arlington was of great assistance to them in dealing with the trauma and tragedy of the fires. They've been helping people with furniture to get through a very difficult time. They've delivered turkeys. They send out a couple to do the Bible study on Sundays. The owner works closely with the crime prevention folks here in Arlington, officers Taylor, Morgan, and others to reduce the demand on police services to come out to the location and help them deal with difficult situations. We know that this is not a referendum on whether George and Anita Terzian are nice people or not nice people. They're passionate in their religious beliefs that rebuilding this 20-unit center meets a need in this community and helps folks 85% or so of the people who were there in the remaining structure are elderly on AFDC or otherwise on fixed incomes. And this person wants to rebuild to meet this need by having more people have the opportunity to live in what's become a very good environment. This is a strange piece of property. The highest and best use for it might be to be acquired by General Motors. It's more or less the bottom 16th or so of their factory plant location. I've contacted GM to see if they had any opinions about being here. The person I visited with in Detroit said they had no opinion to support or oppose our attempt for rezoning. It's a strange shaped piece of property. It's an L-shaped. I question what type of use could one put on it by itself for an existing IEM classification. I also think it serves as a buffer between the GM area and the residential area park view immediately to its west and to any commercial development along Abrams Street. So I think it does provide a benefit as a buffer. I also want to say that the goal is to simply build back as it was on the same foundation to not make greater a nonconforming use. We think that PD classification does not create precedent for other classifications. As to the apartment size, we know virtually all of these persons are single, elderly folks by themselves. For their purposes, for what is the tenant population in this group, we believe that a smaller size apartment would be appropriate for the persons who were there. Most people live by themselves. It's not a question of a room for Johnny or a room for their other children. We also would note that the parking currently takes up 30 cars. We did a survey. There are 87 parking places there. So 30 are being used to serve the existing 56, 57 units which are occupied. So if we added 20 more units, you're more than one for one on parking for those additional 20 units. If we simply extrapolated, you'd be up to 50, 55, with 30 or so still remaining. This is a unique property, a unique circumstance. We ask that you consider those factors, its location, a good value add for the community that its owners provide. And we ask that you to act favorably on this PD application. Thank you, Mr. Miller. Transcript:
And this would only really apply to downtown. And the first two tiers would be by right. And then with the density bonus program, there is also the requirement of four projects to contribute to a downtown beautification fund if they want to get this density bonus. And this contribution to this downtown beautification fund is going to be this fee that's determined by city council. There's going to be another program that's established by city council. I think it's coming to you all on April 21st. And then the administrator is going to make a determination that some projects, if they're doing some kind of public art improvements, they could get up to 50% credit. I think the city is currently kind of working on determining what the fee structure needs to be. And I think Jinsi can answer any questions on that as well. So in addition to the base sub-district standards, in 13.2, you have supplemental standards for height. So you can kind of see what the height standards are in the different sub-districts. We also ended up adding some special street standards. Okay, we're going to move on down to 3.3 on the form-based code. Good afternoon, everyone. For the record, Tarani Devi Palma, principal planner with the Planning and Development Services. Today, Jay Narayana from the consultant team and I will be providing an update on where we are in the process and also highlight some of the discussions that we had with the Municipal Policy Committee last meeting. After almost 18 months, we are almost at the finish line. On March 4th, 2026, the Planning and Zoning Commission unanimously recommended approval of the Unified Development Code Amendment and also the Zoning Map Amendment for the adoption of form-based zoning. At the meeting, we received eight speaker cards in support and four in opposition. Most of the concerns were related to the eminent domain and people wanted to know if the city is taking the property away from them. But we did clarify those questions. We let them know the difference between what the form-based code zoning is and the eminent domain. Form-based code zoning is simply a set of regulations that apply when a property is to be developed or redeveloped. And the adoption of this code does not grant the city authority to take the private property. So we did clarify those at the meeting itself. And after clarification, most of the speakers who came in opposition, they said they were not concerned about it. And these are some of the other frequently asked questions that we have been hearing throughout the process. So we wanted to bring it all to our attention. Will my property be taken through the eminent domain because of the form-based code? No, the adoption of the form-based code does not authorize the city to take private property. Form-based code regulates how a property may be developed in the future. It's just a set of development regulations that will be adopted in the unified development code. It does not involve taking ownership of any private property. Will my short-term rental be affected by the form-based code? This is something we have been hearing too. No. If you are currently having a valid short-term rental permit issued by the city, you may continue operating under the permit. And also if you live within the short-term rental zone, you can continue to apply for the permit and receive them. What is the impact on properties and businesses? Form-based code only applies when a property owner chooses to make significant changes to a building, use, or site, or develop a vacant property. We also send notifications, this is according to the state law, to 965 owners, property owners within the boundary, and also the 200-foot buffer, and to the 63 properties with a total of 168 notifications to both the owners and the tenants, and also 12 PDs property owners within the form-based code boundary that currently have PDs within their location. Out of those notices, we received 17 in support and 9 in opposition, and the opposition was mainly the short-term rental concerns or the eminent domain, and we clarified those. Of the 12 PDs that are existing in the area, 4 have not been built. We did receive consent from 2 property owners to change their PDs to a form-based code zoning so far. Those are indicated in the map here, this property right here, and this property right here. The staff has reached out to the other two properties, and we are waiting to hear back from them. And I'll hand it over to Jay to go through the rest of the presentation. Thank you, Dharani. Jay Narayana with Livable Plants and Codes. Again, I just want to hit the highlights. This will be the new Chapter 13 in the Article 13 in the UDC that will lay out the overall framework for future form-based code. Article 13.1 provides all the general standards, and then Article 13.2 will be the downtown district, and then 13.3 will be the future districts as the city may implement future form-based districts in other areas. It also kind of gives you the toolkit for what's required in the regulating plan, what's mandatory, and what are optional elements as the city kind of identifies future locations for the form-based districts. And then you have four form-based sub-districts that are established. It's kind of like your zoning districts, but they're already kind of pre-established that can be taken and applied in different locations to create the regulating plans. The traditional neighborhood and then the urban neighborhood that's a little more intense. And then you have the corridor mixed use to address some of the corridor frontages along arterial roadways. And then you have the core, which is the most intense mixed use neighborhood. And then you have building design standards, some standards that apply to all building types. And then you have residential building types. And then you have standards that apply specifically to residential building types. We know that it's more than just density and lot size. You want to address garage placement, architectural elements, roof types, dwelling unit entries, porches, etc. So you want to make sure that you're addressing compatibility in the neighborhood. Accessory dwelling units is another important element that we know makes it a compatible issue in the neighborhood. We want to make sure that is adequately addressed in the design standards. Cottage code. We want to make sure that we write standards that make sense within this district, that we don't write a set of standards that can't be used, that cannot be applied. So make it easy to implement this. One-story commercial building standards, we know that they are going to be different than your multiple-story buildings. You have articulation. We have tried to simplify it and make sure there's enough flexibility for architects to bring their creativity. But there are also functional urban design standards that are applied. Parking garage standards are also important because we know that at the end of the day, there will be a lot of multi-story parking garages. And we know at some point you also have to address some drive-through standards because there are going to be some of these parking needs and also the drive-throughs and gas stations and canopies that you'll have to address because we know that some of the arterial roadways will still have these gas stations. There are some cities that have actually done this well. We know in some cities like Fort Worth that have seen quick trips that have actually been able to implement this to some success. So we want to kind of take some of those examples and actually apply them here as well. Street and sidewalks, again, this is really about relating the public realm street and streetscape standards to the private development and really bringing those two together. And so that's the important element of the form-based code that's really critical to the success of development and redevelopment. Especially on existing streets, as redevelopment happens, we want to make sure that there's some consistency for sidewalks and streetscapes to be implemented. But we know that not all redevelopment will really make sense in terms of sidewalks to be implemented. Maybe there's some exceptions, especially if the lot is less than 50 feet in width. So there are some waivers that may make sense, but that's really an administrative function. So we are allowing some flexibility for the administrator to make those kind of decisions as well. Parking is another element that was a different approach that we took that we did recommend a blended ratio. Especially in a mixed use area, we want to make sure that as uses change over time that you don't burden the building and the development with additional parking requirements. So you have the same parking requirement regardless of the use. So all non-residential uses will essentially have the same parking ratio. And so that way, as uses change over time, you really kind of facilitate that highest and best use moving forward. And we actually reducing the parking requirement for all users. So it's a special resolution that says you, as city council, acknowledge that we have more than twice the state average per capita. Several of the properties also fall into the one-mile, three-year rule, which essentially says that within one linear mile, there is another tax credit property that serves a similar population that was developed or is proposed to be developed within three years. So three of the properties fall into that designation. And then there is also a designation for concerted revitalization area. And that is a special designation that gets additional points if you fall within what is called a concerted revitalization area or is governed by a concerted revitalization plan. TDHCA or the staff at TDHCA will determine the merits of whether or not that plan actually meets their criteria for being a concerted revitalization area. Again, with it being a straight zoning designation, all of the uses that are permitted in the light industrial district would be available to any tenant wanting to occupy the space. In addition, the light industrial district does allow for an additional outdoor storage area that is higher than what's allowed under general commercial. That's what you do when you do industrial projects. The only outside storage is behind the south end of the buildings. It is fenced. It is rocked. It is screened. And it only represents 2.25% of the site. There's no more room to put any more outside storage. So that's not what we're asking for here. What we're here to do is ask for basically the uses that were taken away when the UDC was created. Nobody called us and said, which zoning would you like to go to, Jim? Would you like to go to LI? Or would you like to go to GC? They just stuck us down at GC. Those uses that are in GC and BJ Paul, who's our leasing agent, she's going to address those uses because we've had a hard time backfilling when some of the older tenants that have been there. We have some tenants that have been there 20 years, 20 years, and they have some automotive repair. We've had upholstery in there. We've had a T-shirt shop in there. We've got some different uses. We can't put a warehouse use in. Hello, folks. It's a warehouse building. So we're here to clean the zoning up, to get back the uses that we need to have to operate small businesses over there. Transcript:

This is a public hearing, so first staff will present its report, and then I will open the public hearing, and then we will hear from any speakers on the case, including the applicant. Speakers in support will go first, followed by speakers in opposition. If the applicant wishes, he or she will have the final opportunity to rebut or address any concerns raised by the Commissioner or its members of the public. The public hearing will be then closed, and the Commissioner will consider a motion on the request. At this time, I'll call on staff to present its report on zoning case PD 20-16. Mrs. Acosta, is that correct? Yes. Okay. Thank you very much. Please proceed. Good evening, Commissioners. For the record, Nylea Acosta, Senior Planner, Planning and Development Services. This is item PD 20-16. The subject site is approximately 3.65 acres. The site is addressed as 200 East Abrams Street and 325 South Mesquite Street, and the applicant is requesting to change the zoning from DB downtown business to a plan development for a mixed development in downtown business. Here is the location map. The subject property is outlined in yellow, and to the north, south, east, and west, you can see that the surrounding area is also DB. And then to the northwest, there is also another PD DB site for 101 center. Here are the site photos, starting with the top left and going counterclockwise. We have a view of commercial property to the north, view of commercial property to the east, view of commercial property to the south, and the subject property. The subject property is developed as a mixed-use apartment complex known as Park Place. Building 1 is the southern building addressed off of Mesquite Street, and building 2 is the northern building addressed off of East Abram. Both buildings are five stories with a central parking garage with a total of 308 units. The entire building has a gross floor area of 389,956 square feet. The UDC requires at least 15% of the gross floor area to be occupied by non-residential uses in the downtown business district. The gross floor area in Park Place currently has 16.88% dedicated to non-residential use. Half of that space is designated for 45 live-work units, which is considered a non-residential use. So on the site plan shown here, everything in orange is on the first level of the buildings, and those are the commercial buildings, or commercial units, excuse me. Here in the yellow, we have the current live-work units to become residential, and the units in orange will remain commercial. The intent of this application is to reduce the 15% non-residential gross floor area requirement and phase it back in by August 1st of 2030. Here is their compliance plan. This is a five-year plan starting August 1st, 2025, with 15 units until they reach the full 45 units August 1st, 2030. Each of the live-work units must either be leased to a resident engaged in a commercial activity with each live-work unit satisfying all of the requirements of the UDC and having been issued a valid certificate of occupancy for commercial use allowed pursuant to the ordinance. If not currently leased as live-work unit, the same space being held vacant and available for lease as live-work units will apply. And also, just to point out that there are financial implications to doing the compliance plan. If the live-work units were to remain vacant, there is no earned income. However, with this plan, it is allowing the applicant to lease out these live-work units for residential use, which should help generate income, as opposed to the current conditions of all of the commercial and live-work space being unoccupied. For the comp plan analysis, the area is described as downtown university neighborhood, high-intensity. In order to maximize the area's potential, a mix of residential uses and mixed-use buildings are encouraged. There should be retail, educational, office, government, cultural, and entertainment venues to serve those living in and around the area. The park-place development is supportive of mixed-use development that is attractive to students and young professionals and builds the density necessary to support a vibrant urban core. Staff considerations are as followed. This is a planned development with a development plan, which is the compliance plan. It is consistent with the existing development pattern and uses in the surrounding area. If the commission is inclined to approve the request, the following stipulations should be considered. One, require annual monitoring of progress toward compliance with the proposed phasing plan until 15% of the gross floor area is achieved. And two, the following DB uses should be excluded from the site. This would match the permitted uses of 101 Center, the mixed-use development on the north side of West Abram Street. So, the excluded uses would be as follows. Hospital, public park or playground, electric utility substations, accessory garage apartment, heliport, airport, or landing field, temporary carnival, circus or amusement ride, gasoline sales, full-service hotel, motel, and alternative financial institutions. The applicant is Park 7 Group, represented by Christopher Christman, and the owner is CD Park 7, Arlington owner LP. This concludes my presentation. I am available for questions. Should you have any? Thank you, Mrs. Acosta. I believe we have a question from Commissioner Atkins. Thank you for that presentation. Just to basically summarize this, this move is initiated by the applicant, correct, the property owner, to adjust to current market trends. Is that essentially why this is being done? That is correct, yes. Okay. And in order to do so, they're going ahead and the city's suggesting match to what has already been done at 101 Center since they've already faced this same problem with the current retail work-live place, correct? Yes, that's correct. We're mirroring the same method of the compliance plan that 101 Center used. Okay, and then if these spaces that they're converting to, and they will be solely residential, if they're not converted back to retail, is there a penalty for any of that? So they would be out of compliance as far as a penalty. I'm not really too sure as far as enforcement what we could do to punish them, so to speak. So they went forward with the current, you know, at that time, they went forward with the current guidelines put in place where they didn't have to come before P&Z, and they hit all the certain benchmarks. Now they're coming back before us to knock out retail and just go strictly residential on some of these places to be underneath that 15% requirement, correct? Yes, so although the current units are not leased out, there are no live-work units or retail spaces occupied. They are in compliance technically because they are at the 16.88%, so really what the compliance plan is doing is helping them to generate income and then transition those live-work units to residential and then back to commercial. And then if they fail to do so, really what's the checks and balances in place? So this doesn't encourage future developers to propose plans and then come back a year later or before opening day and make changes to their proposed plans. So really they would be inclined to do something one way or another, so right now they're in compliance, although they're not generating income because those spaces aren't leased out. So that's why they're approaching us to transition those live-work units to residential, and so the checks and balances of that would be in stipulation number one of the staff consideration to have a monitoring process where they are providing us with a report after each year saying, hey, these are where the numbers are at at this point. If they were not to be in compliance, then they would be violating the PD, and so they would have to come back in front of you guys and counsel again, and so I don't think they would want to put themselves in the position where they have to confront you and counsel again, so it would kind of behoove them to stick to the compliance plan. Okay. Okay. And like what we addressed during work session with LAPS in 2030. Commissioner Atkins, this is Galen Gatton. Just to follow up on Ms. Acosta's comment, yes, but also keep in mind that if they are in violation of the UDC and specifically this code, then they could be subject to daily fines of up to $2,000 for violating the planning code, so that might be one way to get them to get the report pretty quickly to us and to get into compliance, but certainly worst case scenario, of course, would be to pull the CO on the entire building and say that it was out of compliance, but hopefully we'd never come to that because we could get compliance other ways. Okay. And then how does this compare to the retail that was converted to residential on the Midtown student housing at Davis and Abram? Is there any relation to that, how they converted their retail to residential? Are you referring to the 101 Center, I believe? I think you are. No. The Midtown at Davis and Abram? Well, if you recall, that was Moji's project, and in that case it was just true commercial property, so you didn't have the live-work element that you have here. Okay. So I think that's the big distinction there. Okay. All right. Perfect. Thank you. Okay. Commissioner Reber. Yes. Mr. Costa,

Case number PR 2024-064274 is a Historic Landmark Commission-initiated and Owner-Opposed request for historic zoning. This is the East End Saloon and Eisenweissers, as well as the 1500 Club, Beauty, and Barbershop at 1500 East 12th Street. The staff recommendation is to recommend historic zoning to Planning Commission and City Council. Otherwise, require a City of Austin documentation package before releasing the demolition permit. Staff has found that this item is qualified for historic zoning under the categories of architecture, community value, and historic associations. The 2016 East Austin Historic Resource Survey lists the property as eligible for local landmark listing based on those criteria, as well as individual listing on the National Register of Historic Places for its significance in the area of land development and community planning. The building is a vernacular commercial building, a typology rapidly disappearing in Austin. It was recommended as a preservation priority requiring stabilization in a 2019 letter from the Organization of Central East Austin Neighborhoods. Originally constructed as a two-story store building, occupants constructed one-story rear additions in and outside of the period of significance. It has a hipped roof with a central hip dormer at the 12th Street elevation, one-over-one wooden vinyl windows, and horizontal wood siding covered with vinyl siding that has been partially removed without permits. A shallow frame awning shelters the two entry stoves to 12th Street, while the two Camel Street entrances remain uncovered. The building's second-floor porch was originally open, but enclosed during the historic period. The 2016 East Austin Historic Resource Survey identifies this property as significant for its association with Ernest Eisenweiser and his family, a prominent Austin grocer and saloon operator. The building is also associated with the Alpha Phi Alpha Fraternity, the 1500 Club, and the 1500 Beauty and Barbershop, as well as Christian J. Wilhelm, grocer and politician. It was originally addressed as 1400 East 12th Street, and is estimated to have been built around 1910, per the survey. However, the building's earliest occupant, Grocer Christian J. Wilhelm, is associated with the address as far back as 1889. Wilhelm was a native of Burnett, who lived above his shop and sold groceries and beer. He also bartended briefly on Congress Avenue. Wilhelm was active in politics and ran for several civic roles, including Travis County Commissioner. In 1910, he and his family moved to Houston and sold the property to Dessau merchants Ernest and Louisa Eisenweiser. The Eisenweiser store sold produce and dry goods and had an attached saloon and restaurant. The family lived above the store and occasionally rented out living space for tenants. During Prohibition, the saloon was closed by city ordinance, though it later reopened, and by 1934, it was a popular spot for German food, music, and beer, boasting novelties like a marble beer vault and a resident accordion band. The family stopped selling groceries to focus on the restaurant and made improvements to the building, including the enclosure of the open second-floor porch. In 2004's Austin, Texas, then and now, author Jeffrey Kerr recounts Eisenweiser's history. He worked with Emil Bowles in a Pflugerville meat market before opening his first cafe in Dessau in 1907. Although the streetcar tracks out front are long gone, the name Eisenweiser remains stamped on the concrete steps along the building's front. Good thing I can talk fast. My name is Rosie Truelove. I'm with the Contract and Land Management Department, and we're here this morning to present the finalist for the Airport Boulevard Form-Based Code Initiative. I'm going to ask George Adams with the Planning and Development Review Department to come up and speak more about the scope of the project. Good morning, Mayor and Council. I'm George Adams with the Planning and Development Review Department. I'm here this morning to provide a brief overview of form-based codes and the Airport Boulevard Form-Based Code Initiative. In the most basic terms, a form-based code is a set of development regulations that's aimed at achieving a specific urban form or pattern of development. Form-based codes are typically focused on the relationship and interaction between the buildings and other improvements on private property and the public improvements within the right-of-way, such as sidewalks, streets, and related infrastructure. One principal goal of a form-based code is to create high-quality public space that provides both community benefits and higher values for property owners and developers. Form-based codes are being implemented across the country, partly because they tend to produce a more predictable pattern of development. They're frequently focused on a specific district or corridor, but several cities, including Denver and Miami, have recently implemented form-based codes citywide. A little bit on the project itself. This initiative addresses an approximately two-and-a-half-mile segment of Airport Boulevard. It runs from the intersection with North Lamar Boulevard in the north to I-35 in the south. The corridor links three significant activity areas. There's the Capital Metro Crestview Station at the northern end and the associated Midtown Commons development. There's Highland Mall, the new ACC campus, and Travis County offices near the midpoint of the corridor. And Miller anchors the southern end of the corridor. The Capital Metro Metro Rail Line parallels much of Airport Boulevard throughout this segment. And the Brentwood, Highland, and North Loop neighborhoods are adjacent to the corridor. I'd also like to mention that as part of an earlier resolution, the Council established an advisory group that will help guide this process throughout. The work program, or scope of work for the project, is divided into two phases. There's an initial phase that includes evaluation and analysis of existing conditions, and a second phase that includes the definition of a vision and a conceptual master plan for the corridor. This will provide a framework for the creation of the form-based code itself. Both of these will involve an iterative public review process, and then toward the end, we'll have the board and commission review process and council review and adoption. The major products are deliverable of this project include the vision or conceptual master plan and the form-based code that will implement that vision. And also, recommendations for a strategic set of infrastructure investments within the corridor that could encourage and support redevelopment. That concludes my presentation, and I'm going to turn it back over to Ms. Trulow. So, this RFQ has gone through a four-phase process. The first is the request for qualifications process and scoring, which has been completed, and then panel interviews and presentations with the staff evaluation panel, which has also been completed. This third phase is what we're here today for, which is the finalist presentations to council, and then we have council awards scheduled for October 14th. The timelines associated with this, we issued the solicitation back in June of this year, and did interviews with the shortlisted firms in August. And, again, today is the finalist presentations, and council award is scheduled for the 14th. The top three ranked firms have been invited to present to council today to cover, at a minimum, the team's organization, their work plan, their approach to public involvement, and any similar form-based code experience. I do want to note that finalist presentations to council are not scored by staff as part of the evaluation process. The staff recommendation that will be presented on the October 14th agenda is going to be based on the evaluation panel scoring of Phases 1 and 2 only. Our random order of presentation today is as follows. Gateway Planning Group is going to be the first team up. Then we're going to have Design Workshop, and then Austin Collaborative Design Studio doing business as McCann Adams Studio. Each firm is going to have 15 minutes for their presentation with a question-and-answer session with council following. If not, we'll let Gateway set up and we'll start that process. Thank you. Mayor, it's going to take us just about two minutes to move our materials over here. Thank you. There he is. Great. Okay. This is his mic. Thank you. Thank you. Mr. Mayor, Mayor Pro Tem, Mr. City Manager, and members of the council, it's an honor and privilege to be here. It's also an honor to be here with our competitors. And I wanted to think in terms of how to put Airport Boulevard in context of real people's lives. And so the metaphor I came up with was this is like asking somebody to go back to school and change careers. This is an opportunity for Airport Boulevard to take advantage of what it is, the people it has, its authenticity, its experience over time, but to reinvent itself in a new way to have fun and to be connected to the rest of the community. And I think that's what it's like to go back to school and reinvent yourself. I think that's the metaphor that we are thinking about. In that context, our team is here today, and I'm going to ask them to just briefly stand up. And I'll specifically identify them in a little bit in terms of the roles. But if the team, our team could stand up. Now, this is a, appreciate that, the Gateway Planning, Kim Lee Horn team. This is a little scary, but we added up how many years' experience we have in Austin collectively. 220. Got a little gray hair here. But I think that's important because we're a team that has national experience in doing form-based coding. Of this type of coding, probably as much as anybody. But we're also a team that does understand and lives Austin. And, in fact, the core of this team has been doing the strategic mobility plan and has been putting the connective tissue together that the voters will be considering, for example, this November. This is not about form-based codes. Form-based codes is a tool. This is about co-creation. This is about making Airport Boulevard a place for the neighborhoods around it, an opportunity for the two mall owners to reinvent themselves, for the county to look at real progressive future strategies for public-private partnerships, to activate the transit in the corridor, the two, possibly three transit stations if we're talking about one at Miller Airport someday. And so I think the reason the Gateway Planning team is really the team for this job is because we're about building partnerships, and that's our track record. We know the technical aspects of form-based coding as well as anybody, but today we want to talk about Airport Boulevard. The picture in the upper right-hand corner of this slide, starting a downtown business, we just recently completed with Kim Lee Horn a reinvention of a downtown through a form-based code in Owensboro, Kentucky, on the Ohio River. In a recession, $120 million of real development in infrastructure are under construction today. And the bank said this is key. We want low-risk investment. And so they formed a banking alliance for investment in downtown Owensboro. We used the form-based code to create a master developer environment and predictability in that downtown environment. And that's what we want to do for Airport Boulevard, is to create predictability so that the small businesses in the neighborhoods, the city, and the region can actually facilitate long-term investment, engagement, and so that we can see how the neighborhoods can be a part of that corridor again, which they are not today. And we have a tremendous public involvement team, Armando Reo, Mike Clark-Madison, Glenn Gabois. I'll talk in a bit about why I think that's an important team. Tier 1 is requirements that all PUDs have to meet, and Tier 2 provides criteria in 13 areas in which a PUD may exceed code requirements and therefore be deemed superior. The PUD doesn't have to address all criteria outlined in Tier 2, and there is not a minimum number or individual items that are required. This PUD meets all Tier 1 items and one of three additional Tier 1 items and offers elements of superiority in seven of the 13 Tier 2 categories, being open space and parkland, environment, community amenities, transportation, housing, art, and historic preservation. The applicant's development plan indicates that the building will front Little Road with two access points, which will both be aligned with the access drives on the other side of the street. Diving right into the first topic, I'm going to start with landscaping, screening, buffering, and fences. How good does it have to be? How much do we need? And then take any questions that you have on that topic. So, well, I do want to mention, though, we need to get through all of the topics. So we'll take a few questions on each topic. But at some point, I'm going to kick the conversation to the next. And then at the end, for the remaining time that we have with you, we can revisit each of these individual topics. Landscaping. Alternative landscaping plan option. We say this right up front. We know that no matter how good we draft a code, and we've drafted a lot of codes, somebody's going to come to you with a project that is going to be unique. It's going to have a certain set of site conditions that are different than other properties in Denton. So how do we take care of that? Well, you don't want to require a public hearing where everything gets hashed out and neighborhoods have to get involved. Well, this is an opportunity to talk to the director and to say, look, I've got unique conditions here. I can't meet the black and white letter of the landscaping standard. Here's what I can do that's an equal benefit to the city that still meets the intent of the code but gives us a little bit of wiggle room because I've got utilities where you want me to plant trees. I can't do that. They won't survive. So this is a new procedure. It's a new option. You'll see a lot of flexible alternatives throughout the development standards that say, alternatives may be allowed where the director approves them or shall comply to the maximum extent practicable. That's less than feasible. It's saying this just doesn't make good common sense to require you to do that on this particular property. Another important change to landscaping is how the buffers work. Right now, you do require buffers between incompatible uses, but it's very rigid in the types of buffers that you can provide. Instead, we have proposed an optional point system that allows you to reach a certain point total for a buffer. I'll use the earlier example, single-family residential, if I want to develop industrial next to an existing single-family residential neighborhood, I need to earn 50 points in a buffer. And then there's another table, page 56 of your draft, shows you how you can earn those points. You're not decreasing the quality of the buffer by giving them options for points. You're just saying, you earn the points however you want to. A stone wall gets you more points. Trees get you more points. You keep adding up those options until you've reached 50. Now, if I'm single-family and I want to build next to another single-family, you don't have to do a buffer. That just doesn't make sense, right? We want to protect things from more intense uses. The last one I'll mention here in the landscaping, and then we'll get into some questions about this one, is low-impact development. Green infrastructure. Rather than requiring everything to be in pipes, in piped infrastructure, and putting downspouts directly into pipes, how can we run water across a property to actually improve the water quality, to require less piped infrastructure? This still needs some working out with coordinating with the engineering department, making sure that we can actually do all of these things. But I'll mention, Denton is very proud of, and should be, to be a silver-certified ice swim for stormwater management city. That's important in terms of thinking about how you treat and move water across a site sustainably. We have given you options to do green infrastructure, not mandates, saying you can do these things where it makes sense, where it's allowed by drainage and other departments within the city. Those are the three, the big three for landscaping. I'll open it up to questions before we move to the next topic. Commissioner Beck. Explain rain gardens, just for clarification. Transcript around the quote: We will be supporting the renewal of the SUP for three years, not five years. There were several factors that we looked at before considering this for approval. Since they are a well-established business on Greenville Avenue, we felt comfortable supporting this business for three years. Recently, there has been a high restaurant turnover rate due to increases in rents on Greenville Avenue. This is no fault of the business owner. Recent business turnovers leave the neighborhood in an uncontrollable position when an unknown business concept takes over an existing SUP where the concept may not fit the purpose of PD-842. One, to ensure the compatibility of uses with adjacent residential neighborhoods. And two, to reduce the incidence of crime by discouraging an over-proliferation of regional-serving late-night venues. We have recently seen several well-established businesses close, Crisp Salad, Yucatan Taco, Blind Butcher, Nora, and Dallas Beer Kitchen, just to name a few. We have absolutely no problem with the Libertine as a business. It's just the fact that the SUP goes with the address and not with the business itself. We ask that you approve the request for an SUP for three years, no auto renewal. Respectfully, Kim Comerford, LGWNA. Based, well, with regard to Matter Z189-170, I move that we follow staff's recommendation for approval of the amendment and renewal of SUP 1881 for a five-year period, subject to a revised site plan and revised conditions, which include that the patio would close at midnight and therefore would not be subject to the late-night hours SUP, only the inside of the building. chapters.title: Item C11
chapters.text: You're almost giddy. I am. This is NRD 2014 0100, 500 East 6th Street. And this is an application to put a rooftop use on a building that has been sadly neglected over the years. There are some real good points about this proposal. The front of the building is going to be refurbished. The windows will be refurbished. It's interesting because the windows that are in the building right now, even though they look historic, are not. In your packet, you have a couple of historic photos on page 2 that the applicant provided from the History Center. And the building had casement windows in the late 50s. I'm guessing 1957, just based on the automobiles that are in the picture. And then if you look at the building in 1980, the bottom photo, the current 2 over 2 windows are back in there. So that's not usually the way these things go. So this, I think, this proposal has some really good points in that it really is going to revitalize a building that has been languishing for a number of years. The issue that staff has with it and the reason that I put it on for discussion is the rooftop use. In the downtown Austin plan and our architectural design guidelines for 6th Street, rooftop uses need to be set back from the wall in the historic district. And this one, while the actual construction on the roof, the bar that goes back that you can see there with the glass tower, which staff thinks is a very innovative design for this, that is set back from the front, but the use actually goes right up to the parapet. And there's vegetation along the parapet wall, including a tree. And this violates, I mean, it's lovely, but it violates our architectural design guidelines for 6th Street. So that's why I put it on for discussion. The part of this case that didn't get adequately discussed in the staff report is this also involves the demolition of a small convenience store that is on Natchez Street. It's the Jordania. It's not a historic building. But that will be taken out for the rear part of the addition to this building. So the dilemma here, at least for staff, is that because it is not a landmark, it's just in the historic district, your comments are advisory. So you would make recommendations. The way to make sure, depending on how strongly you all feel about the current proposal, would be to postpone the case until next month. I know the applicant certainly doesn't want that to happen, but that could force a change of design that would comply with our architectural design guidelines and the downtown Austin plan for 6th Street that would bring that use into a much less visible position on the roof of the building. Like I said, this proposal has some great points, the revitalization of this building that's been languishing, but this revitalization probably needs to be stepped back a little bit to comply with the standards that we apply to or try to apply to every other building on 6th Street. Steve, is the setback only from the required or the suggested setback in the district guidelines only from the front of the building? It's a 15-foot setback from the front. It really is up for interpretation as to whether you've got a corner building, whether that should also be 15 feet. It's not really spelled out anywhere. It would be a little bit hard to do 15 feet from the side of this. It would be, and to me, it also would mean that somebody who has a corner building ends up not having the same rights as somebody who has a building in the interior of the block. So I think the side setback could be less than 15 feet, but the front setback is fairly explicit that it needs to be at least 15 feet. And no tree? The architectural design guidelines say no vegetation, no nothing at the parapet. It needs to be a clean, to be able to give the building its historic context. Thank you. This is a discussion item. Did we have anyone else to speak? I was looking to see. Hi, my name is Ken Johnson. I'm with Michael Hsu's office. I don't necessarily need to say anything else. Steve covered it pretty well, but I'm happy to answer questions. Anyone else who cares to speak? I really have a question, I guess, is why the client and you in the process didn't recognize the guidelines for 6th Street? Well, we looked at the guidelines. The building, as Steve mentioned, is only about 20 feet wide. And so in judging the setback there, it seemed like that was, it couldn't be accomplished to get a rooftop deck and set it back from the side 15 feet. From the front, we did hold all the structure back, and seasonally, the plantings will be held back off of the parapet. But one of the great benefits of a rooftop deck is people watching down onto 6th Street. And it seemed that there's a few rooftop patios on 6th Street that have a partial roof and continue up to the street. And I know that they've been built in the last few years. And so it seemed like this was possibly a rule that was not enforced as we drove up and down 6th Street to do our research. And so that's kind of why we tried to hold, we did, we didn't try, we held all the structure back 15 feet. But we thought that the guardrail and adding a little bit of planting to soften the edges of 6th Street and hopefully revitalize this end. Because if you've been to 6th Street, this end is kind of no man's land. So hoping to bring, and the owner's willing to spend a significant amount of money, like Steve said, to bring this back. It's a plywood floor on the first floor. But the second floor has all the original trusses that we're going to keep, all original oak floor. And so it's beautiful. We're going to work around it and insert a new steel structure inside at no small expense. And so we thought that, you know, with the preservation of the windows and the clear delineation of old building versus new building on the back addition, that this might be the one section that had a little bit of leeway as we were designing. And mostly for the fact of the people watching and the appeal of a rooftop deck is being right up there. I think you can kind of see the problem, though. I know that if you landscape your roof edge, everyone else will think, well, okay, we can do the same. And I don't think you're going to find many plannings along 6th Street, to my knowledge. Right. I just, I think we've been trying to interpret guidelines for 6th Street and for Congress to be consistent. Of late, we've had the neon lighting possibilities. And then coming up with this, I think it sort of looks like the hanging gardens of Babylon. I think this is not something that is in keeping with 6th Street or Congress and would detract from the historic character of the building and from the district. And so I would not be in favor of that. Thank you. Also, I mean, we'd like you to consider the fact that you are spending a lot of money to bring the building, you know, back as much as possible. And the front facade is really very attractive. And quite honestly, you know, vines or greenery hanging over the top of it really detracts significantly from that. And I'm not sure that's necessary at all to achieve what you're trying to achieve. Do you think that if the planters didn't have plants that hung down, that just had plants that grew up, that it would be more appealing? I think it would be more appealing as if the rail was back from the facade. And obviously the planters and things hanging over the edge just kind of, you know, are just something that doesn't work as far as I'm concerned. Any other questions? I would just add, you know, I understand that your building is narrow and you can't meet that 15-foot setback on the side. But you can in the front. And I encourage you to do so. I think, you know, your position on that corner there, you're going to have plenty of room for people watching on that side balcony. And it's just the front facade that, you know, we're concerned about here. I guess I'm being optimistic that your presence there will transform. We are too, greatly, yeah. I have a question for Steve. Why would this not have come to the Certificate of Appropriateness Committee? Why did this not come? Uh-huh. Because it's not a Certificate of Appropriateness. It's just a, it's a historic, it's permanent in the National Register District. So it's not a landmark building. I see, okay, okay. Because I was thinking, I would like to have a discussion about these items where we could just sit down and just talk about it rather than having this public meeting. Yeah. And the COA would be a perfect place for that. Would you be willing to come to that, Mr. Johnson? Two weeks? Sure. Okay. I think the chair should be the one to approve that one, though. What do you think? Yes, I would welcome your presence at the Certificate of Appropriateness Committee, and we can, in a more casual setting, kind of work out some of these things and maybe convince you that the planters there at the edge of the building are not in keeping with the historic district. That would be my recommendation. Better not hear an agreement that you'll come to the Certificate of Appropriateness and visit. Like, yeah. Yes. Better enough? So then we need a, we would need a motion. Well, is there anybody else that wants to speak on this item? Okay. Then we will need a motion to close the public hearing and then a motion to postpone the public hearing to 27th of October with the direction to the applicant to visit with the Certificate of Appropriateness Review Committee. Okay. What you said. We need two different motions. A motion to close the public hearing? So moved. Second. Moved. A motion to second. All in favor? Aye. Opposed. Now a motion to postpone action on this and instruct the applicant to come to the next meeting of the Committee of Appropriateness.

chapters.title: XIV) CITIZEN PARTICIPATION
chapters.text: Mr. Buskin, citizen participation. Thank you, Mayor. Citizen participation gives the public an opportunity to make comments or address concerns regarding matters related to city business or affairs that are in the scope of the authority of the City Council and which are not posted on the evening agenda. However, please understand that the Mayor and Council are not permitted by law to respond to, discuss, or address the comment at this time as these items are not included on the posted Council agenda for this evening. The Mayor and Council may only ask clarifying questions and or direct staff to take appropriate action. Speakers who have pre-registered will be given two minutes to make their comments, except that if 26 or more speakers have pre-registered, each speaker will be given one minute to make their comments. Our first speaker this evening is Anthony Moore. Mr. Moore. After Mr. Moore is Andrea Banches. Good evening, sir. The Mayor and City Council. I have a book. My name is Anthony Moore. I'm displaced right now because of a situation with my parents. Unfortunately, my dad's in heaven. My mom's still here, but that's not needless to say. But I have this book. It's called The Unpologetic Guide to Black Mental Health. And me being an African American, I just want to share this one expert and then wrap up my minutes with just a closing statement. The psychological crisis is real. Let's fight for our insanity together. Do you tell yourself like many of us others that black people don't have time to feel anxious or get depressed? We have too much work to do. We have too many situations to manage at our children's schools. Too many coworkers dare us to succeed. Too much family drama. It takes everything in us. Me, you, us, us all. It takes everything for us to keep going. The very effort to deal with our daughters, our sons, coworkers, supervisors, husbands, lack of husbands, our drama with our friends, even friends, family, church members, emotional tank going empty. But it keeps us going and that's what we got to do. And this right there, I just wanted to say that I'm a mental health advocate and a mental health activist. And I just really believe in our black and brown people getting the mental health care that they need so graciously. And partnership with NAMI Texas, NAMI National, Arlington, Virginia. Governor Abbott will love them to death. And I'm also NAMI Tarrant. The unfortunate thing is in Arlington, we do not have NAMI Arlington. That's what I really want to fight for. I just want to make the statement that I think us as people, board members, city council, people and the citizens of Arlington, we can do a great job with having Arlington, have NAMI Texas in Arlington where we can help the Mansfield, Waxahachie, all our surrounding areas, Grand Prairie. Thank you. That's my time. Thank you, sir. Mr. Buskin. Andrea Bunches. Ma'am. Good evening. Andrea Bunch, Arlington resident, my whole life. I own a small business at the northeast corner of Cooper and Mayfield called PRN Uniforms. And I would invite or would like to invite our district person, Mr. Peel, come visit. We are having an increasingly difficult situation with the day laborers that hang out at the corner to the point of this past weekend, and one of my own customers had to call the police because she felt threatened pulling into the parking lot. I'm sorry, I'm not going to get upset. My mother started that business in 2001. We've been in that area this entire time. Lived in Arlington since I was two. My whole life. Love it here. But this situation is not getting any better. Our mail carrier feels threatened to even come deliver the mail to the businesses in our center, which is Arlington Park Square. I just don't know what we can do at this point other than suggesting possibly another place designated in the city where they can hang out. We also have a homeless gentleman that's been living behind the building. We've had vandalism the last two weeks with our security cameras getting knocked off the wall. But I would gratefully invite you to come visit us, especially on a Saturday when it's very busy. And we're the only store open in the shopping center to see the number of people that we have noticed a significant increase since September of 2023. Thank you very much. Thank you, ma'am. Our next speaker is Mohammed Reza Kosh Surat. After Mr. Surat is Brent Warman. I think he's not here yet. I'm Reza, so I'm Mohammed. You're a different Mohammed? We should be talking about this stuff too. Go ahead. Okay. So, you know, we came to the city to have like a new idea to open food truck as a barbecue in Arlington. So we came and they told us to go to the Tarot County to do all the stuff. So we went and all the syrup. And, you know, we built it. We tried to do it all right. And we just built it. And we parked it on Arlington, like across to AT&T Stadium. You know, by approve from the Tarot County, not like just I want to bark there. And one of the health department just came like last week and they shut down us. They said like, you cannot bark. Whenever we came, they told us, you know, you have to deal with the Tarot County. And that's what the situation is. Okay. Yeah. I'm going to ask Ms. Thoppel to get in touch with you to help clarify what the rules are about where the food trucks can be and things such as that. Okay. Thank you. Thank you, sir. Our next speaker is Brett Worman. After Mr. Worman is Gene and Aisha. Good evening, Mayor, Council, Brett Worman, Board of Directors of the Arlington Missile Patrolments Association. For the past few weeks, we have been requesting the Council consider placing the Crime Control Prevention District on the ballot for 2024. We have provided this Council with several public safety concerns, like the lack of training at any of our large venues, the lack of training and security at the Arlington Airport, and the fact that the city has not completed a study comparing the number of police calls for service on event days compared to a non-event days to help understand the amount of strain placed on police resources. The CCPD could help address these issues and can provide much needed revenue for the police training and equipment. In addition, we believe an eighth of a cent for the CCPD will not only provide the much needed revenue, but will free up other revenue within the general budget for other city issues and for hiring additional police officers. Currently, the police department has 730 positions allocated for police officers. We are currently at 690 sworn, not including the recruits in the academy. In addition, we are losing approximately four officers per month to normal attrition, making it a constant fight to get ahead. We think it's important to point out that in 2008, we had 246 officers on patrol. On January 8, 2024, we started our new patrol bid with 241 officers on patrol. We have not increased the number of officers on the streets answering 911 calls for your citizens for 16 years. Yet, we have seen massive growth within the city, including AT&T Stadium, Globe Live Field, Texas Live, Live by Lowe's, and the soon-to-be-open Lowe's Hotel with over 800 rooms. And many other new venues bringing more and more people into the city. We ask that you place the CCPD on the ballot, that you stop listening to certain individuals within the city who are not in favor of the CCPD, and listen to those out there making a difference. The council is playing the odds that nothing will occur. However, should you be wrong, you will not be remembered for the good things you have done, but you will be remembered for what you did not do. Our next speaker is Jinan Aisha. After Ms. Aisha is Shahad Jadala. Good afternoon, council members. My name is Jinan. I'm a resident of Arlington. I'm a UTA nursing student, and I am on top of all of that from Jerusalem, Palestine. One thing the nursing department at UTA consistently teaches us is that a hospital setting is essential for a patient's healing, recovery, and safety. And I would like to emphasize on safety because since the beginning of the genocide in Gaza, there had been 36 hospitals to support 2.2 million people. Mr. Mayor, right now in Gaza, all of the 36 hospitals have either been bombed or raided. And as your future healthcare worker and as a product of your universities, I urge you to not only values life here in America, but all around the world. Mr. Mayor, I want to thank you for being respectful and consistent with our community because for the past four months, we have been struggling to find respect within neighboring city meetings, city council meetings. As we were promised, there will be a ceasefire resolution discussion. And if I would like to ask anything from this council is that you expedite the process because because Palestinians are not only losing time, we are losing blood. And as we stand here tonight, there is a child somewhere in Gaza, buried under the wobble of their own homes, screaming, screaming at the top of their lungs in hopes to be found. I would like to thank you, Mr. Mayor, again, I would like to wrap up by saying free Palestine, free Palestine and free Palestine. Thank you for your time. Thank you, ma'am. Our next speaker is Shahad Jadala. After Mr. Jadala is Mariam Hader. Good evening, ma'am. As-salamu alaykum. Peace be upon you. My name is Shahid. I was born and raised here in Arlington. I completed my graduate and undergraduate studies here at UTA. And most importantly, I'm a grandchild of the 1948 NECPA. To say this started on October 7th is the equivalent of starting a novel on the second to last chapter. You don't even know what led up to the plot. Allow me to mention just a few of the chapters that you skipped over. Haifa massacre of 1937. Jerusalem massacre of 1937. Haifa massacre of 1938. Beled al-Sheikh massacre of 1939. chapters.title: 16. Discussion of Community Engagement Needs (Part 1 of 2)
chapters.text: Great. That brings us to item 16, which was something that I put on our agenda, along with a couple other commissioners. And it feeds into, honestly, the last comment we had regarding community engagement and inquiring within the community for the feedback that we're looking for. As it relates to our new programs, as it relates to needs that are ongoing, as it relates to things that are surfacing in real time. I know we have two working groups right now on within the working group list that are attempting to do this. And one is a bit of a dated group that dealt with the early, the equity working group was really about the launch and the forming of this. In the formation phase of our new programming. And I don't think that it's, we need to carry on that torch in that way. And I'm also seeing that the quarterly working group is just having difficulty, despite best efforts. A lot of energy has been poured into that group, but we're having a sort of stutter step in regards to actually launching those meetings in a consistent fashion. I think we've maybe had two. And because of the work that goes, three. The work that goes into them, not just the coordination of our commissioner schedules, then finding a time and place that works for everybody, thinking about the needs of the community and accessibility, constraints that we are, you know, rubrics for those meetings. We're talking about having different commissioners there, and they're happening in different parts of town. It just, I think, months pass before we've actually been able to bring that idea to fruition. And so what I, along with other commissioners and just people I've been speaking with, like, in terms of ideating and coming up with an idea, what may be the best move forward is to sunset these working groups that aren't, the equity working group is just no longer active. And the quarterly working group, I think maybe we've just worked ourselves into a little bit of a corner in terms of actually getting those off the ground and creating a new working group that is literally community engagement, that can umbrella all the needs of the commission, that allows us to be present in the community without the sort of more stringent parameters that we put forth with, again, best of intentions to be there for the community. But I know that there are groups out there that are already hosting community gatherings, and really the community engagement working group would be the core, as I see it, and again, bringing this for a discussion for my fellow commissioners, it would be the face of the commission. And obviously, as long as we have under six people, all commissioners are welcome to attend. We just need to sort of be organized so we don't hit a quorum. But that working group would then lead the charge in terms of like, hey, there's a meeting within this certain community, and they are inviting the commission to come be present and answer questions, or just to mingle, just to meet the constituents. Back in 2020 and 2021, Commissioner Polgar and I, with expediency and urgency, were able to make that happen and basically just sent up a flare and said, hey, we're available. If you want us in front of your membership, your board, bring us out, and we'll be there. And I think that's the similar, you know, less organized, maybe a little bit more scrappy, a little bit more flexible of a body that we need to sort of shape-shift into, because the rigidity around what we've created is not working. It's just not functioning. I know that the few, and actually Faiza was a host of one of our quarterly, you had at the Cinemakerspace, you hosted a quarterly working group. There were six. There was three. There were six. The Asian Film Society did one as well. That was a community chat, but literally it was a quarter. That's the difference, is I think we've sort of conflated the two. There was community chats, and then there was the quarterly working group. But again, by the time it's locked in, we have a week to promote it, and it's just not doing the thing. So that is my proposal to the commission as a whole, is do we feel like we could shift our modality in the way that we get out into the community, create a little bit more flexibility around the mechanism, and reach out to the people that are our community amplifiers, our partners that are already hosting events. Like, why are we trying to reinvent the wheel here when it's only putting more work on us, and the primary obstacle in bringing this meeting to fruition, are these meetings to fruition, is capacity, is the capacity of us as a volunteer body. So it's really making ourselves available in a formal way, and then reaching out to our community partners at Amplifier saying, hey, we're here, we're ready. Anytime you have an event and you want commissioners there, like the Disneyland characters and handlers, like, we'll be there. So I'm just throwing it out there to my commission. I would love to hear feedback, particularly from members of those working groups. We have the chair of the quarterly meetup working group here. So what are thoughts? I would love to hear from you all. I'll open. I think it would be great to find a community partner in this. And because, like you said, just the volunteer body of what we do and what we're covering and all the working groups we're doing, that community working group, that community quarterly working group, it's been trying to grab ground for a year and a half. And it's, yes, and it's just like something would be postponed or something, and it's just, you're right. And to me, community engagement is number one priority for this body, as well as approving and knowing what's going on. So to find us to reach out to community groups, community groups that are here in the House and listening to this meeting, I think if you can let one of your commissioners know that you're interested in being a part of this community. We are, the Arts Commission and the community are one. We are not separate. We are wanting to join hands to make all of this grow in the right direction. Thank you, Commissioner Gray. Any other? Please, Commissioner Criccini. Yeah, I don't know if this is allowed because I'm still learning, but kind of just to expand on what you were saying, if there was a way to formalize that on the City of Austin website on, like, are you, do you have an upcoming event that you're interested in having an Arts Commissioner at? Because I agree with you, like, work smarter, not harder. When people see, and I'm one of those people because I'm an artist, when you see something that's, you know, the City of Austin, it might not, like, resonate with you. So if there are already these organizations that we should be supporting, you know, generally anyway, that are doing the work to get their constituency there, even just showing up and saying, you know, I represent this district, this is what I do. I think one thing, you know, I haven't been a commissioner for very long, but one question that people have for me is, like, well, what is it that you actually do? And so I think demystifying that and then also offering opportunity just for one-on-one communication is really, really great. And there's so many events that are happening. You know, City Council does this in a different capacity, so I think that that's great. We need to show up for our communities. Exactly, and I think that us trying to create the architecture around how we do it, it ended up being more cumbersome than we anticipated, and it just stalled a need, and that was for us to be available, even just to be active listeners. I mean, that was one thing that I really learned from former Commissioner Polgar was, like, we're not going to have the answers and we're not going to be able to solve any real problems in real time, but being a vessel for these people and knowing that they're being heard and that this feedback is being carried up the chain, like, there is confidence and trust and transparency that can be built through those relationships. And we are all representatives of our community. We all have a deep well of this network that we represent being here. So we need to sort of reciprocate and mirror that back to the people that are entrusting us. Yes, Commissioner Mock. I guess with these new programs, we have funded over 200 programs, right? So, you know, I think I agree with you. We need to work smarter but not harder. You know, I do not want to just go to a meeting for the sake of having a meeting. I do think that the continuous communication is important to build trust. I think when it was started, it was because we were trying to push these new programs out. So there was a lot of anxiety. People were trying to learn all of this. So there is a purpose for those meetings. So I wanted to ask then if we are going to have this community engagement meetings, what are the purpose? And people have very busy life and Austin traffic is not happening, you know. So if we are going to serve the community, what do we offer? What do we offer to the community? Why should they come and meet us, you know, with their busy life? And, you know, so we have to think, I think, about the purpose and how we best utilize people's time and how we as commissioners serve them better. Absolutely. So that's my thought. And so, you know, this proposed community engagement working group would be a body of commissioners that then strategize on that. Who is our community partner? What are the most pressing items that we need to talk about? And, you know, I think that it's, again, having a little bit more flexibility and letting it be more malleable, whereas, like, the quarterly working group is we meet quarterly. We're rotating districts. We have these commissioners. And it's just, like, the rigidity in that was so limiting. Whereas this, the working group can then build out the relationship with community partners. If we're being invited into a space and
