chapters.title: 4. Briefing on Spring Storm Season Preparations - Chief James Davis and Maribel Martinez, Fire
chapters.episode_title: CITY COUNCIL WORK SESSION CITY COUNCIL WORK SESSION
chapters.text: Maribel and I are going to give you a quick briefing. Maribel is going to lead up just talking a little bit about our spring season that we're certainly in the midst of and just answer any questions you may have on our preparedness or procedures. Maribel? All right. Well, good afternoon. We just wanted to provide an overview of what we've been doing these past couple of months. It's been a busy month for the Office of Emergency Management and all our internal and external partners as we get ready for the severe weather season. I know just in March already alone, we've had three different activations for severe storms that have entered our area. So we'll give a brief overview of kind of what our office does as far as it relates to severe weather operations and then the exercises and trainings that we've done and then go over some of the warning mechanisms. Again, our office is the Office of Emergency Management. We have 14 full-time staff. Two of those are on the general fund. The others are supported through the UOC grant program. That's the Homeland Security grant program. And then a few others on our state emergency management planning grant program. We do have currently two vacancies. Those are two duty officers, so we're a little bit short-staffed coming into the severe weather season. But we currently have six duty officers that rotate on a week basis that are that on-call person for emergency management. They monitor weather, and then we activate additional teams as needed. So we're coming into our active season for Tarrant County. From now to last till in the 1950s, we've had about 93 tornadoes hit Tarrant County. Historically, the majority of the tornadoes in Tarrant County have been in the month of April. Of those 93, there's, I believe it was 70, are in the month of April, and then the rest are in the following months. So April or May are our two top months for severe weather. Our time frames that we're usually impacted here in Fort Worth is usually about 3 p.m. to 8 p.m. But we're always ready. We're always working with all our partners, working with our National Weather Service here in Fort Worth. They usually provide a morning email set up to our office by 9 or 10 a.m., kind of giving us an outlook if it's going to be a severe weather active day. We will take that information. We'll coordinate with the forecasters, look at what our county and state partners are doing. And then if we feel that it is of impact to the city of Fort Worth, then we will forward that email. I think most of y'all are on that distribution list, the JOC event notification list. We'll distribute that and outline some of the readiness activities that we're coordinating and the information that we receive in the Office of Emergency Management and the JOC. We also work with all our field partners, TPW Stormwater, make sure they're ready. They have the personnel available on standby if needed. And then depending on the impacts, whether it's a weekday, if it's coming in overnight, if we have a special event going on, if it's coming in the rush hour, we take in all these different factors and what really the forecasters are thinking. You know, if there's a high level of uncertainty on the environment that day, we may activate more people in the joint emergency operations center. Our philosophy is that you can never be overprepared, but we want to make sure we have the right people working in that same room so that we can activate additional people if we need to. I mean, it always helps to have all these people working in the same room and coordinating the issues and getting resources as needed. So we'll go into the activation levels here in a bit, but we will notify some of our key partners if we feel that we're going to be activated later on. We'll get with our StormSpotter liaisons, make sure they're ready should we need to activate them at a later time. And then definitely, if there is a large outdoor event, again, if it's anything over 10,000 people, we are there in the JOC monitoring. That way we get a head start if something does happen at the outdoor event. But definitely, if we have severe weather coming, we have a large outdoor event, similar to what we may have this weekend. We're not sure if the severe weather threat is there, but we have NASCAR TMS operations this weekend. We'll activate additional people so that we're prepared, ready to go. This is kind of an overview of what our activations look like for last year, fiscal year 2018. So we were activated for 14 times in the EOC, but we coordinated with different partners 26 times. Again, we're getting right into the severe weather season, so we expect our stats to be similar this year. But again, for us, it's just making sure that we help work with our partners and make sure we're ready to go if we have any issues come up in the city. These are our different levels of activation as it relates to severe weather. Again, we have a duty officer 24-7. They're monitoring radar. They're monitoring social media. They're working in our chat rooms that we work with the National Weather Service and our meteorologist and other emergency managers in the area, just monitoring to see if the environment becomes more unstable, if the threat increases, if our tornadic threat is going higher, then we'll activate additional personnel. Our general criteria for duty officer is if we are going to have higher winds, greater than 60 miles per hour, or hail greater than one inch. Like I said, if we have an outdoor event, we're going to be there because we would activate the sirens for lower thresholds than this. And I'll go into our siren activation thresholds here in a bit. Again, our EOC limited activation is probably about 10 to 15 people in our emergency operations center. That includes representatives from fire, police, TPW stormwater, MedStar, park and rec, and I believe we're adding code as well for damage assessments this season. We will also have a storm spotter liaison through our Aries RACES group, and we have Tarrant County Emergency Management and the Texas Division Emergency Management will activate as well, so that if we did have issues, we can coordinate a resource request in the JEOC. And then the EOC full activation, we maintain our Everbridge roster system so we can do emergency call-outs as needed. We ideally want to get everybody in the JEOC before severe weather hits. That way they aren't caught in traffic jams or going through hailstorms to get there. But if we feel that it is a high tornado risk day or we have a big enough special event, we would go for the full activation. And I'll show the full activation layout here in a bit. So the Office of Emergency Management, we have several ways to put out warning. A lot of, the majority of the warning products do come from the National Weather Service, so they will issue the severe thunderstorm watches, tornado watches, severe thunderstorm warnings, flash flood warnings, and tornado warnings. The tornado warnings and the severe thunderstorm warnings are automatic. They go out through our Nixle products. I believe, do any of you get the Nixle alerts or signed up for the Nixle alerts? That's something that we encourage our citizens to subscribe to. We do a lot of public events to try to get them onto the Nixle alerts. If we know ahead of a time that it's going to be a possibly severe weather active day, we may issue an advisory to the citizens to make sure that they're tuned in, they have their weather radio ready, and they're listening to the updates should the weather turn worse. But we always, you know, even with Nixle and our siren system, we always promote the NOAA weather all hazards radio. That is so much faster than Nixle, than our sirens. It is pretty much immediate once the National Weather Service does their warning. We've been looking at some of the timelines on some of the warning products, and, you know, I have like five different apps on my cell phone. But with cell, everybody knows, cell networks can go down. There's always delays. But because of the infrastructure that our NOAA weather all hazards radio is, it's on a different structure. You're going to get those a little bit more quicker. There are the wireless emergency alerts. You have probably received those on your cell phone. That is a different infrastructure than what our Nixle products do and the majority of our cell products. Those are only issued, again, automatically by the weather service with a tornado warning and a flash flood warning. So you will not get the severe thunderstorm warnings on your wireless emergency alert. This also goes into a variety of other products available, the EAS cut-ins. I'm sure you've heard on your radios or televisions. Those will cut in. There are, again, social media avenues, mobile apps. The cost of alerts is something that the Fort Worth supports. You can subscribe to those being a citizen of Fort Worth. You can subscribe to those notifications. And then our outdoor warning sirens. Again, this is something that we promote. These are outdoor warning sirens. So they are intended to be heard for those that are outdoors, either at parks or working out in the field. We currently have 149 sirens. 147 of those are City of Fort Worth sirens. TCC bought an additional two, and we activate those for them. I'm sure you've all heard in the media of some of the hackings going around in the area. Last year, thanks to our IT department, we were able to get encrypted. So that project is now complete. And it's nice to know that, you know, hopefully we never get hacked, but we have that to fall back on. We also have our backup plans, you know, should we shouldn't get hacked, but, you know, if we should, how to mitigate that, some of the issues that Duncanville DeSoto have had in the last couple of weeks, that we do have backup plans to deactivate a siren if it was sounded not through the Office of Emergency Management. Our siren activation thresholds, this is part of a two-year project through the region that included meteorologists with the Weather Service, our media partners, and emergency management officials from

chapters.title: III.C) ZA26-01 (300 W. Park Row Drive) - Application for a change in zoning from Office Commercial (OC) to Residential Medium Density (RM-12), on approximately 0.954 acres.
chapters.episode_title: Planning and Zoning Commission - Plat Agenda
chapters.text: Thank you for your family's business and your interest in Arlington. Very much appreciated. Thank you, sir. Thank you. Next, we're going to move on to our final case of the evening. ZA 26-01, located at approximately 300 West Park Road Drive. This is an application for a change in zoning from office commercial, a straight zoning change to residential medium RM12, and approximately 0.954 acres. At this time, I'll call on our staff to present its report on zoning case ZA 26-01. Good evening. Alex Van Amberg, Planner Planning and Development Services. This is case ZA 26-01, addressed at 300 West Park Road Drive, and the site is just under one acre. They are currently zoned office commercial, and the request is a change in zoning to residential medium density, or RM12 zoning district. Here's a location map showing the site and surrounding areas. There is a single-family neighborhood to the north across West Park Road Drive. To the south, there is a multifamily development. To the west is a parking lot and, I believe, a church property. And then to the east is zoned single-family, but it is Grace Lutheran Church. They own that property and also the subject property. And here are some images showing the surrounding area. Here are the uses that are permitted in the RM12 zoning district. The applicant's intent is to build eight townhomes on this property. The comprehensive plan designates land use goals for this area as established residential. This property is also in the Heart of Arlington Neighborhood Association. And it is within the South Cooper Corridor Strategy, specifically Zone 1, which is an area around UTA. The applicant is Yvonne Gonzalez with Place Strategies, Inc., and the owner of the property is Grace Lutheran Church. Staff did receive two letters of support and no letters of opposition, and I'm available for any questions. Seeing none, thank you very much, Alex. This time I'm going to open up the public hearing and ask for the applicant to come forward and speak on their behalf. I have two cards here. Who's going to come first, Donna or Yvonne? Sir, come on up. If you'll both introduce your name and the city that you live in, we don't need your address. Donna Van Ness, Arlington resident. And go ahead and introduce yourself, Dan. Yvonne Gonzalez, Fort Worth. All right, thank you. All right, Donna, take it away. Thank you so much, commissioners and staff. I appreciate the opportunity to see you tonight. Housing Channel, I'm the president. We're a nonprofit partner with the city of Arlington for over 34 years, helping with mixed income housing and the Arlington Homebuyer Assistance Program, which provides up to $20,000 for low- to moderate-income households to purchase a home. We also provide housing counseling and education to help create sustainable homeowners. Our business model includes development of for-sale, single-family, detached and attached homes to help revitalize communities and strengthen neighborhoods. We're unique in that our organization has an in-house property and HOA management team to help ensure our owner-occupancy requirements and long-term maintenance of our properties. Typically, for our developments, we place a soft-second lien on the units for up to 20 years, which helps ensure that the home is exclusively used for owner-occupancy. Leasing and other non-owner uses are prohibited, and as the community developer, we are in charge of developing the HOA rules and regulations, which expressly prohibit all forms of rental activity, including short-term rentals. I'll let Yvonne take over. So Yvonne Gonzalez, urban planner and principal of Place Strategies, we're an urban planning and architecture firm specializing in infill development and walkable neighborhoods. So the first thing that we wanted is, being urban planners, we wanted to take a look at what's around, what's the neighborhood, and then how does it comply, or how does it stack up with adopted city policies and documents. So the request is going from office commercial to residential medium density to allow for the townhomes, like staff mentioned. All the units will be for sale for working families, owner-occupied requirements for the townhomes, like Donna said, and act as a transition between the multifamily rental and commercial to the west and the church to the east. And Park Row also, on a lot of the adopted documents, is the transition from kind of the downtown area down to some of the residential areas. So it also becomes one of that transition. So, again, being an urban planner, I wanted to take a look at how does it stack up in the comprehensive plan. And so three things that I just wanted to point out really quickly was promote land use patterns. I reflect a mix of integrated community uses, encourage appropriate redevelopment and reinvestment that creates lasting value, and increase the visual appeal within and around residential and commercial developments and along corridors. We've also been following the city on redoing that comprehensive plan. So we were able to take a look at that. Although it's not adopted, there's a vision framework that also speaks on infill development and just trying to reinvest into existing neighborhoods. So we think that it fits well within that as well. And like staff mentioned, this is also part of the Heart of Arlington Neighborhood Association. So we took a look at that plan, too. They have a neighborhood action plan. And so we wanted to just briefly look over how does it fit in within that plan. And so, you know, there is a Cooper Street Park Row redevelopment study. The study envisions a compact development that includes different arrangements of commercial uses, townhomes, apartments, student housing, and senior housing. We feel that it fits in well with what that neighborhood was envisioning for that area. It also was classified as a high-priority redevelopment area within that area. And so, and like I mentioned before, it is the boundary between the downtown university neighborhood and the medium density transition with residential area going south. And so a lot of mix with the church and with the multifamily rentals, you know, just to the south. But we feel it's a good transition. They also had some representative imagery within that action plan. So I just wanted to kind of take a look at that and see what they were envisioning at that time. Again, this has been, you know, since I think 2013, since this plan was envisioned. But variation in facade, prominent landscaping, pedestrian access priority, architectural features such as stoops and porches, and then a combination of materials. And I'll let Donna talk a little bit about kind of how we're envisioning that facade and kind of the working with the neighborhood to really try to hone in on what would be appropriate along that stretch. We understand Park Row is a prominent street within that area. And so we want to make sure that this is a prominent development that is a good entryway into the neighborhood. And with a focus on, again, we specialize on infill development in walkable neighborhoods. So making sure that that presence onto the right-of-way is appropriate. We're, again, it is straight zoning. And one thing I wanted to mention here, too, that I neglected to mention on our request at the beginning was when we looked at this, we looked at, you know, the use of townhomes and what is the least intense zoning district that would allow that by right. That's how we chose the RM-12. Again, just best practice for planning. What is the least intensity that would allow that use? Making it simple for staff, but also, you know, trying to streamline that development. And, again, with the partnership with the city, you know, a lot of trust with, you know, the partnership and making sure that, you know, with the first-time homebuyer program, there's a lot of connections with the city in trying to develop this. With that, I'll give it back to Donna to kind of give some examples. So these are some of the photographs of some of our projects. And you can see that, you know, one size doesn't fit all. We try to work with the city and the neighborhoods in every development and every neighborhood that we go into. It helps inform our design materials, our colors that, you know, fit within the character and the context of the neighborhood. You might recognize Bel Air on Abram, the lower photograph, which was championed by former Mayor Jeff Williams and the unofficial East Arlington Mayor Sue Phillips, who, with East Arlington Renewal, helped us choose the materials, the colors, landscaping, fencing, and we incorporated a butterfly garden and some seating in the common green space. So a lot of that was informed by several meetings and working with the neighborhood to come up with that context for that community. In the right photo, you'll see that easy cake. That is a live-work unit that we built. It's a community of live-work townhomes that we developed in partnership with the city of Irving. It was a catalyst to initiate their new mixed-use zoning in the heart of the city's Heritage District, which is one of the oldest neighborhoods in the city of Irving, and they wanted to revitalize that to create not only rooftops but opportunities for small businesses and entrepreneurs. And you'll see it's a little bit more of a modern, I guess, urban kind of look to that townhome. And then in the top photo is just actually a couple of blocks down from the right photo is an infill townhome development community, and it was surrounded by single-family homes. We built 18 communities, 18 homes, and we gave them more of a traditional townhome look and worked with the neighborhood with the colors and the materials for that as well. So it is our plan to obviously work with Hannah and Councilman Boxall to inform the materials and the colors for this project as well. Any last words or I guess we're done? Take some questions. Thank you. Questions at this time? Commissioner Blake? I don't sound too dumb with this question, but what is a soft lien versus a lien? There's no payments and no interest. It just sits on the property as a soft second lien. Okay. So you have your first lien, which is your mortgage, and then the soft second. So you can't make any adjustments. You couldn't sell the property without. Gotcha. Yeah. Sorry. Other questions? So let me ask one. So let's assume, I'll use the example I used upstairs. Family purchases this, they qualify. Contracts are signed. You've got the second lien in place. And four years go by, and this family has to move

tags.definition: Third places and public life: Informal social gathering places and the everyday public life of a community.
Parks and recreation: Parks, trails, recreation facilities, and access to everyday outdoor space.
Infill and redevelopment: Reuse or intensification of already-served land within a city.
Traffic calming and road diets: Street redesigns that slow traffic or reclaim excess roadway space.
Walk, bike, and transit access: Walking, cycling, transit access, or multimodal connectivity.
Missing-middle housing: Small-scale multi-unit housing between detached homes and large apartments.
Housing supply: Policies or projects intended to increase the amount or variety of housing.
Road widening: Road expansion, lane additions, or capacity projects that change street geometry.

Adaptive reuse: Converting existing buildings to new uses rather than replacing them.

Rezoning (individual case): An individual property or site-specific zoning action: rezoning a specific parcel, a planned development (PD) zoning case, a specific/special use permit, a replat, or a variance request tied to one property or a small set of parcels. Do not use this for a citywide or district-wide change to the zoning code text; use the "zoning-reform" tag for those instead.
Neighborhood planning: Plans, codes, or investments organized around a neighborhood-scale area.

chapters.title: Public Comment ( Part 2 of 4 )
chapters.text: All right, let's continue on with speakers. First in speaker person is Roy Whaley, speaking on several items, followed by Ben Sudeby. Thank you. Howdy, y'all. My name's Roy Whaley. I'm here for the Austin Regional Group of the Sierra Club, and I sent all of y'all an email not long ago talking about the Open Meetings Act and the Texas Attorney General's ruling, the rules you were supposed to be going by, that you're not required to have a state-mandated amount of time, but for each item, you're supposed to get that amount of time. So I'm not here on multiple issues. I should be here on individual issues. But that said, I ask y'all to support and pass item number 45. I know Watershed has worked on this for a long time, and these are regulations we can't afford to delay anymore. Also, on item 15 and 17, that needs to be put back in the oven, too. We need to have more time to upgrade those standards from 1980. We can be a leader not only in water conservation, but what we put back into the water stream. Thank you. And I know y'all worry about the state coming down on y'all all the time, but y'all don't seem to worry about it when it comes to citizen input. And that's a cry in shame. Not only is it a shame, it's also illegal. Mr. Whaley, thank you very much. Ben Sudeby and then Gus Pena, both speaking on several items. Good morning. My name is Ben Sudeby. I use he, him, el pronouns. I just want a disclosure. I'm not here representing any organization that I sit on the board of, my employer, or anyone else. I'm here as a citizen. And although I'm no longer a renter in this city, I was for a long time, and many of my friends are. We are a majority renter city. So I'd like to encourage all of you to support these measures that help renters. Very reasonable things, like giving them time to cure, time to get it right, and proper notice in English and in Spanish. We know that we're facing housing crises, and as a homeowner, as a house owner who pays taxes, I see this as a measure that will help us save money. An ounce of cure, or an ounce of prevention beats a pound of cure. Keeping these people housed will save us money, so we're not having to find them and get them rehomed. So again, very reasonable measures. Please pass them. This is one thing that you can do right now to help people stay housed. Thank you. My time. Okay, again, on number 20, El Buen Samaritano for service to a whole household, not to exceed $400,000, is a great expenditure, our expenditure. On number 31, 32, is an agreement with Sunrise Community Church. I stopped at the bus stop over there on Slaughter and Manchaca, and so they do a great job of housing and finding housing for the people and also food. Number 39, approve a resolution relating to mobile homes, et cetera. Please pass that one. And number 40, approve resolution directing the city manager to draft an ordinance that authorizes the property located at 2400 South Congress Avenue, et cetera. And I will tell you this much. Even under Bruce Todd's administration, we were talking about affordable housing. We had a lot of people being booted out of their homes, their rental homes. So please, por favor, usen la chaveta. That means use your brain housing group and help the people out. Thank you very much. On item 23, Sydney Beatty, followed by Emily Blair. Hi there. My name is Sydney Beatty. I am a researcher with Texas Housers and speaking in favor of item 23. Evictions negatively impact renter physical and mental health, employment and financial stability, and housing stability. These impacts can be long lasting. Research has shown that children in evicted households experience worse educational health and financial outcomes later in life. Evictions to stabilize communities. Rehousing programs for residents facing homelessness due to eviction are more expensive than preventing evictions in the first place. Evictions are also a racial justice issue. Black renters face a 6.2% national eviction filing rate versus 3.4% for white renters. And one in five renters likely to face eviction are black women. Right to cure is an increasingly common approach to eviction protection. New York State and the cities of Chicago, Minneapolis, and San Francisco have all passed right to cure ordinances in the last few years. A key feature of right to cure is that it prevents eviction filings. Even when a judge rules in favor of a tenant, eviction filings can follow tenants for several years and result in rejected apartment applications and housing destabilization. The proposed ordinance helps all us and renters avoid the personal, family, and community harms of eviction and remain stably housed. Thank you. Item 23, Emily Blair, and then Jao Paulo Connolly. Good morning, Mayor and Councilmembers. Thank you for your time. My name is Emily Blair, and I represent the rental housing providers affiliated with the Austin Apartment Association. I'm speaking today on item 23, the notice of proposed eviction. The Austin Apartment Association is unable to support an ordinance mandating additional day's notice for lease violations and non-payment of rent as it is out of sync with the Texas Property Code. But what we can support is alternatives, and specifically the recommended notice of tenants' rights ordinance that was proposed in lieu of this ordinance or a narrow application of this ordinance, for example, to those properties receiving city benefits or city incentives, such as density bonus program participants. We understand that there are some amendments being discussed, and I just want to speak in support of those, including an amendment that would put a maximum number of curing per lease period, for example, for lease violations during a lease term. We look forward to continuing to work with you all on housing items that both support our renters and rental housing providers. Thank you for your time. Thank you. Item 23, Jalpa O'Connelly, followed by Lindsay Haynes. Thank you, Mayor and Council. Good morning, and I am here to speak in favor of item 23 and item 25. I do want to quickly note that additional days to zero is zero days, and so just want to make that clear. I also want to state that Austin right now has over 1,000 active eviction cases right now. So when we talk about preventing homelessness in our community and when we talk about addressing homelessness, the most effective thing we can do long-term to address homelessness is to create solutions that will keep people stably housed for the long term. And so Right to Cure is one of those solutions. It's an important tool. We need to pass it. We need 21-day cure period, and that is more than reasonable. As has been noted, other states and cities all around the country have 21 days for cure, and so I'd like to show my strong support for a 21-day period to cure. I also want to note that Austinites, 55% of Austinites are renters, and yet all too often we do not show up, we do not participate in these conversations, we're not invited. So I'm excited to see all of the renters who have showed up today and who are calling in and adding their voices to this conversation. Thank you. Thank you. Item 23, Lindsay Haynes, followed by Erica Johnson. Hello, my name is Lindsay Haynes, and I'm a general partner on 321 apartments in Austin in Districts 1, 4, and 9. Though I own apartments, I am a very small company, and I provide quality workforce housing because it is my passion. The mortgage on my properties is $210,000. The income potential is $294,000. To pay the mortgage on time and avoid being in default of the loan, 71% of the rent payments would have to be made on or before the first. In workforce housing, that is impossible. We learned in the pandemic that time does not cure rent delinquency. Adding an unproven notice to cure will give residents that regularly pay late the illusion that the rent due date has changed. It will cause me to be in default of my loan every month, jeopardizing the availability of quality affordable housing in Austin by 321 homes. It is also unnecessary. The Travis County Justices of the Peace have proven that they are fair and reasonable in dealings with residents and housing providers. I ask that you trust our elected JPs to use their knowledge of the law and discernment in eviction matters. There's already a natural period to cure with the timing of the courts. Please don't terrify residents with additional notifications. Thank you, Mayor, and Council. Thank you. Item 23, Erica Johnson and then Raul Ubedes. My name is Erica Johnson. I'm a representative of Austin Apartment Association. We would like to speak to the specifics of an alternative policy to have offered, which is working well in other cities such as San Antonio, who's canceled past a similar policy in 2020. This alternative requires rental housing providers to provide defaulting renters a notice of tenants' rights along with the notice to vacate. The notice of tenants' rights documents explains that a notice to vacate is what the eviction process is, what the renter's rights are, and most important, provides the defaulting renters with resources for rental and legal assistance. In other words, it actually points them to real help when they need it most rather than leaving them in the unknown. Anxiety, waiting for three more weeks to pass, or seven weeks if they are a carer's property, with hoping for some kind of solution. None of us in this room want anyone to be evicted, but when it becomes necessary, it should be handled in a way that provides meaningful support and resources within the law. Thank you. Raul Ubedes, and then Katya Watson, item 23. Katya Watson. Good morning, and thank you, Mayor and Councilmembers. My name is Katya Watson, and I represent the rental communities in Austin. I'm here today to speak on item 23, the notice of proposed eviction. I want to speak to the late fee statute under Texas law and bring attention to what is currently in practice. Late fees cannot be charged at least until the fourth day of the month. For example, if rent is due on the 1st of November, the late fee cannot be legally charged until at least November 4th. This grace period already means there is an opportunity

Anti-displacement and equity: Anti-displacement, fair access, tenant stability, or distributional equity.
Housing supply: Policies or projects intended to increase the amount or variety of housing.

chapters.title: Item 32
chapters.text: And now we need to backtrack very slightly to item number 32. And we have two citizens signed up to speak on item number 32. And the first is Debbie Russell, who has signed up neutral. And you have three minutes, Ms. Russell. Thank you. And somebody left their glasses up here. Debbie Russell, Central Texas Chapter, ACLU Texas. And over the last few months, it's become apparent with the Board and Commission appointments, as we've been doing them in bits and pieces, that there is a lack of coordination. And as we're getting our final appointments done here today, and I just want to emphasize that I'm not coming here with any beefs about any particular appointees being made to these Board's commissions, except for in one case in which I'll get into, but there are, it's more about the overall process and the way in which we're getting there. I don't think we're ensuring diversity, broad diversity on each Board or Commission, because none of the Council Members, it seems, are coordinating with the others. There's no one person at the city appointed to oversee the process and to check each person to see if they, in fact, fit the parameters of the ordinance of that Board of Commission. And so, in fact, this list was handed to me at about 10.30 this morning. Y'all aren't even seeing these names most of the time when you're voting on consent, so you're not even knowing who you're voting on unless y'all are getting an earlier version than the public is. Of the appointments. I had suggested a few weeks ago when we did some changes to City Council procedures that we actually look at perhaps doing this all in one shot at one meeting each year that we have a Council election and that spawns more appointments. So that we, that all the Councils turn their names in well ahead of time. We have a few weeks to look at those names to vet that out and that it spawn a public hearing. That one meeting in which you do appoint on the total list. So we can see this as a total, as a whole. So we're not seeing, there's, there's language in the, in the charter that talks about these boards being balanced, being broad in their diversity, so that we can adequately participate in the government, the city's governmental process. And the one example I did want to cite is something that just hasn't been answered yet. The community has talked about, Council Member Cole's appointment of Babette S. Ellis to the Animal Advisory Commission. And her appointment is supposed to have somebody that is an animal welfare organization representative. She owns a dog, a dog grooming business. And I'm not sure how getting the proper poodle cut actually lends towards an animal's welfare. But thus far, we haven't heard any answer from anybody in regards to that question. And, of course, my, my, the thing that led me into this was watching very carefully the appointments to the Public Safety Commission, which I, of course, applied to and hope to be appointed to. And, in fact, was told by police entities that they were assuming I would be on there when we've been talking about bringing things forward to the Public Safety Commission. But we have several organizations. Nobody is representing those organizations. There's a lot of fine people being appointed. But there's no African Americans, no East Siders, nobody from the organizations, although four did apply from those organizations. So I think we need to look more carefully at that, find some solutions, and appreciate your time. Thank you. Thank you, Ms. Russell. Also, Mayor, I think it should be mentioned that Dr. Nelson-Linne, Dr. Linder was offered a position on the Public Safety Commission, as well as me discussing it with Mr. Flynn Lee. But since Flynn is an investigator with the city's HR department, there was some concern by his supervisor in serving in that role. So there were at least two approaches. Dr. Linder respectfully declined because he didn't want to give up his position on the African American Advisory Board. So, you know, we're doing everything I think we can to ensure diversity and make sure that we have a well-represented commission. And with today's appointment of Ramey Coe by Council Member Morrison, we finally have the Public Safety Commission fully appointed. And the mayor and I will be hosting a press conference just to introduce them to the public and let them know that this is our new Public Safety Commission moving forward. Thanks, Mayor. Thank you. Next speaker is Marcello Tafoya. Mayor, I had a comment. Council Member Coe. Ms. Russell, I wanted to tell you a couple of things about my appointee to the Animal Advisory Board. She does represent an animal welfare organization, and we have a certified letter on file in the clerk's office to that effect. And I also presented that to the legal department because that actually is a requirement. And I was told that her service was in compliance with the law. And I also emailed the ethics commission about that based on your email to me. And I thought that you were actually included in that email. I did not realize that you didn't have that information. And I also wanted to let you know that she is a long-standing citizen on the Animal Advisory Commission. She started with Mayor Pro Tem Betty Dunkerley. She was an appointment of Mayor Lee Leffingwell, and now she serves as my appointment. Mr. Tafoya. Welcome. Good morning. Marcel Tafoya with LULAC District 12 as the director. I, too, have concerns over issues when commissions are formed. I will go straight to the point of the Public Safety Task Force. I was there for two years as one of the individuals representing LULAC. We had asked that organizations such as LULAC, NWACP, ACLU, people from EMS, Travis EMS, and Police Department also be part of the task force, although we were told that a lot of those individuals would be coming before the task force. In turn, although the ordinance says may be part of it, I look at the list that was appointed. I don't want to be on it again. Believe me, although I did at one time submit my name, but in reality, two years of work trying to accomplish something and ending up at the other end of it, East Austin organizations such as LULAC, NWACP, who defend East Austin or defend the community, should be somewhere in this commission. We were not at it, so that's fine. I will continue doing what we were doing, but I'm just saying lack of representation of people who actually are involved. When most of the issues, when it comes to safety, are in East Austin, the higher crime rate, the higher drive-bys. We had two in the Latino community of which we stood before the police department asking the community to help us with that, and there was nobody else there except us, so what I'm saying is that when it comes to something as important as public safety, East Austin is in dire need of help. So by not having somebody there that truly represents East Austin community, yes, there is an individual, a Latino there, more involved in other issues than what we are. I still say that lack of organizations that do that kind of work, not being on these commissions, should be considered, and I want to thank you for your time. Thank you, sir. Council Member Morrison. I want to make a few quick comments and thank Ms. Russell and Mr. Tafoya for coming down and raising this issue. I think it's important to realize, from my perspective anyways, our boards and commissions are one of the most important, critical elements of our city government and identifying and appointing or nominating for appointments as a council member is a huge responsibility. It's also a rather large job. I think it's important to point out that, I guess it was in December of 2007, there was a change. I might have the date wrong. There was a change to our boards. It was before Council Member Shade and I got on the council, there was a change to the ordinance that removed, for the most part, consensus appointments, and it also removed requirements for representation from most of the boards and commissions. And there were reasons that the council did that. But I think that both of those were probably things that were in the ordinance that helped ensure diversity. I'm not sure that they were totally effective, and helped ensure that we achieve some of the things that Debbie and Marcella have brought up. So, in a way, we're in a learning curve right now because we're just going through, it's just really the second time after Council Member Shade and I got on the council, and now Council Member Spellman and Riley are on the council. So, I think those are important points. We need to ensure diversity. We're in a learning curve with a new system in place that allows more flexibility, and we should all probably, I hope that we'll all be thinking about and mulling over how we might improve this process. Mayor Pro Tem. Yeah, I want to speak briefly. My appointee to the Public Safety Commission is native Austinite. Moses Saldana, who was born and raised in East Austin, he just happens to live in South Austin now. And Hispanic issues and issues with policing and public safety aren't just East Austin issues. They happen all over the city. And so, I think part of the diversity you have to take in mind is having folks from different parts of the city. So, picking someone who's living in South Austin now, who is a Hispanic, and who was born and raised in East Austin, I think is an ideal candidate for serving on the commission. And I dare you to find anybody that would say that Mr. Saldana won't serve well in that capacity with his commitment to our community. So, I look forward to working with the Public Safety Commission and all of our other boards and commissions. Is it Mr. Saldana also the mayor of South Austin? He is. I thought I'd heard that. Yeah. He carries around business cards, letting you know that. Council, before we take up a possible motion on this item, I'm going to go ahead and read into the record the nominees to the various boards. First, to the 2006 Bond Oversight Committee, Moses Garcia by Council Member Spellman, Paige Hill by Mayor Pro Tem

chapters.title: III.B) Zoning Case PD24-6 (4901 South Cooper Street) - Application for approval of a change in zoning from Community Commercial (CC) to Planned Development (PD) for Community Commercial (CC) uses, for a Restaurant with Drive-Through with a Development Plan to address commercial design standards on approximately 0.611 acres.
chapters.episode_title: Planning and Zoning Commission - Regular Session
chapters.text: Our next zoning case is PD 24-6, addressed at 4901 South Cooper Street. And, again, Mr. Charles will be presenting. It's a public hearing. So, again, first we will have staff preventives report and then I will open the public hearing. We'll hear from any speakers on the case, including the applicant. Speakers in support will go first. Those in opposition, next. If the applicant wishes, he or she will have a final opportunity to address any concerns raised by the commission or members of the public. The public hearing will then be closed and the commission will consider a motion. At this time, Mr. Charles will fill us in. Good evening, Commissioners. For the record, Principal Planner Kevin Charles. As well as planning and development services this evening, we'll be looking at 4901 South Cooper Street, also known as PD 24-6. The site is approximately 0.6 acres. Addressed at 4901 South Cooper Street. The current zoning on the property is community commercial. The request is a PD for community commercial to address the design standards for franchise architecture. As you can see from these photographs, this is a little bit of the development history of the site. The site was developed back in, excuse me, 2000s, in the early 2000s with the big box retail, with restaurants and convenience type uses adjacent to the public right-of-way. That pattern of development has continued in this uniform manner up to the current time, with restaurant and commercial uses continuing to develop both north and south along South Cooper Street. Here you see the site highlighted in yellow. The property to the north of the site is zoned general commercial and currently developed with a restaurant use. The property to the east is zoned community commercial and currently developed as general retail. The property to the south is zoned planned development for neighborhood commercial and is currently developed with restaurants with drive-thru. This site was originally the location of the District 9 fire station prior to its relocation to Harold Patterson's Park at 1000 West Barton Road and was originally zoned residential single family. That's the reason for the PD at this location. And the property to the west across South Cooper Street is zoned community commercial and developed with general commercial uses, including restaurants with drive-thru as well. If we start at the upper left-hand corner and move clockwise, you'll see a photograph of the existing site as it is right now. It's currently just a parking area. Looking north, you'll see a restaurant developed, fully developed. The next photograph shows an existing restaurant across South Cooper Street that is fully developed. And the view to the south is the same with a restaurant with drive-thru. The request, as far as the use is concerned, is consistent with the adjacent uses. And restaurants with drive-thrus uses are allowed by right in community commercial zoning categories. Here's an aerial photograph of the site with the site plan overlaid onto the site. And the intent of this particular slide was to show that the site does not have any direct points of access off of South Cooper Street. The intent is to use the existing access easements, which runs along for the full length of that property to gain access to the site, as well as showing the circulation that's going to be provided for the parking lot to the east. Again, this talks about shows landscaping. As I mentioned before, we did get a revised drawing for that. I did send it to you all with the memorandum. One of the only differences that I really saw for the landscaping was the incorporation of additional landscaping along the island there to the east. However, the applicant is here, and they can specifically identify any other changes that were presented with that new rendering. Okay, so the elevations of the site, excuse me, so these are the elevations or a few of the elevations from the site. As we can see, the applicant proposes a unique design that incorporates a containerized look that they refer to as cans to establish their unique identity. It is their concept to maintain brand recognition by using a painted vertical 1x6 fiber cement rain screen. Again, this is a cementitious fiberboard type of product, so it is an accepted product that covers a minimum of 80% of each building elevation, with the remaining 20% being pre-finished metal panels. What this case is really about is the deviations from our required design standards that are identified by the UDC. We'll try and run through these pretty quickly. Again, 5.6.3 required developments composed of one or two building materials shall be oriented so that the front facade faces the street from which the building derives its street address. As you recall with the elevation drawings that I showed, there is no entry points into the building. Now, I will say that the franchise concept for this is that they do not provide an interior seating because they don't have anyone that will be seated inside. Everything is on the patio. So, the site is not providing access to the inside of the structure. The only entrance provided is for employees due to the nature of the franchise architecture and the concept. That is, small sliders. Section 5.6.4 required flat roofs shall incorporate a parapet that adhere to the articulation requirements for the main facade of the structure. Again, this is a very unique development. The structure is designed to look industrial in nature and proposes no parapets along the roof line. However, they are aware and are providing that all roof-mounted equipment shall be screened from the public right away in the parking lot. Section 5.6.4, materials and colors. No single building material shall cover more than 80% of the front of the building facade. The applicant is proposing a painted vertical 1.6 fiber cement that we spoke of that's going to cover 80% of each building elevation. However, it looks as though on the front elevation, and they can probably clarify this, that it may be 100% of a single material. So, 5.6.4, building materials and cover and colors. Structures 20,000 square feet or less require a minimum of two distinct building materials from the approved material list or preferred material list to be utilized on all facades to provide architectural detail and interest. They are proposing the use of 20% pre-finished metal panels on all elevation. This is now one of our preferred materials that is identified by the Unified Development Code. 5.6.4, again, facade colors shall be low-reflectance, subtle, neutral, or earth-tone colors. The use of metallic colors, black, or fluorescent colors is prohibited. The applicant is proposing the use of orange as the main color. Again, this is their franchise architecture, which they are trying to stick to, which gives them their uniqueness to make them stand out. And finally, 5.6.4K, at least 25% of all walls facing the public street shall contain windows or doorways. There are no street-facing windows or doors based off of the proposed franchise architecture that they sent in or are proposing. The applicant is KFM Engineering and Design. The owner is Slink Holdings, LLC. Staff did receive a letter of support that should have been attached to the staff report. And we are available if there are any questions or comments in reference to this particular project. Thank you, Mr. Charles. Any other questions that didn't come up at work session before we move on here? All right. Thank you. One question. Oh, I'm sorry. Mr. Commissioner Talambas. So, given that this project is in the middle of common access points, will there also be common signage for all these restaurants? No, sir. This is not a unified development. Okay. They would be eligible for their own ground sign and wall signs. They are not tied to any of the other developments that are currently adjacent to them. And also, the other question I have, right now the entire area is blacktop. Yes, sir. Will they be required to rip out all the blacktop and come back in with concrete? Our unified development code identifies approved surface materials as concrete or asphalt. We can, I mean, maybe you would like to make that a stipulation if you feel free to do so. However, the UDC only calls out concrete or asphalt in the code. Okay. Well, they are both approved materials. And I think on either side of the, each restaurant on either side is concrete surface structure. Yes, sir, it is. So, I'll ask the applicant about that. Thank you. You're welcome. Thank you. Other questions? All right. Thank you. Thank you. At this time, I'm going to open the public hearing and call the first speaker. And it looks like I have two speakers and an applicant not wishing to speak. So, Hank Hopkins, would you like to be first? If you'll give us your name and your city of residence. Hi. Good evening. Hank Hopkins, Dallas, Texas. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Charles, for your presentation. And thank you, everybody, for your time. I'm Hank. I'm the franchisee operator of Smalls Sliders. Is there a way to scan through? Okay. There we go. You may ask yourself, you know, what is Smalls Sliders? The purpose of Smalls is to make everyone's day a small bit better through its vision of becoming the cheeseburger brand that shakes up the burger industry. We keep it simple by delivering a craveable cooked-to-order cheeseburger slider to guests as quickly as possible with unexpected guest interactions. Smalls Sliders currently has 12 locations throughout Louisiana and Mississippi with over 200 locations currently in development. This project here will be the first small sliders in the state of Texas. So, we're excited to bring it to the city of Arlington. We keep it real simple, like I said. It's, you know, our menu items, one, two, three, or four cheeseburger sliders. You can upgrade your combos, have a couple of ancillary items, and then we also do our 25 slider party packs that you may be familiar with, like with the Raising Cane's or some other concepts. Why do we stand out? As I mentioned, you know, we're a single product concept. We provide an overall, you know, positive guest experience, similar to what you would see at a Chick-fil-A with our employees out taking orders on iPads, interacting with our guests. We have quality and convenience, and also, you know, at a reasonable price point. So, we like to, you know, as I showed here, we like to categorize ourselves in some of these other brands, Chick-fil-A, Raising Cane's. chapters.text: Is that correct? $3.52 a year? No, $3.52 a month. $3.52 a month. Okay, well, in the line it said annual cost. Oh, did I? That was probably an error then. Still fairly minimal, but anyway, it's good to get that clarified. On reclaimed water, which is a program I totally support, and that's a part of the 2007 recommendations, you mentioned that the cost of reclaimed water is very low, and of course it should be. Are we talking about arriving at a cost of reclaimed water still much lower than treated water that basically reflects the cost of delivery of that? Are we still subsidizing it to some degree? I might have David Anders try that one. With the rate increases that we are projecting through 2016, we project that the total at 2016 would probably still be 50% to 60% of our average potable water rate. And so that still could go up a little bit higher than that, so we could be a little bit more aggressive. But it still provides an incentive for those customers that want to irrigate with reclaimed water as opposed to the higher rates that they would have on the potable water. Yeah, and it's a bargain. It's something, as I said, I totally support because it has an impact on the amount of water that we draw out of the Colorado basin, which in turn has an effect on when we're going to have to start paying for water when we hit that trigger point. So it's all good. I just wanted to ask for clarification if what we're planning on charging, 50%, 60% of the cost of treated water, reflects the cost of building the infrastructure and treating the water to a point where it can be used in that system. Do you understand what I'm saying? I'm back. We could definitely come back on that, but I think there would still be, at 2016, probably some subsidy of the water and wastewater utility of the reclaimed system. Well, again, as I said, I think it's a good thing we ought to continue to do it. We just need to know where we are in relation to cost-benefit. And finally, the question is on the wastewater averaging, what are the three months that we use? It's three months from a billing period of about mid-November to mid-March. But typically, some of them might be mid-November through December and January, and some will start in mid-December or in December, and it would be December, January, and February. So it takes us about five months to get all of the billing cycles to have a three-month period during that time. Yeah, well, I just think it's a good thing for our customers to know exactly when that wastewater averaging period begins, especially if we're going to talk about removing the highest month. And we do bill stuffers and other advertisements so that we try to signal them. I mean that everybody reads those stuffers, yes. I always pour over those myself. Okay, overall, I think it's a great report. I appreciate it. And Mayor? Mayor Mike? I just have a couple of questions. First of all, thank you for the report. It's very informative. It helps me understand the future of our water utility. I want to go back to one of the very early slides, slide 22, because I caught a little something that you said, and I want to get the true impact of our service delivery. You said in that slide where, you know, the vacancy rate is hovering about 10%, that you're finally seeing service delivery being impacted. And I just want to know, I'd like for you to give us an example of what that means. Does it mean a slower response to water main breaks? You know, what exactly does impact on service delivery mean? Yes, we set a goal during the last drought to try to respond to all leaks in the same day. And at the 10% vacancy rate, we're really struggling to keep up with that same-day response goal, and that's really important, particularly if we're in another drought. And, you know, we would like to be able to do that. We implemented a second shift, and, you know, as you have vacancies, it's hard to keep that second shift as focused. So we're then shifting resources around. As an example, one of the things that isn't as urgent is valve turning. We like to exercise our valves on a regular basis, and we set some performance goals there, but sometimes we have to sacrifice those service levels to do a better leak response. You know, hydrants is another high-priority area. We like to put hydrants back in service as soon as possible. So there's other goal areas that we may relax the service level a bit. We sometimes, we might have a maintenance contract that you have in place, and you might say, well, I'm going to skip a year on that maintenance contract. I won't maintain that piece of equipment for one year through a contractual basis. I might try to skip that for a year, and you don't want to keep doing that. I mean, maybe one year is okay, but two years wouldn't be wise, or three years wouldn't be wise. So it's a combination of those factors, but particularly in our pipeline area. I mean, if my AD here, George Calhoun, would say, you know, that he's really struggling to keep up with some of the service areas, because pipeline grows every year. I mean, every year our network gets bigger. It gets more geographically dispersed. There's more travel time to get to that, and he's probably carrying now, geez, 50, 60 vacancies, and that's a lot, and we just don't want to stay in that state of affairs chronically. And I agree with you. So what I'd like for us to keep in mind as we go through this budget process, city manager, is that I think there's an economies of scale that we tip over where by having this many vacancies, it's actually costing us money because we're not able to respond and mitigate, you know, water leaks and water mains that break. So I want us to keep that in mind. And if we are reaching that tipping point, it might be prudent for us to fill those vacancies and actually save money by hiring more employees as opposed to this little savings, this little vacancy savings we're creating but costing ourselves exponentially more in lack of response to service. And it's another example of, like, the concept of volatility. The need to repair our system and respond to leaks rapidly doesn't change with how much water we sell each year, but our revenues can go up and down. And so, you know, when you lose $53 million in a year, I mean, you kind of have to deal with that. And, you know, one of the ways we do that is by manipulating vacancies a bit. And, you know, I'd like to decouple that a little bit where we could. Sure. So. I appreciate it. The other question I had was regarding the sustainability fee. I do think that that is an area we need to begin discussing, and obviously you're making that proposal this year. But I wanted to ask, does something like a sustainability fee, would it have to go to the Public Utility Commission for approval? No, we check with law, and this is something that we can implement as a home rule utility, that it's really at the council's discretion. Now, jump in, David. That's correct. But is there any exposure to a potential appeal of initiating such a fee, and would that go to PUC, or would it have to go to court? I'm just trying to look at any potential exposure we might have with creating this, because I can certainly see a lot of folks in the community not being happy with this new fee. Where we are at risk from a legal perspective on our rate challenges would be that our outside city customers or our wholesale customers that would be charged this fee could challenge our rates. Now, this proposal assumes that we do not charge this particular fee to our wholesale customers, so we would try to deal with them from a volatility standpoint in another manner, like just raising their regular minimum charge a little bit higher. But our outside city customers, which we have a few thousand of those customers, they could challenge our rates to the, not to the PUC. We don't, they, the TCEQ actually looks at our rates if they challenge, and our outside customers would have to get a petition of at least 10% of the outside customers would have to sign a petition and send that to the TCEQ to challenge our rates. And then typically at that time, we would work with those customers to come to some sort of a settlement before it would go through a complete rate challenge. But that's the risk that we would have. But I would add the fee, the numbers are real. I mean, it's justified. And by implementing it based on your meter size, that's a cost of service type implementation, which is the standard you need to meet. So implementing this fee, we think, would meet any legal standard that we may have to work through. Could I, I'm just following that a little bit. As I said, the things that are paid for with the sustainability fee are not core utility functions. So if it came right down to brass tacks, the alternative of the water utility could be to not perform these functions at all, to not incur these expenses at all. So if you didn't have the fee, you wouldn't perform that service. You would not maintain the wildlands division, for example, within the water utility. That'd have to be funded in some other way. And that is, to me, that is the alternative. Yeah. And Greg, in the absence of the fee, why don't you remake your point about what happens to rates? Well, without the funding of the fee, assuming we didn't drop any of these services, I think the other response would be you could just raise the volumetric percentage higher. That would be another way to respond. So this helps balance between those two. To me, it's transparency. You know, what are we spending this money on? People know what they're spending their money on, and then they have some basis for making a decision about it. And then just a brief comment to follow up on Mike's remarks

chapters.title: 6. Proposal to Sell Tax Foreclosed Properties - Jay Chapa, Director, Housing and Economic Development Department
chapters.episode_title: HOUSING AND ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT COMMITTEE HOUSING AND ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT COMMITTEE
chapters.text: Mr. Jay Chapa, Director of Housing and Economic Development Department. Good afternoon. It's a really big presentation. It will take a little bit as far as size of bites. This afternoon, I'm going to go through a proposal from city staff on how to move forward with exposing of tax for closed properties. We're going to provide a recommendation, go over some of the basis for the recommendation. Then also what we're going to propose is we have target areas that we target in each district for development and for land banking, and then a timeline to implement the plan. The issue is on tax for closed properties is that it results in lost tax revenues, of course. Maintenance costs for the city go way up. We have illegal dumping and illicit uses, especially with the amount of tax for closed properties we currently own. It is very difficult to manage the amount that we have with our current resources. And then there's a loss of opportunity for development when we just hold them because of our concern for what could result in the type of development that could go there. Our recommendation is to create target development areas, and we're going to be proposing some here in a minute for each district that we'll use for land banking for our infill and community development side. And we will target those areas for redevelopment and development overall. We will allow only direct sales in those, direct sale properties in those targeted areas so that we can ensure quality development. And then we'll use priority foreclosures as we go forward in those areas to try to land bank where we do have back taxes on property so that we can put larger tax of property together so that we can try to bring in developers to help us do the development. And then finally, we would have a mass, especially on the front end, you'll see in a minute the amount of properties we have, a citywide bid sale for all the properties that are not in the target area so we can get those back on the tax rolls as soon as possible, and then we can spend more time trying to target those areas for development with our current folks. These are maps outlining all those red dots that you see here, and I'm going to run through these pretty quickly. But these are the properties that are in foreclosure in each district. This is District 2, Councilman Espeno's. District 3, Councilman Zimmerman's. District 4, Councilman Skarth's area. You'll see there's the red dots here. Councilman 5, Councilman Moss's area. You see a concentration here. Councilman Jordan's in 6, 7, 8, and then 9. All those red dots that you saw there look like measles were basically about 1,030 properties, 1,027 properties with a TAD value of about $22 million. We don't believe that's very accurate because they have been on our books for so long. TAD just doesn't go back and revalue them because they're not currently taxable. And you can see the breakdown of the properties, where they're located, and you see some concentration of the properties in District 2, 5, and 8. If we were to take those properties there and basically what we're proposing is about 75% of the properties would be sold, our estimate is that we could add $141,000 or so to the city's coffers. And a lot of those properties and the majority of those properties are vacant. So we believe that once you get some of those turned around and some development occurred to them, there would be a lot more annual dollars there. And then on the actual sale, we believe since we'd be doing bid sales and we would just take the best bid, we wouldn't put any minimum requirements on it, we believe about $1.8 million would come to the city. The overall sale of these properties would be about $5.9 million, but the city only receives about 30% of those revenues because you break it out to all the taxing entities would receive the remainder of that. So 75% of these properties, our estimate is that nearly $1.8 million could come to the general fund next year if we went forward with this plan. Going into the actual expenses that we incur on an annual basis, these are the departments that are most impacted by the whole system, including my department. We didn't put that on there because we do manage the properties. We have four land agents, and each of them is assigned two of the council districts. But the police department, really their issues has to do with calls that come from the issues that happen on these tax-for-closed properties. During the last six years, seven years, there's been nearly 7,000 calls concerning police issues. On the fire department side, they've responded to 230 incidences in the last three and a half years or so, and they've actually broke out how those work and what the costs are. And as you can see there, when you break it out by incident, it's about $222,000 has been spent, the fire department responding to those 230 calls. The parks department does the mowing for us. You can see in the last year or this current year alone, nearly $550,000 was spent on mowing. Code compliance, who does the board-ups and fix-ups on those properties, $16,000 to date. They also deal with cleanup and abatement when there's dumping and those kind of things. And the environmental department gets calls for illegal dumping and also on the properties that we have. And finally, they also have to go through and pay the cost of cleaning those up. At times, we have had squatters move into tax-for-closed properties. And when we find that, because of the liability that the city could incur, we have to move forward to try to get those squatters out of the homes. So we have eviction costs that occur there. There's an example here. An eviction costs us nearly $5,000 to get folks out of there. Now, going forward, what we're proposing is that each council district have two, maybe three, target areas. And Cynthia's going to pass out some bigger maps for your individual council district so you can see it up close. These magenta or purple lines you see here are what staff is proposing be our targeted areas. The green circles that you see there are proposed future TODs. Those we are recommending would become automatic target areas where we would do priority foreclosure. You're not going to see many foreclosures in those, but we would be targeted priority foreclosures in that area so we could land bank for future TOD-type development. So those green dots are kind of by default, but these maroon or purple lines that you see here, squares, is what we're proposing that each district we would have the priority central city or community development occur. That was District 2. This is District – oh, this is a close-up of District 2. So you can see where the areas are. The areas on Northside Drive, just west of 35W, the area over on Northside Drive, which includes a West Haven project where we're trying to get a project created, and then the Six Points area here. District 3, we're proposing that the western end of the Camp Bowie development, where it's not really as active as further east of there, be a targeted area. So if tax foreclosed properties would come in that area, that we would only do direct sales so that we could hopefully control the type of development. They went there and make sure that it was quality. It's a close-up of that. District 4. District 4. District 4, we're proposing the area just east of Woodhaven, along I-30 – I-20, the Woodhaven redevelopment area, and then the commercial area around – or just south of White Lake Hills. Of course, part of the Six Points is in here, too, so it would also be involved. This is a close-up of those areas. District 5, we're proposing areas in the Stop 6 area where there is already a lot of vacant land and tax foreclosed properties. We'd like to continue that land banking and actually try to get interest from developers to move in there. And we also – the HFC has a project, the Burger Street project, for infill housing that's going to be moving forward. And then the area here just south of Barrie, along Miller, between 27, where Mr. Moss has a commercial redevelopment activity going. And in this case, we'd also keep the old Cowtown Inn site, just to protect the uses there. This is a close-up of those two areas. District 6, we're proposing the Altamesa-McCartt Avenue intersection in that area where there's a lot of vacant retail that we want to target in there and make sure we are able to control the types of uses that go in there. There's a close-up of that. District 7, we're proposing the Como area where we have the bulk of those, but we'd like to have an infill project in the future, next year or two, that we can move forward, maybe with some help of developers, to go through and start utilizing some of that vacant property, sort of infill housing. That's a close-up of that site. And then District 8, we are targeting the East Barrie-Renaissance TIF area and the Terrell Heights, where we'd like to begin an infill project as we move forward. Close-up of those. And then District 9, we are proposing the Magnolia-Rosedale Corridor and the South Hemphill area as two of the target areas for that district, and that's a close-up of there. Now, the issue is that those areas that I showed, everything outside of those blocks and or the TODs, we would actually go forward with the bid sale. And so all those other properties would go out for sale. In the past, I think we've ended up with so many properties because of the concern associated with this type of housing that has occurred. And you all saw this. It's almost all this coming together in that the DAC came in last week and had a presentation on this and on the issues that we're trying to solve. And because of those issues, there's been holds by city council members. There's been concerns from communities on the sale of these properties that we're going to end up with this type of development that are somewhat modern-day shotgun shacks. This house here, you have to walk through a bedroom to get into the living room. And then you walk through the living room
