chapters.text: Hello, sir. Mr. Van Dino. All right. Uh, well, welcome back, Mayor, Mayor Pro Tem, members of the Council. Again, I'm Ed Van Dino, Deputy CFO and Budget Officer for the city. Our, uh, next policy discussion for today is, um, is a very important one. One about our city's Health and Human Services Department, um, and our social service contracts that we support in this city. Uh, the programs provided by the Health and Human Services Department, some of the challenges we're facing in this area across the community and, and some of the funding needs. And, um, I'm joined today by our Director of Health and Human Services, Shannon Jones, um, and Assistant Director, Kimberly Maddox, and Assistant Director, Stephanie Hayden. They're going to do the, uh, um, all of the present, presenting here. But I did want to start this presentation off with, um, you know, just a little bit of an acknowledgement that, that, uh, we as staff are 100% aware that this is a high priority for the city council. So we know that because we have at least three, I think actually four different resolutions that have been passed over the years from, uh, this council and earlier councils indicating a desire to increase funding, um, in these areas. And we also witnessed last year as part of the budget adoption, uh, this city council made significant increases in the funding for Health and Human Services and social service contracts over and above, uh, increases that city staff, um, um, had already, had already proposed in the proposed budget. So again, um, we're well aware that this is an important topic. And so the policy discussion here, um, for us isn't so much of does council feel that these services are important, but, um, you know, you've seen a lot of the dynamic here that in any budget we end up with priorities that are beyond our ability to fund all of them. So I think really the policy question here is about, um, the degree that these are our priority relative to, you know, perhaps desires to see, um, tax rates, um, be held low or desires to see homestead exemptions be increased, senior exemptions to be increased. Um, um, um, you know, you saw last week we had presentations about significant needs in, uh, facilities maintenance and IT needs. And so we're really just really need to hear from council, um, to have you all help us prioritize, um, the desire to increase funding in these areas. I mentioned these various resolutions, uh, prioritize increases in these areas against all these other needs. And I, I mentioned those resolutions, um, we sent out a memo perhaps a month or two ago indicating that if we were to stay on track with all the different funding goals that were established in those resolutions, we would need to increase funding in fiscal year 17, um, for health and human services and social service contracts by $8.3 million. Over and above any built-in cost drivers for wages and health insurance, we would need to increase $8.3 million over and above those amount in order for us to keep pace with these goals that have been laid out by council, uh, vis-a-vis these various resolutions. So I just wanted to introduce this topic in the, in that way and, um, I don't know if there's any questions about that. If not, I'll just pass it over to Shannon to, to take you through the presentation. Uh, good morning. I'm Shannon Jones, as, uh, Edith says, uh, director of Austin-Travis County Health and Human Services Department. I'm joined here also by our deputy director, Stephanie Hayden, and our assistant director, um, Kimberly Maddox. I'd like to start off by saying that Austin-Travis County is one of the healthiest, fittest, and wealthiest communities in this state and in this nation. And that's important to understand as we talk about the role of health and human services in addressing the issues we face in our community. Today, we will give you a road map that outlines and overviews some of the issues and challenges we face in our community, despite falling in those categories. We have significant areas that we have to work on, and so we will talk about those as we look at and address the issues we face. I will define the social determinants of health would play a critical impact in terms of the conditions that we find in our areas. We will focus on, despite being one of the healthiest, wealthiest, and fittest, significant disparities in our community. There are significant, stark differences within our community, despite the overall health of our community. We will look at chronic disease epidemics among populations of color. We will look at our role in public health preparedness, threats such as Ebola, chikungunya, Zika, and we'll talk about efforts to address key issues that we face in the budget process regarding current funding and council resolutions that have been put forth. When we look at Austin and Travis County, and particularly Austin, we look at it primarily in terms of demographics. And if you look at the slide here, what we see is what our city demographer provided for us. In 2000, roughly the Asian American landscape in terms of population was primarily north and west in our community. We've seen over time that migration, as in all population, further in and certainly on the north side of our community. District 6 has a significant number of the Asian American population, close to 15%. District 7 and 9 are close at 10%. When we look at our Hispanic population, here we see the changing demographics among Hispanics from 2000 to 2010. If you look at that very clearly, we see particularly in the inner city core of Austin, a diminution of that population moving further to the east and northeast, as well as south, within the city of Austin. We look at this by share, by district. What we clearly see is district 2 has the largest percentage of Hispanic population, followed closely by district 4 and district 3, and followed by district 1. And yet, throughout all of our districts, we see the Hispanic population has a significant population number in terms of those districts. When we look at the African American population, we see clear diminution of the African American population within the center core of Austin between 2000 and 2010. Basically, that population has significantly been moved outside of the center core and more for the east and northeast part of the county. When we look at population, clearly, we see that district 1 has by far the largest population of African Americans. However, district 4, district 2, district 3, and district 7 all have relatively larger numbers of African Americans in those districts, as well. The Health and Human Services Department provides services throughout the city of Austin and Travis County. However, if you look at historically our service model, what we see is that most of the services historically have been provided on a line roughly 600 yards off of I-35 corridor. And so, as a result, over time, we've had to expand and look at other areas to do that. Towards those efforts, we provide services in various community settings, including churches, recreational centers, schools, and at local shopping centers, such as Walmart and HEB, as an effort to reach out to the changing demographics and changing locations of communities. Health and Human Services is partnering with our assistive department, parks and recreation, and community care to deliver services both in Colony Park, Runburg, Dove Springs, and Santa Barbara in the eastern part of the county. In an effort to provide those services in the new areas that we've identified with the changing demographics. HHSC is to identify future facility needs as we go forth with developing our capital plan for expanding services for this changing demographics. I'd like to spend a little time briefly talking about the social determinants of health. It is important to recognize that many factors affect the health in terms of our communities, not just health care. The environment, lifestyle, behavior, genes, and other factors play significant roles in terms of that. Poverty and unemployment, or employment where exists, also plays a significant role in terms of the health outcomes of our community. An example, an adult 25 or older without a high school diploma are primarily located in certain parts of our community. We look at districts, we see District 1, 2, 3, and 4 have significant populations that do not have a minimum of a college degree. We look at District 2, 1, 23.8% has. We look at District 2, 24% has. District 4, 22% has. District 5, 43% has. So we see that there are significant differences in terms of educational levels. We look at poverty, particularly District 3 has a significant, Department of District 4 has a significant burden, as well as District 3 in terms of poverty. One in four children in Travis County live in poverty. One in four in this county, one of the wealthiest counties we see. And children under the age of six are the fastest-growing living in poverty. One-third of Travis County residents are low-income. That means they're 200% of poverty or below. That includes, for the definition that may not be familiar, a family of four with an income of less than $24,000 living in poverty in our community. In this community of affordability, that's a real challenge for our community. When we look at the median family income by district in our community, over the last 10 years, rents have risen 50%, while the median income rose roughly 9%. The median family income is lowest in Districts 1, 2, 3, and 4, primarily those on the eastern part of the county, which means the average income in these districts are below the poverty level. When we look at our investments in terms of trying to address some of these, we see clearly that the department, over many years and currently, are focusing in on those areas. Basic needs, funding in the neighborhood of over $8 million. Behavioral health, $3 million. Children and youth, $6 million. HIV. Travis County has the third highest rates of HIV in our state, as we'll talk about in a few moments. We currently have investment in closely to $600,000 in our social service investments. Homeless services, $5 million. Workforce, $3 million. So there are significant investments in these areas. National studies have indicated that demonstrated investments in these areas have significant return on those investments. Every dollar invested in workforce program returns $2.74 over 10 years. chapters.text: Now that we're all here, before we get to our cases, we do have a presentation. Mr. Yeah, Mr. Sure. Come on. Well, we were nodding at each other in a friendly manner. I thought that was it. Just make sure the line is on on the microphone. There we go. But I have a presentation. It's actually a voice. Okay. It's my presentation. The city council back in May. About saving city all. Yeah, I can't hear. You may need to point that up to your mouth. Well, it's not. This will speak for me. The project is a bold architectural proposal presented to Mayor Johnson and the city council to reimagine Dallas City Hall by preserving and revitalizing the existing historic I. M. P. designed building. Instead of demolition, the plan calls for the restoration and modernization of the iconic brutalist style structure after the completion of a complimentary addition. This new addition takes the form of an inverted C, which, when combined with the original linear city hall, creates a powerful symbolic gesture. The letter D representing Dallas. The project transforms city hall into a renewed civic campus that preserves architectural integrity, strengthens functionality, and enhances public engagement, aligning with Dallas greening initiatives through renovation and adaptive reuse. The new design features clearly defined public, private, and secured zones to ensure an efficient and transparent civic environment, meeting modern operational and security standards. Once the addition is complete, all 43 city office divisions could be consolidated there, allowing the original historic building to undergo thoughtful renovation without interrupting municipal operations. The addition is also envisioned as the first net-zero ready-mass timber civic building in Dallas, targeting high certifications like LEED Gold slash Platinum and LEED Zero Energy, distinguished by its curved form geometry and large roof wing accommodating solar panel arrays. The design utilizes a monolithic concrete base to honor the original building's materiality, and sets up an architectural dialogue with nearby projects like the Dallas Memorial Arena renovation and the KBH CCD master plan. A key feature is the elevated public courtyard between the two structures, which will be a dynamic civic green and event space. A thoroughfare street will preserve short-term parking and service access, but is intentionally designed to close for large-scale city events like the Dallas Marathon or festivals, transforming into a pedestrian promenade. The project is positioned as an urban anchor to help reconnect downtown Dallas to the Cedars, Deep Ellum, and South Dallas neighborhoods. Architectural designer Rand Scheer, the proponent of the project, argues that preservation with thoughtful evolution is the path forward, not demolition. He urges the Council to vote no on demolition and yes on the Big D project, calling it a win-win-win opportunity for heritage, civic identity, and future generations. That's it. I'm basically here to try to save City Hall and also be, let me say that I'm against any kind of demolition by neglect and so the letter I wrote today was speaking on that regard. I know that in August, I believe, they had come with a commission. I don't know if they went in front of the commission or not, but they were talking about demolition by neglect and from my history, I know that demolition does not work. Demolition by neglect does not work. It doesn't preserve the new building or the old building. It doesn't do anything but keep it in a stable, locked state for nothing to get done until it gets knocked down. So that's pretty much. That is your time, sir. Well, thank you, sir. Obviously, the commission has already expressed its concern for the preservation of City Hall by our initiation of it to be a city of Dallas landmark. Is that me? And until we, you know, at this point, there's not much in our purview anymore to do about it. But we have all been following closely the various arguments and events that have been occurring related to City Hall. Well, I came to make my statement and then also to have you follow the design because I'm already in the fourth generation of this design. And hopefully it'll go public and hopefully they'll have other architects come together to come up with ideas to keep City Hall here in Dallas. Thank you. And we wish you luck on that. This might be a good time for a little update for commissioners is that we have started the demolition by neglect investigation. And so we've started with our first meeting with facilities and we are reviewing the report from the building. All right. Thank you, Marcus. I know that's quite a legal path. Would it be appropriate for the landmark vision to have a support statement for saving the building and doing an addition to it? I don't think that's appropriate at this time. We've already essentially made our statement for the value of preserving it by initiating it. But at this point, it's probably we've done what we can do and other parts of the city government are now discussing what they're going to do. Thank you. I think we've made our opinion clear. Can this commission vote on the big D project? We cannot. No. Okay. I think it wasn't on our agenda, but we cannot vote on anything like that for this ongoing. Okay. Thank you. But as you said, you're exploring the demolition by neglect. Any other questions? I think that's it. Okay. Nice to see you guys again. Bye.

chapters.title: Item Z28
chapters.text: Item Z-28 is a public hearing and an ordinance granting a CR, Community Retail District, and a resolution accepting deed restrictions volunteered by the applicant on property on the south side of Greenville Avenue, east of Lyndon B. Johnson Freeway. Mr. Mayor, we sent ten notices to property owners within 300 feet of the area of request. We received zero replies in favor of the request and zero replies in opposition. You do have two individuals who have registered to speak on this item. Each speaker will be given three minutes to speak. First speaker, Andrew Rueg. Good afternoon, Mr. Mayor, Honorable City Council Members. This is Andrew Rueg, 2201 Main Street, Dallas, Texas, 75201, representing the property owner in this request. This is a, just to kind of give you a really quick overview, this was a site that was impacted by the 2019 tornado, which caused the building to, the existing office building on site to be damaged beyond repair. So, this is an effort to redevelop and revitalize the area with a mix of personal service uses for the benefit of the surrounding community. We did volunteer some deed restrictions at City Plan Commission, and I'd like to thank Council Member McGue for working with us to further refine those deed restrictions. And I'd like to read our amended and expanded deed restrictions into the record. For condition number two, I'd like to amend that to read the maximum number of restaurants with drive-in or drive-through service use permitted on the property is three. I'd like to volunteer a condition that a minimum, a minimum of 350 square foot outdoor patio area must be installed in conjunction with each restaurant with drive-in or drive-through service use and restaurant without drive-in or drive-through service use. Add a volunteer condition that states pedestrian connections to adjacent office uses and open space areas are required. And finally, add another condition stating, if the most easterly parcel of the property is not being developed within six months of the issuance of a final certificate of occupancy for the adjacent parcel to the west, the most easterly parcel must have a sod and a minimum of two of the following pedestrian amenities installed as a temporary use until work commences for the development of the most easterly parcel. And those pedestrian items would include benches, pedestrian lighting, walking trail, trash receptacles, or bicycle parking. So that's the revised volunteer deed restrictions with this case. Again, I'd like to thank Council Member McHugh for working with us on this and happy to answer any questions should you have any. Thank you. Thank you. Dallas Cawthorne is not present. There are no further speakers, Mr. Mayor. All right. Do we have a motion? Oh, is there anyone in the audience who wishes to speak? Oh, it's, oh, yeah. Thanks, Chris. Thank you, Chris. He's watching out for us. That being said, we have a motion. I move to approve the zoning change as recommended by the City Planning Commission with the amended deed restrictions volunteered today by the applicant. Motion to second. Discussion? Just quickly, I want to thank the development team and Andrew for your work on this. I think we've made some improvements and look forward to moving it forward. Thank you. All right. With that being said, all those in favor, say aye. Any opposed? Motion carries. Next item. Item Z-29 is a public hearing and one, an ordinance granting an MF-2A multifamily district and two, a resolution terminating deed restrictions on property on the west line of Mark Trail Way southeast of Swansea Street.

chapters.title: C. ID 17-761 Receive a report; hold a discussion, and receive departmental presentations in preparation for the FY 2017-18 Proposed Budget, Capital Improvement Program, and Five Year Financial Forecast.
chapters.text: in preparation for the FY 2017-18 proposed budget, capital improvement program, and five-year financial forecast. We want you to sing your presentation. It's going to take too long for that one. I'm sorry. Good afternoon. I'm Emerson Vorl, Director of Parks and Recreation. Thanks for the opportunity to run through the budget with you today. I'll try to be brief. Our 17-18 budget, starting with general fund, FTEs, you'll see a couple of reductions up there. Those relate to an admin. Two of our positions went to facilities management to help us handle our CIP projects in the future. We moved that over to facilities to take advantage of their skill. One of those positions went back to park maintenance. That's the increase that you see there in park maintenance. You'll also see a reduction in aquatics. We actually had a retirement of a custodian out at the water park, and we elected to contract that position instead of refilling it so that FTE, the funds from that FTE are used to contract that out, and there's a savings here that we'll get to as we progress. Organizational chart, Parks and Recreation split up pretty much three ways. On the left, park maintenance, 46 full-time, 1.36 temp seasonal positions. Our admin there in the middle was six full-time positions and a half of a temp seasonal position. And then on the leisure services side, 31.5 full-time positions and a whole bunch of temp seasonals. That's 72.37. Most of those folks do not work for us year-round. That's how we get to between 200 and 300 folks that we hire every summer to work our summer camps and to work at the aquatic facilities. Some accomplishments that we've already been able to complete this year. Of course, we opened the wave pool a couple of weeks ago. We've completed a departmental strategic plan that Pat Smith from Serve Denton was kind enough to help facilitate. We replaced a playground at Evers Park. We replaced a playground at the north end of Southlakes Park, the London area playground. We've installed some shade at the golf driving range. One of our folks, Chris Escotto, won a regional award from TRAPS, a Horizon Award in TRAPS as our State Recreation and Park Society. We also won a regional award for excellence in programming, a design award for the work that was done last year at Civic Center Pool. We won a media award at the state level for the work that we did on Eureka II. A good one, a fun one that we did this year, we partnered for the first time with the AmeriCorps Summer Vista Program. That allowed us to add some staff positions to our summer camps. It allowed some folks to also to get some work and some employment this summer. This year that was free to us. I'm not sure we're going to be quite that fortunate next year, but it was a great program. It's been a great program. It's worked very well for us. It allowed us to put some more hands and some more eyes on our summer camp programs at no additional cost. So that's been a good one for us. A couple of things that we want to try to still accomplish this year. We're going to complete construction of the concession stand at Waterworks Park. We're hard at it with that one. The construction of the 9-11 Firefighters Memorial in front of Fire Central. That's in progress. Replace is probably the wrong word at this point. Launch our new registration software for our department. We're real excited about this one. There's been a ton of work that's going on behind the scenes. Anytime you make a shift in software, there's a lot of data that has to migrate from one system to the other. And we're just about ready to go live with that. We'll talk a little bit more about that. We'll get the spray ground completed at Carl Young. We broke ground for that the other day. We'll get that completed in September. And we have an athletic field that will be playable in Carl Young Park. I'm sorry, Fred Moore Park. This September. Time for some football. Goals for 17-18. We want to complete construction of the trail that we've been working on. That was a $1.3 million grant. About a $1.6 million project. That trail extends from Evers Park all the way up to UNT. And then ultimately over to North Lakes. We want to start construction of the Vela Soccer Complex out at North Lakes. Also on the south side of the McNatt Animal Adoption Facility, we want to build the city's second dog park. We are funded in the CIP to start design work for the city's new tennis center. With rec fund money, we're going to replace marquees at all four of our recreation centers and the civic center. They have timed out. They're not functional anymore. We'll use some funds to do that. With the funds that council has given us and some CIP money, we'll make improvements at Oakwood and IOOF cemeteries. We're going to build a restroom at Carl Young Park. That will be in conjunction after we build the spray ground. We'll come back and build that restroom. And in the CIP, we are funded to replace playgrounds at Dena and Fredmore Parks. Council Member Briggs, do you have a question? Will there be a part in the presentation where we can ask specifics about these items listed or is now the time to do that? Now would be the time. Okay. About the dog park. Yes, ma'am. Because I've had, it's been on people's radar for a long time. Yes, ma'am. And I've had questions from my constituents in anticipation about when it's going to be open. So do you have any more specific information on a complete, estimated completion or start or? I don't at this time. We initially thought we were going to jump out and do that project in-house. And as we did a little bit more homework on it, we decided because of the parking lot and the lighting involved, that it would be best if we took that through the planning process, did a site plan and all the approvals that would go with it. So right now we're waiting on a proposal from Teaknall Perkins to help us with that part of the process. And I'm going to hold off on comments on timing until we see that from them. Okay. I can tell you it's moving forward. You're just not seeing any dirt turning. That's all. Okay. Thank you. Council Member Gregory. Thank you, Mayor. We acquired some property on Industrial Street for a pocket park. Yes, sir. Do we have any goals for that in the coming year? There are no funds identified for that at this point. I have been meeting. I've had some requests. I've been meeting with folks over there on Industrial Street, the Industrial Street Guild, talking about some potential designs. But at the moment, there are no funds identified. I did get a form today to talk about the TIF and maybe requesting some funds from the TIF that could be applied toward that. Along those lines, did we use money from the parks dedication fees? Yes, sir. Development fees to purchase that property? That property was purchased with park dedication fees. And so have we basically exhausted that money for that sector of TIF? Well, I'll jump ahead here a little bit. If you recall, there are two fees, park dedication and park development. The dedication is supposed to either the developer would give us property or give us cash in lieu of. The park that's dedication, the development fee are the dollars that we use to construct the parks. There are some park development dollars that are available to use. All those dollars have geographic restrictions on them. Currently, they must be expended within a mile of where those dollars were generated. And we're actually in some discussions right now with our legal staff to look at maybe making some changes to that, to expanding that a little bit so that some of those dollars could be more readily used. Well, we've received some of those fees from apartments that have been built in the district. Yes, sir. We have used, but we've also used some within a mile of that park. Fred Moore, Carl Young parks are both within that distance. So, you know, some of those dollars have been used. And just along with that, in terms of money to do those kinds of things, at the present time, do we have any policies in place if a major donor, if a corporation or a foundation wanted to donate, you know, $100,000 or $250,000 or a million dollars for a park development, do we have any policies in place that would allow a recognition by naming the facility or naming it for a limited period of time after the donors? The city has a naming policy. And I'm fond of saying it goes through all of the text in the last line. It says basically council can do whatever they choose to do. Okay. So should that person with a million dollars come forward, it would wind up in your laps to make a decision on that. Okay. Thank you. Yes, Mayor Porte. I have a question about some of the different park funds. So, for instance, I know with the Splash Park, we utilize some of the recreation funds to pay for the overage over what was fundraised and the bond. And so we have about $500,000 left in the recreation fund. What are some of the things that can be used with the recreation fund? Well, the rec fund, and I don't know that we used a lot of rec fund to do the Splash Park. Okay. There's a couple other funds if you want to go through them. Okay. And I'm going to get to those later in the presentation. Let's hold off on the rec fund. I've got a slide on that. Okay. And I'll speak to that in a minute here. I'll hang tight then until we get to the slide. Thank you, Mayor. I have a question about the Legion Hall. Is that going to be in this presentation? This will not be in this presentation. Okay. That's a capital. I'm sorry. It's a supplemental that I think you're going to see. And I'm going to look for a head nod from Chuck. That's going to show up when Chuck addresses supplemental packages with you all at a future date. Okay. Got it. It is in the

chapters.title: Item 20
chapters.text: Okay. So we're going to move forward with item number 20. Mr. Guernsey, you want to lay that out? Yes. Um, thank you. Um, item number 20 is case C14-2015-0133A. Uh, this is at 1204, um, San Antonio Street. Um, it's proposed for downtown mixed use zoning and the, uh, Planning Commission, uh, recommended the, uh, downtown mixed use zoning or DMU CO, um, with a condition, uh, that was placed on the height of, uh, six or excuse me, 90 feet. And that the, uh, additional uses would be made prohibited, including bail bond services, cocktail lounge, pawn shop, liquor store, and outdoor entertainment, and also prohibiting, uh, amplified sound, uh, on the premises. Uh, the property is about 11,000 square feet in size, and it's located within the downtown planning area. Uh, the staff recommendation was for 60 feet instead of, uh, uh, 90 as suggested by the, uh, commission. And originally the, uh, applicant was not asking for a height limitation, which could take heights up to, uh, 120 feet, but the applicant is now agreeable to the, the 90 feet. Uh, there's existing development of a one-story office, and there's a variety of office buildings that surround this on all sides. Uh, the, um, zoning for the most part in the area, uh, is zoned GEO, um, or, uh, LRCO, and there's some, uh, DMU as well, uh, in this area. Um, as, as I said, it was in the downtown, uh, planning area, and it's in the Northwest District that was adopted by plan in, in, uh, 2011. Um, being in an area where most of the height restrictions under the GEO and LR, uh, would be 60 feet or, or less. In height, uh, staff recommended the 60-foot height limitation. It was part of the adopted plan. It's, uh, similar to the zoning in the area. In addition, this would be probably more sympathetic to the historic structures, uh, that are, that are nearby. Um, I'll pause if, uh, you have any questions. Uh, Alice Glasgow is, uh, here with Alice Glasgow Consulting to speak on behalf of the owner, and I believe we've got some neighbors here that would also like to address you on this case. Any questions before we move forward with the testimony? Okay. None. Okay. Ms. Glasgow. And, let's see, is Kim LaPierre here also? And, Josh Benavides? Okay. So, Ms. Glasgow, you have nine minutes. Thank you. I just want to mention, too, we're talking about tract A. Okay. So, as you're looking at your backup, for your ease, we actually combine both items 21 and 20 in your backup, but we're talking about tract A at, uh, 1204 San Antonio. So, just so we're clear. Good afternoon, council members. Alice Glasgow representing the Texas Association of Counties. Just a little history about the, um, association. The Texas Association of Counties was formed in 1969 in order to improve and promote the value of county government on a statewide basis. TAC is the representative voice for all Texas counties, all 254 counties in Texas. Through TAC, counties communicate the county perspective to state officials and the general public. This cooperative effort is managed by a board of county officials, and every county is represented on the board. The board establishes the scope of TAC services and the amount of money that will be allocated to provide services. The services that are provided by TAC include a toll-free legal hotline, training, continuing education programs, representation at the state and federal government levels, health and employment benefits, risk management pool, unemployment compensation group account fund, and health and wellness programs. The two sites that are on your agenda are 1244 San Antonio, which is the one we're discussing now. The site is currently zoned GO. It was built in the mid-80s, and at the time, this zoning ordinance did not have flow-to-area ratios. So the flow-to-area ratio today of GO is one to one, which would give us less square footage than is actually existing on the site. The building currently at 1244 San Antonio at its tallest point is approximately 50 feet. So DMU 60 gives us the same height we have today. Under GO zoning, we're at 60 feet. The building is approximately 50 feet or so. So the benefit of getting DMU zoning gives us additional flow-to-area ratio. We get additional square footage for the building. The height allows us to accommodate more square footage. Which means you don't have to have the parking garage go underground. It saves you money. So you can have, you know, above-grade parking and then offices above that. And that's where the height comes in because we already have 60 feet today. The total square footage that would be allowed under DMU zoning would give us 55,000 square feet on this site. This is one of very few sites in the city that is not in a capital view corridor. As you can see, the yellow fingers that spread out show you those are the areas. The properties that fall under those arrows are controlled by the capital view corridors. The areas that are white that do not have any of those overlays are those properties that can go up in height, should you allow it, but do not affect the capital view corridors as adopted by the state. The Planning Commission used this map to help them come up with the recommendation they did. They looked at the surrounding properties that have heights ranging from 120. So the build sites that have 120 feet of height can build tomorrow at 120 feet that are zoned. And those that are at 120 feet, we're showing them in bold as existing heights. So the Planning Commission looked at this map and looked at equity and felt like the subject site is surrounded by tall buildings already, ranging all the way from 80, 120 feet, and 100 feet on the most recently built building that is called the St. David's Association Building on San Antonio and 13th Street. So this is what the Commission looked to guide them as to height. Some of the justification for height is that a new building at this location will replace an aging structure. The additional space with ground flow retail will help consolidate some employees in one location and accommodate future growth. And any additional spaces that are leased, those funds are used by the county to help serve Texas counties. That's what they serve. The site is not in a capital view corridor. DMU zoning will allow Texas counties to continue to provide cost-effective services. We have support from the adjacent property owners, the majority of them, with the exception of one. This map shows you, and in your backup, you do have letters from the majority of these property owners. Some gave us their verbal support. So this shows you everything in blue that we've highlighted, shows you the support we have for DMU 120 on this site. We would like to offer a community benefit as we were making our rounds of visiting with council offices and with the economic development staff. We, and you spoke very eloquently, some of you recently, about the need for affordable or reasonably priced spaces to house the creatives in Austin on a recent case. And this is an opportunity where the applicant would like to, if you support DMU 90 on this property, they would like to provide 50% of the gross square footage. At least 10% of the gross square footage will have rents reduced to 50% of the CBD rates for a period of 10 years. This offer is really the same as what you typically get on multifamily projects, where applicants offer 10% of units to be affordable at a certain median family income. So the process would be the same here, where should you accept our offer of a volunteer to provide space so that a nonprofit, I'm sorry about that, can use it to accommodate those entities. We have spoken to the Austin Creative Alliance. There's a letter that they sent to you indicating that they would be interested in partnering with us. So they could be the recipient of that space where they can look at creating or managing co-working space for creatives. You've indicated in the resolution that you adopted in March that you would like to create hubs for creatives in Austin. And we would like to explore this with the Austin Creative Alliance. So we'd appreciate your support and I'd be glad to answer any questions you might have at this point. Any questions? Council Member Poole? Thanks, Ms. Glasgow. Could you go back to the slide where you were showing the heights of the buildings in the vicinity? I don't know if you're able to tell us. This is showing some taller buildings in the area. Can you talk about the height of the buildings that are not marked on here? The heights of the buildings that are not marked, their zoning would allow them to go to 60 feet, 60 feet five to six stories. And do you know what they are now? What they are? Some of them are two or three stories approximately. Okay, so that would be about 30 to 40 feet. About 30 to 40 feet, correct. And then if you could jump to the slide that had two forward. Go forward. Go forward by two. The next one. That one there. All of the blue there are the people that are supporting your change in height request, with the exception of the building that is immediately adjacent. Correct. And I think that is that party here to speak to us? Yes. Mr. Tollette is here, and I have enjoyed meeting with Mr. Tollette and Ted Siff. We've had lots of coffee cups together, and we've been trying to reach a compromise. So it's not that we have not spoken. I respect those gentlemen. I've worked with them for a long time. But unfortunately here we're in disagreement on the height, and I was hoping that we can reach some accommodation on the height. But we have met several times, at least five times, and so. And then I've walked along San Antonio Street numerous times, and been in Mr. Tollette's building, and also in the TAC building in the past. Yes. And one thing that strikes me is, especially along San Antonio, you have a lot of fairly mature trees and a good tree canopy. What is the fate of the trees on this site with the redevelopment? I believe we can say because the building is already there and the trees that are there, so it will just basically

chapters.title: 1. ZC-13-162 N. LUCILLE GILKEY 4023 E. Berry St. 0.16 ac. CD 5
chapters.text: That's great. Thank you, Steve. Yes, ma'am. Mr. Chair, and Mr. Zonis, this is the existing building. Could you pull that microphone up just a little? Yeah, that's great. Thank you. The existing building or the proposed building that we are discussing on today is... Can we have your name again? Lucille Gilkey. Okay, address then? 10-25 Lindstrom Drive. Great. Thank you, ma'am. Go ahead. The existing building is 1,400 square feet. It is currently indicated as a restaurant with occupancy of 45. The total occupancy for the proposed land use is 107. We propose a sanctuary seating with a capacity of 70 people. If capacity exceeds 70 people, we will coordinate with the family or with the client, and this will usually be at a church location or some other location that the family agrees to. Soft music will be played within the facility itself and will be contained within the walls of the facility only or the proposed land use. The surrounding zoning and land use is to the north and south, A5, one-family, single-family, and to east and west, ER, neighborhood commercial restricted. The existing pole sign, which is approximately 12 feet, will be removed and an attached sign will be installed for proposed land use. I have a ladder containing 14 signatures of individuals who are in support of proposed land use. Of the 14 signatures, six of these signatures are from individuals within the 300 feet buffer area. And with that, I will submit these individuals who have five in control. Thank you. Great. Thank you. From an environmental perspective, I've talked with Mr. Alphonse Newton with the Fort Worth City Plumbing Department, and from an environmental perspective, he has indicated to me, basically, that for a funeral home, we have to install two RPZ valves, and these are backflow valves that will be put, one, on the main line, which will prevent any contamination to the main sewer line. And then a second RPZ valve will be installed inside the building or the proposed land use, and this will prevent any contamination within the building itself. These particular RPZ valves must be installed and inspected by a licensed plumber and also part of the inspection for a certificate of occupancy. Also from an environmental perspective, the State of Texas Funeral Service Commission does his inspection, and it's a list of over 25 items that he inspects for. He does all his inspections after the applicant has received a certificate of occupancy from the city, and the city has done all the inspection that it needs to do. After passing all inspections from both the city and from the State Funeral Service Commission, the applicant is then provided a license to set up as a funeral home. From a parking space perspective, a minimum number of required parking spaces for proposed land use is 14. This is based on a seating capacity of 17. However, the current facility now has a land use of about 11 parking spaces. We have paper agreement or a letter agreement from Mr. Bobby Boone saying that we can use his space across the street to the west, and that's about 28 spaces. So between the existing 11 parking spaces and Mr. Boone's parking space across the street, we're talking about adequately enough or more than 14 parking spaces that is required as far as parking space is concerned. And here's the letter from Mr. Boone. Lastly, in addition to that, we have – would you please put up the buffer picture that shows the – very good. If you will look to the proposed location, which is 4023, the one that's highlighted there, to the east of that, there are two lots, and they are 4025. I have acquired those particular lots to use for parking spaces and also other uses as needed for the proposed land use. So in actuality, the 4025 can be used for parking spaces, which, if you notice, the long one is 210 feet by 50 feet. And this particular one will house up to as many as 52 parking spaces. Here is the documentation. Oh, I'm sorry. Is – all right. Does – does anyone have any questions for Ms. Gilkey? Yes. So – I actually have a question of clarification for staff, if I may. Sure. These – can you go back to the one that has the actual addresses? 4025, I believe she mentioned. Let's see here. 4025. Can she park cars there if it's a residential lot? Or would that be considered yard parking? 4025 is zoned ER, Neighborhood Commercial. Oh, okay, okay. Sorry. I didn't see that. Okay. So you've secured some parking across. And tell me again where exactly you're saying you've got that parking? It's 4019 currently. 4019. Words. Can you point that out, Stephen? Which is right across the street, right across Noah Street. Across – okay, I see. Directly to the west. And that's where the other existing businesses are, correct? Yes, ma'am. And then on your site plan, you've indicated that you've got 11 spots. However, there's requests for site plan waivers with regards to the parking. And I do have some concerns about that. You can't park necessarily on the side there. I'm not necessarily willing to allow parking on the side of the building. But let me ask Jocelyn or staff to clarify. The way it's worded is it says in the staff report a maximum of seven spaces and that she's providing 11. So she is providing more than the minimum. But I want staff to confirm that wording is correct. For our – for the city standards, yes. For the – for the use – for the gathering use that it is intended to be. Yes. So there's not a deficiency of parking per the zoning ordinance. Okay. Is there still a waiver for side yard parking for this site plan? Along Noah Street, yes. Okay. Having that in the projected front yard. Okay. And I'm not necessarily looking at that waiver there. You did say you are planning on removing the sign. I'm sorry. You are planning on removing the sign. Yes, ma'am. And so what other locations might you have secured if you have more than 70 people in occupancy? That would depend on the family. On the family? Yes. And you did say this is a 24-7 operation? Well, it's only 24-7 from the standpoint of death calls, actually receiving death calls. But as far as meeting with the family, that time spot can be between 8 o'clock in the morning and 5 o'clock in the evening. But death calls are only 24 hours around the clock. Okay. And just show me one more time, if we can go back to the map with all the properties. Zoning map. Yeah. Will you please point out to me where you've secured parking? Is it just in that 4019 and 4025? 4019 is the barbershop beauty shop. Okay. Okay. Okay. That parking, we have a letter from Mr. Boone saying it is okay to use this parking space. And we're looking at a number of 28 parking spaces there. If you look to the east of where the current site is, there is two lots, 4025, which is a smaller lot, which is 67 feet by 100 feet. That I have acquired. Right next to it is another lot, which is 67 feet by 210 feet. If opposed land use, we intend to put a parking lot on the farthest east lot, which is within the 500 feet for an auxiliary parking space. Is there anyone else that would like to speak to the applicant? All right. Thank you, ma'am. And is there anyone else in the audience that would like to speak in favor of this case? Is there anyone that would like to speak in opposition? Yes, sir. Do you need to? Can we get him a microphone? Yeah. You can stay there, sir. You can use this microphone that he'll bring to you. Yeah. That's okay. Just. Sir. And if you could give us your name and address for the record, that would be great. Okay. One second. Try it now. Yes, sir. Great. Thank you. All right, go ahead. Thank you very much. My name is C.D. Jackson. I live at 4024 Burden Street, 76105. I'm in opposition of this funeral home business. We believe that we have a zoning that already fits our case. The zoning requires that no, any kind of junk be put in our neighborhood. We went along with the restaurant deal. And when the business was good, it created nothing but problem after problem. Because when you park on both sides of no street, you leave nothing but an aisle. They did. We did go and race there. And they got a parking. It said no parking this side of the street on the street that the restaurant's on. But that's just like I said, welcome to park any day. They didn't pay no attention. But I am saying, first of all, we don't need a zoning change. The next thing, the place that she wants for a funeral home is really not big enough for what they call a funeral home. Now, you can throw some stuff up there, junk, and assign all the doors of a funeral home. We're tired of that kind of stuff being in our neighborhood. We live in Polly, but we love Polly just like people love in these other neighborhoods. So, we are asking that y'all don't let these things just come in here. People come in here and just throw up something in our neighborhood just to say they're in business. Another thing I want to point out is she talked about the parking. I've been over there at the beauty shop. And the lady, one of the ladies' names, I have a petition here with one of the ladies' names on it. The beauty shop works in there, rent from them. And she told me that she do not have any space for nobody else. They don't have space for themselves. Let me tell you, over all, even at the barbershop, they got the park side of the road. They don't have parking for their own stuff. They're parking side of the street. So, when you park over on her side and our side, that just leaves out. She can probably hold about, she said, 12 cars. If it was a sidewalk, you remember there's no sidewalk there. It's just a place where a sidewalk's supposed to be. If the sidewalk was there, like it should be, she couldn't probably put, she might get 12, but it'd be covering the sidewalk

tags.definition: Zoning reform: A citywide or district-wide change to the zoning code text itself -- a text amendment, a code rewrite, a unified development code update, or a comprehensive rezoning that applies broadly across many properties. Do not use this for an individual property's rezoning, platting, variance, or planned-development case; use the "rezoning" tag for those instead.
Walk, bike, and transit access: Walking, cycling, transit access, or multimodal connectivity.
Infill and redevelopment: Reuse or intensification of already-served land within a city.
Adaptive reuse: Converting existing buildings to new uses rather than replacing them.

chapters.title: 8. ZC-14-108 JAMES JACOBSON 2735-2737 Purington Ave. 0.37 ac. CD 8
chapters.text: CC-14-108, James Jacobson, 2735 and 2737 Purington Avenue. Request is from B-2 family to PDB plan development for all uses in B-2 family, plus the four-plex site plan included. Yes, sir. Yeah. I'm Jim Jacobson. I actually live in Haslett, 2653 Blue Mound Road. And I purchased some properties in Southeast Fort Worth. There's two existing four-plexes. One was built in 1921 and one was built in 1931. The corner house, you see in that display, I guess, was actually a house. And it converted, eventually, to a four-plex. The other house is a 4,400 square foot four-plex that was built in 1931 as a four-plex. It's got a matching floor plan right and left side, and it's in quite disarray. It's been neglected for years. I purchased it as an investment with the NEZ program. It offered some pretty good benefits. In that program, I'm required to have five doors, and this is qualified with two four-plexes. And also, it requires an investment of around $200,000 for updating, and so it will increase the tax base. And I guess what I've gone through, I guess, in this initial application, I started the NEZ application, and then I found out that the area was zoned for duplex only. And so in renovating it, I have to get, I guess, a zone change to make a four-plex a viable option. But what I did look at is the parking, and it is a fairly constrained area. It's 140 by 100, basically, and over half that is occupied with structure and entrances. And so I actually laid out a plan that I could get 12 parking spaces on the property. Adjacent to the east side, there's a park, and so we'd like to have no parking in the street. And so what I've done is I've modified that corner house to actually convert that to a duplex instead. And it would be a rather large duplex, around 1,880 square feet per apartment, and actually I'm going to do a right and left-hand side split on it. And this is just a recent change, so I haven't really developed floor plans for it. But it would allow me to still qualify for the NEZ program because it's still got five doors or more. And so I'm requesting the zone change to a lot of four-plex, and actually the duplex would be in compliance. Okay. Any questions for Mr. Jacobson? Yeah, go ahead, Juan. Yes, I do have one. Okay. With absolute admiration for the fact that he took on these two old buildings that have been a code compliance nightmare in our neighborhood for years. Thank you for that. But I do have one question. Sure. When you finished, you did get your NEZ application approved, didn't you? Right. It's on hold until we settle this issue. Until we do that. Okay. Right. But our neighborhood is in support of this. But the question that I have is, once you get these renovated and leased, who will, will you be managing these? You're not going to just sell them off. You're going to be managing these because we would like for them to be maintained and for the landscaping around there to look nice. Yeah, I plan it, man. Actually, it's a retirement investment. Okay. So you will be in constant watching to be sure they're not falling down again like they were. And actually, the way the purchase of the, I guess, the deed to this property, they're very difficult to split up. It had to be, you had to purchase both of them or, you know, or none of them. And so it's kind of locked in. And so I guess I'll have to ask for a waiver as well because in the requirement, it's just the one property side. If you look on the west side on this property, it's lot 19. I've got a requirement that has to accommodate eight parking spots. And what I've done is I've bled the parking spots into lot 20 to accommodate the eight. 20 will be just a duplex and that will only require, you know, actually be four parking spots for that one. So the way it was written in the request is that I need to take parking spots for the length of lot 19. And I won't be able to come back to ask a waiver for that clause, I guess. We don't have that listed as a waiver. What do we do about that? There's comments there, but it doesn't say. Put it in motion. That's why we had left it because we had thought about maybe pulling the corner lot off because it was a duplex. Therefore, it was permitted by ride in B. But we left it as the PD. So the PD showed the parking across. So it wasn't a waiver for that lot as much as the PD was intended to accommodate the parking for both. Okay. All right. That clears that up. Go ahead, Dan. And that's all I had. All right. Thank you, Juan. And to that point, I wanted to clarify or ask Jocelyn if she would agree that since the revision to have the corner, the east lot become B2 family, then the change, the PD zoning change, since it would retain that as a duplex, that that would be compatible with surrounding land uses and would be consistent with the comprehensive plan for that eastern lot. So it would be somewhat of a maybe splitting hairs, I suppose. But really, it's just now the one structure, not both structures that are proposed as a fourplex. Oh, okay. So I wanted to make sure the commission's aware of that. Okay. And then secondly, I don't know if this would be of interest, but there's, before you make your investment, there are some tax freeze options if you were to designate it as a historic property. And so, you know, so that may be something if you're interested in our historic preservation. Is that separate from the NEZ program? Yes. Oh, yeah. Okay. So it would be, it basically would freeze your tax, your city taxes, at the pre-renovation value. And then once you made your renovations, the tax rate would not go up for a period of time. But it takes some time to get the historic designation, so I don't know what your time frame is. It may or may not be. All right. Thank you. Thank you, Kate. Okay, any other questions then? And I did have another comment. This is probably really a good thing that's happening along there because West Meadowbrook has not had any really good rental property. This is on a bus line real close to East Lancaster, which is the most traveled bus line in the city of Fort Worth. So this kind of goes along to our pedestrian-oriented developments. All right. Thank you. All right. Thank you, sir. We have just a few seconds of time for anyone else that would like to speak in support of this application. Is there anyone that would like to speak in opposition? There being no opposition, then we'll close the public hearing, and we're ready for a motion. Well, and I'm certainly ready to make one. All right. I'd like to send the ZC 14-108 to Council with a recommendation for approval. We have a second by Ms. Reed. Wanda was jazzed up on that. I am. All right. Let's go ahead and vote. That motion passes 8-0. CC-14-109, HDMM Investments, LLC, 2310 Avondale-Haslett Road. The request is from unzoned to e-neighbored commercial. In this case, it will be heard by the City Council on November 18th, 2014. Great. Good morning, Commission. My name is Gene Capps. I'm with Barrett, Hampton & Brown Engineering at 4550 State Highway 360, Suite 180, Grapevine, Texas. I'm here representing HDMM Investments, which is a child company of Castle Development. I'm here to answer any questions you guys might have.

chapters.title: 8. PR-2026-053670 – 1109 Travis Heights Blvd.
chapters.text: congratulations. And that is well-deserved. So the next item for discussion is item number eight. That's right. That would be 1109 Travis Heights Boulevard. All right. This is a proposal to demolish a certain 1920 house located in the Travis Heights Fairview Park Historic District. This American four square house with Prairie School stylistic influences was constructed around 1920. The two-story house has a low-pitch hipped roof with broad overhangs. The full width hipped port, hipped, hipped roof port, excuse me, has a long open span supported at corners by large square columns. The second floor had recessed corners that had been infilled and converted into interior space. Much of the house has been covered with aluminum siding. Wood windows appear throughout the building with larger multi-light fixtures appearing at the front elevation and simpler one-over-one units more common at the sides and rear. Early owners of the circuit to 1920 house were Elmer Elmer and Cora Young. E.E. Young was a co-owner of an automotive dealership, Harton Young, Willys Knight, and Overland Austin agency. He later bought out his partner and continued operation under his name. He served as president of the local automobile dealers association, and shortly before his death in 1928, Young became secretary of the Stacy Realty Company, developer of the Travis Heights neighborhood. Later owners included Charles and Catherine Brunner, who owned the house from 1929 until 1947. Charles Brunner operated a jewelry business on East 6th Street beginning in the late 1890s. After his death in 1933, Catherine Brunner continued to run the jewelry store for another 10 years. It appears that she leased out the house following her husband's death but moved back in around 1941. In the 1950s, the house was occupied by Robert and Gwendolyn Hill. Robert Hill was a foreman at the Calcasieu Lumber Company. Some department comments here. A demolition permit for this property was originally referred to HLC in July 2019, and the case was subsequently withdrawn. A demolition application for the garage at the rear of the property was submitted in 2024, but this was later withdrawn upon the subsequent owner's purchase of the property. This property also attended the January 15, 2025 Architectural Review Committee meeting to discuss a potential remodel, though no permit application was submitted for the scope of work. Documentation, including agendas and backup materials for these three previous applications, can be found in backup attached to this case. Per City Code, the Historic Landmark Commission has 180 days to review demolition permits of National Register Historic District contributing structures starting from the date the application was submitted. This period is set to time out on October 27, 2026. The property contributes to the Trappist Heights, Vareby Park, National Register District. Properties must meet two criteria for landmark designation. Staff has evaluated the property and determined that it does not meet two criteria for landmark designation. Therefore, staff recommendation is to encourage rehabilitation and adaptive reuse, relocation, or deconstruction and salvage over demolition, but approve the demolition permit application upon completion of the City of Austin documentation package. The Historic Landmark Commission must review new construction drawings prior to permit release in National Register Historic Districts before those demolition permits are released. Thank you. This concludes the staff report. Thank you. Any questions of staff? Yes, Commissioner. This particular house lies on two legal lots, as I understand it. That's correct, yes. Is there anything, since there wouldn't be a demolition unless it's part of the garage, since there isn't anything on the adjacent lot, is there anything that prevents the owner from moving forward, other, well, is there anything that prevents the owner from moving forward with something on the adjacent lot? The only thing that we would require is a review for new construction. Because it's in the National Register District. That's correct, yes. Okay. That's it. Thank you. Okay. Any other questions? Okay. Commissioners, this was, we heard first at our meeting in June, this was postponed, so it's, the clock has only just started. And I don't believe that the applicant was there. Do we have, is the applicant here this evening? He's listed as Gabe Joseph. It would appear that they are not here. They have also not signed up to speak. Okay. And we did encourage a visit to the Architecture Review Committee, and my understanding is that they did not do that either. That is correct. So, Mr. Joseph, if you're listening, we would like to hear from you. There are options, perhaps, that you might have to preserve this building, as staff has noted. And we will still reserve an opportunity to initiate historic zoning, even if we continue to postpone up until the last couple of meetings. But at this point, I think we can certainly listen to any discussion if anybody's signed up to speak on this item. Do we have any speakers? If I could just jump in here very quick, just for a staff note, because of the July 4th holiday and city services being closed on the 3rd, any referral to Architectural Review Committee at this meeting would have to occur in the August 12th ARC meeting. Okay. Got it. Thank you. All right. Thank you. We could do that, potentially. Yes. Let me go ahead and see if there's anybody else signed up to speak. Yes. We have four speakers signed up in opposition, and our first speaker is Clifton Ladd. Okay. Mr. Ladd, please come forward and introduce yourself for the record. Good evening, commissioners. My name is Clifton Ladd. I'm here to represent the Historic Preservation Committee of the South River City Citizens Neighborhood Association, which I co-chair. I'm also a resident of Travis Heights Fairview Park National Register Historic District. Thank you for this opportunity to speak. Our committee is pleased that you have pulled this item from the consent agenda to discuss it thoroughly before you make a decision. We believe this house merits historic landmark status. It meets the requirements for historic landmark designation included in the city code. This house is a 1920s American four-square and contributing structure in the Travis Heights Fairview Park historic district. Its balance of proportions, prominent front porch, and traditional massing embody a residential forum that helped define Austin historic streetcar suburbs. It is located on a highly visible corner lot, contributes significantly to the character of the surrounding streetscape, and serves as an architectural anchor within the district. Our other committee co-chair, Ms. Barbara Silley, will also speak regarding the importance of protecting homes on Travis Heights Boulevard. Our committee is concerned that we could easily lose important houses like this one, and also on 2009 Travis Heights Boulevard, which is also on tonight's agenda. Several other members of our committee are also signed up to speak concerning these proposed demolitions. Travis Heights Boulevard is the most prominent street in the Travis Heights Fairview Park National Register Historic District. We must protect the historic homes on the street, if possible, in 1109. In 2009, Travis Heights Boulevard are prime examples. Unlike many historic homes that have lost their integrity through extensive alterations, 1109 Travis Heights Boulevard retains much of its original character and historic fabric. Our committee sent you a letter last week regarding this house, and we included many of the reasons why we think it is worthy of protection. Our letter also included several photos of the interior of the house. The photos show the house is in good condition. It could be improved with modest effort. I hope you've had a chance to read our letter. We understand that property owners want to improve their properties, but we have seen too many examples of owners tearing down old houses and building something modern that doesn't fit in the neighborhood. We're not opposed to modern architecture, but modern structures would be out of place on Travis Heights Boulevard. We request that you invite the owner to the architectural review committee and show them what could be done to improve this home in a way that honors the original architecture. It is truly a diamond in the rough and could easily be improved in a way that retains its unique architecture. Thank you. Thank you. Okay, anybody to question the speaker? Then let's have the next speaker, please. Our next in opposition speaker is Barbara Silley. Silley? Welcome. Before I get started, I had a lot of images, but I didn't realize I needed to get them in advance. I do have them on a whatever those things are. A flash drive. Yes. Thank you. Yes. Okay, before we get started, I want you to set a note. We don't have really great Christmas decorations, but I live in the middle of Travis Heights Boulevard, and so we have a huge Halloween affair. I mean, I had probably 500 kids in my house last year. So, and that has some historic context, I think. I want to talk to you about the concept of a boulevard, because we do not spend enough time, I think, talking about early urban planning, and the boulevard was one of those really important concepts. Travis Heights was planted in 1913, and the ideas that shaped civic pride in the early 20th century are incorporated in this newly minted boulevard. The boulevard was a central avenue designed to both beautify and enhance the circulation of the neighborhood. This urban pattern was inspired by the city beautiful movement that was the organizing idea of the Columbian Exposition of 1893. The sweep of the avenue was designed to impress and enhance the living space of all the residents. This property, located at the entrance to Travis Heights Boulevard, is one of the gateway properties that helped to define the idea of a boulevard. It is located adjacent to the fully restored Stacy House, and is also adjacent to other important bungalows. The avenue is defined by the landscape that incorporates crepe myrtles that are now 100 years old. They are planted in the carefully designed tree lawn located between the curb and the sidewalk. Although there are gaps in the blocks, much of the historical landscape remains intact. It is the combination of structures and planting that characterizes the experience of the boulevard. We are facing the demolition of two structures on each end of the boulevard that are going to diminish our community. Preservation is both individual structures and their context. We are incrementally destroying the early 20th century civic pride that was invested in the development of our boulevard. And the slides were I did a crepe myrtles tour. And you can see how beautiful these crepe myrtles are that line our Travis Heights Boulevard. So I will be back, and

chapters.title: 23. Staff briefing regarding Austin Water Environmental Resource Office and Wildland Conservation Division, which involves the management of the Balcones Canyonland Preserve and the protection of water quality and quantity in the Barton Springs segment of the Edwards Aquifer– Sherri Kuhl, Austin Water Environmental Resource Officer, and Justin Bates, Austin Water Environmental Conservation Division Manager
chapters.text: And we can move on to our next staff briefing. It's item number 23, and it's the Austin Water Environmental Resource Office and Wildland Conservation Division. All right. Thank you, commissioners. We, you, I'm happy to be here today. We also briefed our Climate, Water, Environment, and Parks Committee of Council this morning on this same topic. An update on the Environmental Resource Office and Wildland Conservation Division. All of you, as commissioners, are aware that we manage 49,000 acres of water quality protection land and Bocconi Canyon Land Preserve. And so, we're happy to be here today to give you an update on that work. Good evening. I'm Sherry Kuhl. I'm the Environmental Resource Officer for Austin Water. And I'm going to talk a little bit this evening about our Environmental Resource Office. Next slide, please. So, we have a number of programs that we coordinate through the Environmental Resource Office. Part one of the things we do is coordinate some of our climate mitigation and climate resilience work. I know you're very familiar also that the water resources team does a lot of that with Water Forward. But we're kind of focused on, internally, on our engineering design guidance and things like that and our wildlands efforts. We have the Center for Environmental Research at Hornsby Bend. And I'll talk a little more about that. The Bocconi's Canyon Lands Conservation Plan and Permit. And then the Wildland Conservation Division. Next slide, please. So, understanding and preparing for climate, Austin Water for Climate Change. Next slide. We do a lot of things. We work across the city, especially with our Austin Climate Action and Resilience Department on a number of items. But one of the main ways that we work within our team on climate change is with the Water Utility Climate Alliance. And this is a group of utilities across the country, 14 utilities that are looking at climate change and trying to be prepared for the future and looking at things like heat, increases in heat, increases in cold temperatures, flooding, sea level rise for some of the coastal cities and so forth. Next slide, please. Next slide, please. So, one of the projects that Heather Darumple and my team just co-managed recently was this putting together a manual for climate resilient engineering design guidance. And so, it was very well received. One of the benefits of WUCA is that we contribute money to that organization, but it's pooled with the money from all the other utilities. And we're able to get a lot of incredible work done with great teams of smart people from across our country and with the consultant teams that work with us. So, this manual, I think, will be very helpful for Austin Water. And the next step, the next phase, we're going to look at some specific checklists and flow charts that we can maybe incorporate directly into our CIP planning process. Next slide, please. So, out at Hornsby Bend, hopefully you're familiar with Hornsby Bend operations. Next slide, please. I believe it's one of the great examples of sustainability at the City of Austin. So, we take the sludge from Walnut and SAR and work together with Austin Resource Recovery to bring in all the branches from this, particularly from the winter freezes that we've had recently. And those are mixed together to create Dillow dirt, which is an award-winning compost material. We also have a biogas facility there where we generate and utilize the biogas. We have reused the water on watering hay fields on the track. And then we have a series of ponds so the water is treated naturally before it's not discharged to the Colorado River. So, because of those ponds and just the land that we have there on the Colorado River, it's a very popular spot for birding. It was discovered by birders and birdies, I guess, back in the 90s. And so, our team helps kind of coordinate the public involvement there so that the plant superintendent and others don't have to deal so much with that public involvement. Next slide, please. So, it's open from dawn to dusk. We love having people out to see that facility. There's about three miles of trails right along the Colorado River where you can walk along the trail. There's about 1,200 acres of land. And then, as I mentioned, the ponds that are good. You can drive around the ponds to bird. Next slide, please. So, this has been a longstanding center for environmental research there that was created back in the 90s. And some of the first research was really on waste and compost and sludge and things. And then, also, for the last 20 years, we've been working with the Jackson School at UT on looking at river hydrology. We have a series of groundwater wells where we can work with students on what's happening with the river when it's pulsed with the releases. So, it's been a great place for research with those universities and also just for citizen science projects. Next slide. We do a lot of education and outreach as well, monthly lectures and bird walks and river trips and so forth. So, a big part of what we do is just Endangered Species Act compliance for the city and for Austin Water. Next slide. We wanted to let everybody know a big effort's going to be going in in the next four or five years on permit renewal. Our Balcones Canyonlands Conservation Plan and Permit was established in 1996. So, it was a 30-year permit that just expired in May of 2026. But we worked with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to extend that while we're in the process of renewal. So, it will be extended until we finish our renewal. So, what is the BCCP? We've talked about it here before. It's what created the Balcones Canyonlands Preserve that Justin will talk about. But, it's basically, it's a, when you have an endangered species, you can have what's called incidental take. If you have a project, like you're building a subdivision or a water line and you don't intend to harm the endangered species, but it's incidental to what you're doing. And so, there's a mechanism to permit that. So, if you don't have a regional permit like ours, you have to go into the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Every Project and get it permitted. So, our local leaders back in the 90s decided it would be best if we had a county-wide habitat conservation plan and permit. And so, they created the Balcones Canyonlands Conservation Plan. And that effort took almost 10 years. So, we're hoping four or five for renewal. But, we'll be looking at all the aspects of the permit as we go through this process. Next slide. And this map just shows you the permit area because all the current species on the permit are in the west. So, what does it do or what are the benefits? Some of the benefits I'm going to talk about a little bit. But, the preserve is where we do all the conservation efforts of the Balcones Canyonlands Conservation Plan. As I mentioned, it's an incidental take permit coverage. It's the main mechanism for that for the city of Austin and Travis County. And then, we're able to permit other developments that are going in that go through our staff. And, therefore, it's much more streamlined. And, it's a local mechanism, a local control over that permitting. Next slide. This is one of our caves on the preserve. So, over the years, we've permitted quite a bit of development. We've had over 1,500 developments and 400 infrastructure projects and about 12,000 acres of development. If you look at the slide in 96, the photo, and then 2026, you can see the difference in the amount of development that's gone in. And, we've been able to do that with a local mechanism that saves money and saves time. And, also, then, we were able to, back in the 90s, create that preserve system as the mitigation for that development and able to create a whole system of preserve. So, it benefits as a way to locally permit a development in a streamlined way, but also create a good preserve system. Next slide. Oh, next slide. So, permit renewal. As I mentioned, the permit expired. So, in order to renew it, we have to look at everything that was pulled together for the original permit. There have been a number of species that have been listed since our permit was issued, and also some that are proposed for listing. So, we'll be looking at all those species and seeing if we want to add them to the permit. If we do decide to add them, then we'll be able to have kind of a one-stop shopping for developers and infrastructure. We're going to look over the whole county, because some of those species occur in the eastern side of the county. And, we'll have to look at all the current U.S. Fish and Wildlife regulations. We'll need to do a climate change analysis. We didn't really, weren't really thinking about that back in the 90s. So, we're looking forward to going through this process. Next slide, please. One of the things that you'll hear about right away is we issued a press release, a joint city-county press release yesterday, to ask for citizens who might want to participate in the Citizens Advisory Committee and the Biological Advisory Team. Those, we had them in the original permit, and now they're required by Parks and Wildlife Code, Chapter 83. So, we'll be standing up those committees again. So, we're looking for people that would be interested in serving on those. We're going to issue a notice for request for interest back in January of 27. And, those committees will help with the technical advice in terms of the Biological Advisory Team, and then also with the community engagement. Next slide. So, the BCCP, we have those two acronyms, but the Bacones Canyonlands Conservation Plan has been a great tool, very successful over the last 30 years for having this streamlined, locally controlled permitting mechanism, but also being able to create a preserve system that was best for those species that are covered by our permit. So, we're looking forward to being able to modernize the permit, get some GIS maps instead of hand-drawn maps, and be able to maybe expand on our public engagement. It seems like even though we do so much public engagement, there's still so many people in Austin that don't even really know about these lands. So, we're looking forward to this opportunity for more public
