chapters.title: Item 4
chapters.episode_title: Comprehensive Planning and Transportation Committee – Apr 07, 2014
chapters.text: Next, we have an update on the process timeline for Code Next, the city's initiative to revise the land development code. And we have several speakers on four and five. We're also going to have a briefing on Code Next on number five. I think we'll go ahead and take the speakers first. Laura Presley. I have a quick question. Can people donate time? I have Daniel Yanez would like to donate time to me. Yes. Let's just do that. Okay. Thank you. Thank you. And so you have a total of six minutes. Who donated, David? Daniel Yanez. Daniel, he's back there. Oh, I see. Okay. You have six minutes. Thank you. Well, thanks for bringing this topic up again. We really appreciate all three of you and Council Member Tovo for being here. I want to talk a little bit about the alternative code approaches, and that is what this council is slated to potentially vote on. And you guys have talked a little bit about how that would work. Would maybe the sitting council do a first reading and then let the 10-1 council do a second and third reading? But I want to kind of more talk about the process. The alternative code approaches is a big deal, and it is going to be voted on by one of these councils. And there are three major entities feeding into that alternative code approaches. I have that flow chart memorized, so that's the part of my brain that does that. And I want to talk about three components that the neighborhoods are supposed to be having feedback into. The first one is listening to the community report, and you're going to hear an update on that. And I want to let you guys know that if you look at the statement of work that OptiCoast has put together, there are major stakeholders from the community. And the two major ones that are kind of in my view, the neighborhoods, Austin Neighborhoods Council, and environmental groups. I want to let you know that the Austin Neighborhoods Council, and I am an executive committee member of ANC, and I am speaking for ANC as I speak today, we have never been approached by the consultants for ANC. And that concerns me, given that that is one of the main key inputs into the alternative code approach, if you look at that flow chart. And also, I question the consultants, have they reached out directly to environmental groups? And how did they do that? Did they talk to SOS? Did they talk to Sierra Club? Who did they get with Texas Campaign for the Environment? Who do they talk with in our community? If ANC is being missed, what other stakeholders are being missed? So that's number one. The other key input that's going into these alternative code approaches is the neighborhood plan summaries. And we've talked a lot about this. The neighborhood plans, in some cases, my neighborhood plan of Windsor Hills, I'm president of Windsor Hills Neighborhood Association. Our neighborhood plan is 126 pages. The city staff boiled that down to 145 words. That is a little problematic. And so we've asked for some extended time to go review that and have an iterative process so that this summary that gets put into this entity of the alternative code approaches and gets evaluated is accurate. If we don't have back and forth feedback, those 145 words are really critical and they better be correct. And right now they're not. So that's a problem. The Envision Tomorrow scenarios that are, it's a simulation of Austin's code and applying, if we use our code today and we completely build out to that, what does that look like? That's the Envision Tomorrow deliverable that's going to be given to you guys. And it's also going to be used in this alternative code approach. There are multiple problems with the scenarios that they're looking at. They are not including compatibility standards into that simulation. They're not including neighborhood plans, future land use maps, into that simulation. They're not including heritage tree ordinance. Now that's a difficult one I give them. It's very hard to do that. They're not including the Capitol View Corridor. And I want to quote Steve Oliver at a meeting last week. And he said, if you do not include these, it's not Austin. The alternative code approaches is supposed to be, is to come out of these evaluations. And those four major components of our code today will not be incorporated in that Envision Tomorrow scenario. That's a problem. So here I've given you, listening to the community report, ANC was never in outreach to directly. The neighborhood plans are being summarized to 145 words. We're not sure that's accurate. The Envision Tomorrow is not including the code that we have today on deck for our city. These are three major inputs, entities that are feeding that alternative code approaches analysis. And they're not being done. So we are, as Austin Neighborhoods Council, we have addressed all three of these. We've gone to the CAG. We've gone to the city manager's office and asked for these things to be done better and more accurately. And it's not happened. So now we're coming to you. We're asking you, as a city council subcommittee, to ask and direct the city manager to do all three of these things, to include ANC, direct the consultants to include ANC, and potentially include the environmental groups we just mentioned. To have an iterative process for the neighborhood plans to be accurate, the summaries, and to include these current code components into the Envision Tomorrow simulation. Now, the Envision Tomorrow consultant said, well, that is not incorporated in the contract to put these things in. That's problematic. When you're not including neighborhood plans and you're not including compatibility standards, that's Austin. That's why people love Austin. This is why Austin's weird. Because we have different neighborhoods with compatibility standards that are their own character. So, the bottom line is, who wins here? And I can tell you from Windsor Hills standpoint, there's a direct competition right now for the neighborhood plan and the growth corridor of Dessau and Cameron Road. And I will address that in my next item. Can you explain what you mean by there's a direct competition in Windsor Hills for the neighborhood plan? Yes. Thank you for asking that. So, in my neighborhood plan and on my future land use map of Windsor Hills, on Cameron and Dessau, we have single-family three-zoning. The corridor, the growth corridor along Dessau and Cameron calls for high density. Which wins? The neighborhood plan or the growth corridor model? We asked the consultants this question. In the Envision Tomorrow scenario, which are you going to pick? Are you going to pick the neighborhood plan, which is SF3, which existing homes, very affordable homes in that part of town? There's your affordable housing in Austin. It's northeast Austin. Or are you going to pick more expensive density? We asked which one's going to win. Mayor Leffingwell has always said neighborhood plans are going to trump. But the consultants are not being told that. We need your help. Give them direction. Which do they pick? Okay. Thank you, Laura. Any further questions? Thank you. The next speaker is David King. Good afternoon, and thank you for the time to address this important issue. To me, this is one of the most important committees that will be looking at the new Land Development Code. You're all about the future, about our infrastructure, about the long term. And that's exactly what Envision Tomorrow is. It's the long term. It's 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 years or more down the road. And we're going to be spending millions of dollars to do this. So I think we should get it right. And there are some things that I think need to be done to help make sure that we spend this money well and we get good value for what we've done. In the interest of our future here, the model depends only on the quality of the data that it receives. And right now, we don't have the infrastructure data at the level of granularity that's necessary for the model to be accurate. The infrastructure for our roads, for our water, for our wastewater, for our electricity. That's not available yet. And yet here we are pushing. Let's run the model. Let's do it. Let's go. We can't wait. But I think we need to wait. We need to make this right so that when it comes time to map in the new zones that we're going to work hard to produce, that that part of the process will be done more precisely and more completely and with less problems, fewer problems. This is crucial. So right now, Austin Utility and Austin Water Utility, Electric Utility and Water Utility do not have that data ready. But we need to have that data. And it needs to be at the most granular level possible, at the lot level, so that we can do this accurately. So I would ask that you please address that and help us make sure that we get that data. And that data is produced before we run these scenarios. And we've already heard about some of the components that the model cannot handle. The other concern I have is that the default data that's in the model is five years old. And that's the data about housing types and costs. And I think that's a little old. Things have changed in five years. That data should be updated. The other concern I have is that at the CAG meeting the other day, there was, I believe, some misinformation about the fact that developers do not pay the full cost for new development. They do not, not even with the new impact fees, they do not fully go into effect for several more years down the road. And not only that, they don't cover roads or stormwater. So if we're going to calculate what the affordability, what the impact of this Envision Tomorrow is going to be on our community, on our families, we have to get the data right. So I would just ask that you please address those key concerns in addition to my cohort's concerns. And thank you very much for your time. Thank you, David. Next, we have Frank Heron. All right. Thank you, Council Members. I, too, would like to talk about small area plans, including neighborhood plans, in relation to Imagine Austin and the Land Development Code. A small area plan clearly should only influence or control issues that

chapters.title: 7A 2025-0009 To receive public comment and consider an ordinance amending the City of Pflugerville Code of Ordinances Title XV Land Usage, Chapter 153 Planning, by amending the Future Land Use Map in the Downtown District Overlay from Suburban Residential to Mixed-Use Neighborhood for the following Travis County Property Ids: 276146, 276147, 276127, 276126, 276125, 276124, 276123, 276122, 276023, 276129, 276133, 276132, 276131, 276130, 276177, 274586, 274585, 276186 and from Suburban Residential to Institutional for Travis County Property Id: 276023; all to be known as the 2025 Downtown FLUM Amendment (CPA2024-00499)
chapters.text: All right. Now, we have item seven. We have a public hearing this evening. So the commission welcomes comment on the following items. Each person providing public comment will be limited to three minutes and will be asked to state his or her name and address for the public record. All right. Jeremy, our principal planner, will be, uh, presenting item seven A, uh, to consider amending a city code of ordinances for the future land use map. Dean, Dean chair and commission, and thank you for, uh, being here tonight and welcome to our two new members. Um, this is a comprehensive plan amendment. This is something that we don't do on a regular basis. We, we typically, we approve a comprehensive plan and that it establishes what our vision is of the community. But there are certain times where we find that there are discrepancies or inconsistencies or something like that, that needs to be addressed. And so, um, an applicant can pursue a comprehensive plan amendment. Um, in this instance, this is actually a city initiated comprehensive plan amendment. So we're looking at a, uh, the future land use map, the future land use map is in, um, sub chapter three of our comprehensive plan. And that helps to identify what the different land use categories are for, um, the city and within our realm. Um, it's typically kind of a broad brush stroke kind of painting, if you will, of what the different land use categories would be throughout. Um, but there are times where we have to get into the specific details and zoom in onto properties. And sometimes that's where we find those inconsistencies. And so sometimes that can be a mapping error, um, that we want to come back and revisit. This happens to be a situation where we looked at some properties and we found some inconsistencies with what the land use categories are and with what the current zonings are. And so bringing forward tonight, um, proposed amendments to address something, uh, it's approximately 18 properties inside of our downtown core area, as well as the transitional compatibility zone. Um, the downtown district overlay, um, just to give you kind of a bigger picture of what this is on the left hand side of the screen represents what that area is inside of that area. We have like five different, um, sub areas, if you will, the Western extent becomes like 10th street. Um, and our Eastern extent becomes 685. Um, the, the downtown East properties inside the Pflueger tract is an example. Um, on the right hand side of the screen is our downtown core and also shows the transitional compatibility zones. That's the hatching. Um, those are the areas that we're talking about tonight. And so specifically it's the areas that are circled in red. So, as I mentioned, we were looking at the, the future land use map and we found on the left hand side of the screen shows the future land use map. And we saw that there were some inconsistencies when you compare to the zoning that's on the right hand side. Um, the properties that we're talking about are outlined in black. You can see that they have that yellow color on the future land use map. We also have the pink that's in the downtown core area. That's our, um, mixed use neighborhood, um, classification or category. And then the blue is the institutional category. The right hand side then shows our zoning map. So trying to put a side by side is kind of a lot of colors for you, but, um, to show what we were looking at and where we saw those inconsistencies. Um, the, um, transitional zone, I should back up and talk about that for a minute. So that transitional com, um, compatibility zone is, is an area that we envision as that true transition, right? To go from where the more vibrant mixed use things might be inside of our downtown core to where the neighborhoods are. And so we identify that there could be, um, an area or those are the areas that we could see some transitioning happening from say a single family home that would transition into an office or something like that. Um, that would be more compatible with the neighborhood, but it wouldn't maybe be as, as intense as what we might find in the downtown core. So some of those properties are shown on the zoning, um, on the zoning map. Actually, I'll zoom in on in just a minute onto those. Um, the future land use categories that we're talking about today, that everything that was in the yellow on that left hand side is the suburban residential that was intended for a hundred percent single family types of development. That's what we see as our, our single family neighborhoods. Um, the non-residential would be considered when you were talking about some type of civic or amenity or amenity center or something like that. The mixed use neighborhood is intended to create the vibrancy that we would anticipate. Um, mixed use doesn't mean that it has to be vertical mixed use, meaning stacked on top of one another, but it could be a horizontal mixed use. Um, mixed use does not remove single family from its equation. Instead, it looks at, you could do small lot single family, which is what we find inside of these areas. Um, there could also be transitioned to town homes or duplexes, triplexes, that type of um, that makes compatibility. It also allows for the opportunity to do some type of office or retail or neighborhood commercial type of, um, developments there. And that type of vibrancy is what is envisioned inside of the, the downtown area. That's what's, um, established in our downtown vision plans. Um, and that's pulled into our unified development code and all of its, um, development requirements. So that's why we're looking at making that adjustment for those areas. The institutional is another, um, it's one lot that's proposed to be moved into that category. And it's basically because the property itself, um, was owned and controlled by the church property. It's, it's the property on the left hand side. That's that light blue color. Um, the rest of the property, well, the property itself and the adjacent property is, is all zoned office today. And so this would, the future land use map shows it as a suburban residential. This is just to give it that conforming, um, land use category on the left hand side of the screen. What's, um, highlighted in pink are those properties that are inside of the transitional compatibility zone. That's just north of Pecan street on the west side of first street. Um, on the zoning map, you can see on the right side, there's yellow and green on the, um, on that west side. It's those properties that are highlighted in the blue. Um, two of those properties are currently zoned office. One is used as an office. The other one was zoned for office and had the intent of moving forward today. They don't have an office in there. Um, but that's, that's afforded to them. That's an area that we've identified inside of the unified development code in our downtown district to be that transitional piece. And so putting a mixed use neighborhood into that section helps to establish that transition and put that compatibility there, um, compatibility and conformity. Um, on the right hand side, you can see the pink, that's where the east side of first street is currently zoned retail is what's reflected on the right hand side of the screen. Um, that again, the, the proposal is to change that from the suburban residential to the mixed use neighborhood to be able to provide that conforming, um, classification. The last parcel that's on this, um, screen is down at the southwest corner of main street and railroad. Um, today it's a two story building. It has the taco house, uh, the tattoo shop, and then there's an office that's up upstairs. Um, that would be to take that from suburban residential to the mixed use neighborhood. Today is on general business one. Um, the last area that we're looking at or that we looked at found, um, was on just south of Pecan street between second and third street. There's just a little three parcels there on the north side of hall street. Two of them are zoned, um, for the non-residential, there's an office and then the retail zone property. And then one suburban residential property that's adjacent to it. Um, again, it's in that compatibility zone that's identified to potentially transition. And so it's just that one little block that we were looking at making the adjustment to it, not, not anything else on hall street. Um, when we look at the rest of the comprehensive plan, there's another chapter in there that talks about neighborhood districts. And so those neighborhood districts kind of take the city and break it off into different parts. This one is the central district and some of the aspirational actions that are inside of that. We're really looking at creating vibrancy, increasing the walkability and creating that pedestrian atmosphere, um, creating the communications with the neighborhoods so that we're having compatible elements, um, and looking for ways to increase the aesthetics. Making these adjustments doesn't change anything in this. Um, what this would do is can continue to retain these aspirational actions, um, and, and be more consistent again with what the downtown area was intended to be and what it continues to be zoned today. Um, the proposed request does not make any requirements to change anybody's land use that's on that property today. It does not change any of the zoning on it. Instead, what it does is it provides consistency of a land use category that was anticipated to be on those properties. So the transitional corridor, just those different small pieces that we were looking at is intended to transition. And so we want to make sure that that is, is consistent. Um, the properties that are currently zoned for the non-residential, we need to make sure that that's also consistent there. Um, staff does recommend approval. This is anticipated to go to city council at the end of the month. Um, be happy to answer any questions for you, from you. Have the, um, have the owners of these properties been notified or have they provided any, uh, feedback? We sent a notice to, um, the property owners that were specifically affected by this, and we have not received any other feedback

chapters.title: Arts & Cultural Advisory Commission on September 18, 2025.
chapters.text: Okay. We now have a quorum at 432, and I call to order the meeting of the Arts and Culture Advisory Commission. We're going to go straight down the agenda, and we're going to start our meeting. Today, we actually have two public speakers, and our first public speaker is William Allen. So, Mr. Allen, you can have a seat right here. And what are, is it two or three minutes? It's up to you. Three. Three minutes? Okay. We're generous. Three minutes. How's that? It's perfect. All right. Timer. Yes. You may begin. Awesome. Good afternoon, Chair, Arts and Culture Commissioners, Parks and Recreation Leadership, and guests. My name is Dr. William D. Allen, the founder and CEO of TISMAC, which stands for the Texas Supremacy of Music and Arts Conservatory. Thank you for this opportunity. I am a 14-year educator, former head band director at South Oak Cliff High School, during the back-to-back state titles, a Grammy Award-winning band director, and also a Presidential Lifetime Achievement Award honoree. My assignment is simple. Field Leaders Through the Arts. TISMAC serves at scale. Last year, we reached 1,500-plus students across 59 schools. 98% of our students passed, all classes, and graduated. 90% enrolled in college, military, or trade school. Students logged 850 hours of rehearsal and performance time. This past April, we was able to secure $3.3 million in band and dance scholarships, and we're tracking $5 million by summer of 2026. We just don't teach notes. We teach discipline, responsibility, and pride. But from 3 to 6 p.m., too many kids have no structured place to go. As budgets tighten, arts are cut first. When structure leaves, risk enters. Our solution, a community, you can not completely cultivate, hosted at a Dallas Parks and Recreation Center in Southern Dallas. Open citywide, instruments and uniforms, daily instruction, mentorship, healthy snacks, transportation support, and a safe place to belong. As momentum builds, we add on jazz band, mariachi bands, and also orchestras. Our ask is clear and collaborative. Priority access Monday through Thursday, 4 to 6 p.m., fee waivers where possible, secure storage, rehearsal field access, modest operating support for instruments, uniforms, buses, and snacks, city visibility through festivals, parades, and artists residencies. A team jobs pipeline so advanced students serve as paid junior coaches will report quarterly enrollment attendance, GPA gains, incidents, reduce performances of scholarships. Real results on the record. If we wait, another cohort slips through the cracks. If we act, we change trajectories. Let's give our kids something to march toward, not away from. Let's band together and march forward, Dallas. Thank you. Excellent. Wow. That is excellent. And you've come to the right place because I'm sure we're going to have some real band nerds here on this commission. Joe Band when I was in high school. Joe Band. Okay. Awesome. And in fact, so I want to make sure that we have, that all the commissioners know how to contact your organization. So how would they do that? Yes, I actually have my brochures where everybody wants it. Contact us. I've been working with Councilman Zarin Gracie, also with Councilman, what's the name, Mrs. Blair, and also Maxie Johnson. He was working with me at South Oak Cliff High School. So a lot of our students in the southern sector, now we've reached out to the north side of Dallas. They all come to our events. We give our scholarships. Like I said, easy access to those colleges is whatever's hard for them to overcome. We bridge that gap for those students. Okay. And for everybody that's virtual, his office is at 4041 West Wheatland. So is that close to Friendship? Yes, it's close to Friendship or Redbird Mall. And we're actually in partnership with the mating twins, with Terrence Mating. So we're working on some things as well with the cities for the economic ability side to be able to host all these students because we have a lot, a lot of kids. And so now we've just outgrown our spaces. And once again, TISMAC stands for? The Texas Supremacy of Music and Arts Conservatory. Okay. Well, I am very appreciative of you coming. We have a tight schedule today, so we're not really taking questions, you know, to you, but we certainly want to be able to get a hold of you. Yes. We can do that. So everybody that's virtual, we do have a way to contact Dr. William Allen. Yes, sir. And also I'm a member of Kappa Alpha Psi and a member of the NAACP, so we're moving in the right direction. Excellent. Excellent. It's great to have a divine nine member here talking to us. Thank you, sir. Thank you all. Thank you. And we have another public speaker, Mr. Randy Shear, and he is going to update us on the Electronic Arts Sculpture Portal. Nathan is going to speak for me. Okay. So it will take me a few seconds here. Who's now, you are the public speaker, but if someone is going to speak for you? I'm the microphone. Oh, okay. Okay. Yeah, that's the name of the device. Okay. I thought, I didn't know. Hey, man. I thought you had somebody online. It's 2021. There we go. For sure. For sure. Yeah. That's right. That's right. Timo should be here for this. Please be patient. Honorable chair and members of the Arts District Advisory Commission, thank you for allowing me to speak with you about this great opportunity to bring this incredible sculpture to Davis. I have been working with the Portal organization for over a year now, located in Berlin, Germany, as the local ambassador, I have been tasked to make Portal a reality. At the same time, the Portal will revitalize downtown Dallas with this technological sculpture, designed and created by a Lithuanian artist, Benedictus Jailis. The Portal's organization is a network of global sculptures that use a 24-second live video stream, connecting cities around the world. They have connected people from Philadelphia to Dublin, Philippines to Dublin, and soon, Ipswich, England, to the world. Presently, with upcoming milestone events like the FIFA World Cup and America 250, Dallas has the chance to house the Portal in 2026, but the window of opportunity is rapidly closing. Just imagine a person stepping into the DNA Portal Plaza with a single glance, locking eyes with a friend thousands of miles away, whom they have not seen in over a year. Imagine a rock-paper-scissors competition. Imagine a marriage proposal. Imagine school children sharing a moment to interact with pen pals in Brazil. Imagine groups of two-step dancers being shared with Calgary. Imagine the unimaginable. For Dallas, urbanistically, the Portal in the DMA South Plaza would create an anchor for the Arts District and be a dynamic hub, transforming the DMA Portal Plaza into a vibrant urban space. The Portal promises to support a multitude of unexpected activities. The Portal also ties into the DMA's future renovation plans, the Connect 2020 Master Plan, and the 1983 Sasaki Plan of creating an Arts District to reflect a multinational character. For the arts community, the Portal represents a simple step forward. It is more than just art. It's an immersive, interactive window into multiple cultures. It will cement Dallas's reputation as a city that embraces and of a global public art, putting the city on the world stage alongside cities and countries. This Portal will stimulate global dialogue and cultural understanding, and will fulfill the promise of the Arts District as a nationally and globally connected to the local economy. The Portals will be a magnet, attracting a predicted 25% increase in footfall of visitor counts per month. This increase in foot traffic to the Arts District will bring new energy to local businesses, theaters, museums, restaurants, and shops. In turn, this sculpture will invigorate the South Plaza into a lively gathering place that benefits the Ross Original Plan and the entire downtown economy. For the people of Dallas, the Portal is a chance to participate in a shared global experience. For families, groups, and schools to connect with people far away, learning about different cultures in real time. This project will foster a sense of shared humanity and civic pride, reminding everyone that we are all part of a larger global community. Finally, the Portals have the power to redefine a public space, spark imaginations, and build connections that transcend geography. Working together, we all can bring this transformative experience to Dallas, not just as a great American city, but as a great international city. Bring it to Dallas and they will come. All right. chapters.episode_title: Moving Forward on Homelessness: Miamis Lessons for Austin Discussion – Oct 23, 2012
chapters.text: Well, thanks so much, Heather, and thanks so much to all of y'all for being here tonight. Let me start off by just recognizing those folks who made that trek to Miami with us. I know there was a Mayor for Ken Cole and Councilmember Tovo, but there are a number of other folks who went there with us. Can you just raise your hand if you've been to the Center of Miami? So a lot of you folks have been. I want to thank all of y'all who have been able to make it. And for those of you who haven't, I want to encourage you to consider a trip over there. It's a great city to visit, and it's an amazing experience to see exactly what they have done with respect to this issue. Let me start off by just saying a word about the situation that we have in Austin as compared with the situation that you see there in Miami. We have, in Austin, we are blessed with an amazing core of people who are dedicated to dealing with homelessness. And they are doing the very best that they can in very, very challenging circumstances. But the reality, I think we all know, is that we're struggling on many fronts. On virtually every aspect of the homelessness situation, we are having difficulty in meeting the demands that are out there. You can see it every time you go by the corner of 7th and Natchez, the arch. And it's not the fault of the arch. I want to emphasize that. But it is a system that is simply overwhelmed. You could see it in Woldridge Park until we finally put up the fences around there and got the park fixed up. You can see it on many corners throughout the city. We have a system that is simply overwhelmed in many respects. And along with that comes a certain sense of hopelessness. And you see it on the faces of our homeless population, even right there at our homeless resource center. It's not a place that is real uplifting when you go by there and you see the folks that are out there. It is uplifting talking to the folks who are working there just to see the sense of determination and the energy and the commitment they bring to the job that they're trying to do. But the reality is it's a very discouraging situation to see the problem that we have there. The scope of the problem and the inadequacy of our response to it. And I say that as an introduction to what we saw in Miami. And the most striking thing we saw in Miami is a little hard to describe. But it is the opposite of what I just described in Austin. You go into the center in Miami and you see smiling faces. The slide that you saw here of the two women sitting and laughing around an ice table. That's for real. You actually see people smiling. It feels kind of like a college campus. You don't have crowds sitting out there out front milling around. You've got people inside as if it's a college campus. It is a bigger facility that's able to offer a lot more services. You've got an area for men and for women. You've got a place for kids. Housing for families. Playground in the middle. When you go in to actually see the area with the kids. They will come running out to you smiling and hold out their hands and greet you. The place has the atmosphere of a place that has its act together. And that is treating the people that are there with respect. And that there is a sense of purpose and accomplishment in the facility. Now, what is it that they are doing that enables them to do that? Let's just do a little bit of compare and contrast on some of what they've got going. The biggest single thing is the housing units that they have available to them. On every way you look at that, they are in a better situation than we've got. If you add up all the types of housing units together. From emergency shelter, transitional, and permanent supportive housing. They currently offer about 6,229 beds. We are currently around 2,000. Of that, they have got, on permanent supportive housing, we are somewhere around 870. They are up to 2,851. And another element of the housing situation, Dan mentioned, and it's very important. The fact that they have been the number one city for foreclosures. They, not too long ago, were down to 15% occupancy on their condos. That's a very significant difference. Because what that means is that the providers actually have some leverage. The service providers actually have some leverage with the housing providers. Because those housing providers desperately want customers. They want to get folks. And so folks who are in the business of placing clients actually have some leverage. Because they can say, we know this client may be a little challenging. But if you take this one, then we can send you four that are going to be market rate and pay you. And the housing provider has an incentive to take that. Because they are so hungry for customers that they'll take a risk with one so that they can get other solid customers. So the folks who are trying to place folks have an easier time than we do, frankly. Because here, none of the people who have the housing are having a hard time billing it. We're over a 95% occupancy. We don't have that stock of housing. So one thing we need to focus on. Well, we need to remember that the housing problem we've got is not just about permanent supported housing. It covers the whole spectrum of units that we've got. Another thing that you'll notice right away, and I think a lot of providers will appreciate, is the fact that we are woefully short on funding. Most every element of funding here is completely inadequate compared to what they've got there in Miami. The continuum of care in Miami is calculated to get about $29.4 million a year. Here, we're down to $4.7 million. Now, a lot of that has to do with the restaurant tax that Dan described. I want to emphasize on the rent-to-restaurant tax before you just say, oh, well, they're different. They've got that restaurant tax. When they started down this road and committed themselves to addressing the problem of homelessness, they did not have that homeless tax. They got their heads together, identified the problem, and figured out a solution to it. And I want to emphasize that because here it would be very easy for us to say, well, it's Texas. We're not going to be able to. We can't offer those taxes. We can't do it. But I would encourage you to stay focused on that and think about ways that we might come up with proposals and work to get those proposals passed to open up new streams of funding. Because it's going to take that kind of funding in order to adequately address the problem that's before us. What it enables them to do is, with a combination of housing units and that funding, they are able to put in place a very elaborate case management system. Dan mentioned that the 26 case managers that they've got there at the facilities at the Chapman Partnership. At our Arch, we have six case managers who do a great job of placing folks, and it's extremely important work that they do. But they can't take on the whole problem. And so what you've got there at the Arch is you've got a large population that is showing up every day seeking housing. We simply are not able to deal with everybody who's there. And so a number of those who are in case management, who we are able to offer case management to, they get to have extended stay. But because we're not, our case management just is not at the level it needs to be. The average stay now is about nine months there within that case management program there at the Arch. That's in terms of people who are being case managed and we're trying to get them into housing and jobs. Now, Dan, what is the average stay at Chapman? It's much shorter. They start with 60 days. They aim to get everybody placed within 60 days. And then if you're not placed within 60 days, you go onto a list. And they have weekly meetings with the case managers to talk about everybody who's on that list and to focus on getting those people placed. And that's what I really want to emphasize most. It is a very client-centered and personalized approach where they're able to focus on the folks who have been there for more than 60 days and figure out how to get them placed in both jobs and housing. And that is critical. Because when you are short on resources, you have to run the kind of triage that we see every night at the Arch where we actually have a lottery system to decide who's going to get to stay at the Arch for one night. Now, that is a contrast to a program in which your facility is set up as a program where you call and get informed and you get to stay for up to 60 days and you're going to be actively case managed and you're going to get individualized focus and care through the help of those case managers. And that, I think, is what really makes the most difference in terms of bringing about that atmosphere of respect and success and accomplishment. Because everyone is getting personal care. They know they're being tended to. People are actively working on helping them find jobs and get placed in housing. It's that personalized individual approach through active case management that is really the key. And, of course, it depends on having a stock of housing that you can get people placed in. We've actually got the supply of jobs that we ought to get people placed in. And we have a leg up on Miami in that regard. The big challenge is going to be finding enough housing to get people into. And then getting the case managers who can help identify the appropriate funding streams that will support the people to be in housing and get where supportive services are needed. Identifying the funding that's going to help provide those supportive services on an ongoing basis. So that is the big

Just to introduce yourself for the people watching on TV and the like. Sally Van Sickle. I am the District 9 appointee to the Commission on Seniors as well as the chair of Age-Friendly Austin Work Group, which is the commission, AARP, Austin Up, and a number of community partners. So we have three asks today. We'd like to ask City Council to adopt the plan that we've put in place, act as a sounding board for us because it is a living, breathing plan that will change over time. And be a resource to us. So I'd like to give a little history about the Commission on Seniors in Austin Up. Thank you. For those people that were not involved in city government, possibly back in 2010. Austin, in the 2010 Census, Austin had the nation's fastest growing population of ages 55 to 64, and second fastest 65 and over. Between 2010 and 2014, Texas, percentage of people 65 and over increased 50%. So it's not slowing down. It's actually increasing. And Austin is still key in that. In 2012, Mayor Leffingwell put together the Mayor's Task Force on Aging. This was a 23-member group spread across the community. We had government, we had nonprofits, and the public sector involved in this, as well as a 15-member advisory council. Out of that year-long task force came a report that they titled Embracing an Age-Diverse Austin. There were a number of recommendations that came out of that. Goals for the city, specifically, to focus on age-inclusive policies, integrating those policies into the city decision-making. And I think we made a great step when you added the two amendments to the Imagine Austin plan a few weeks ago. And then joining the AARP, World Health Organization's Age-Friendly Communities Initiative. So we did get that designation because we had the Mayor's Task Force on Aging. It's five years later, and they are looking at us and asking, what have you done since? So that is why we put together this strategic plan as the next step for the city of Austin. That we focus on affordable housing. As you know, this is an issue for everyone in Austin, but it is a key issue for a large portion of our senior population. And integrating older adults into civic life. We really want to be engaged, and I say we because I'm hitting into that age group. But we want to be engaged in what is going on in the city. We want to be involved. We've got a lot of experience that we can bring to the table. And I will say that while you always hear about the silver tsunami, it's not a tsunami. It's a reservoir that needs to be utilized. So please try not to think of it as something that's going to come in and wipe everything out. But something that can be used. So of those recommendations, there were two for vehicles of implementation. One was to create the Commission on Seniors, which was done. One, thank you, since you've been doing this for me. So the result was our commission, and we have had, well, let's, all right, so we put a mission statement in place. The commission has been implemented about three years ago. First, we're to focus on issues related to the senior population for the Austin area. Evaluate and recommend programs, practices, policies that create a positive impact and reduce the burden on seniors. Look at the needs of seniors in our community and advise city council on what those needs are. And then promote the contributions of seniors that are cultural, economic, and historical of value to Austin. So the accomplishments that we have made as a commission in those three years, we supported ending the homelessness for veterans. Forty-five percent of the homeless veterans in Austin are over the age of 55. We reviewed the tax swap proposal for AISD, and we support the conclusions of city staff that it would negatively impact our seniors. We've advocated to you on behalf of the older adults for improvements in the sidewalk, mobility, signage, signals and lighting, and expanding social service contracts. We've formed a number of workgroups around the domains of what constitutes an age-friendly city, and we've included community stakeholders in that to move us forward in building that age-friendly Austin. We have also, at our commission meetings, hosted a number of presentations. We had a very interesting presentation on cooperative housing. It's the Boomer Collaborative, really focused on the Boomer generation and doing co-op housing. Mobility has come in several times. And then a great presentation from Jackie Onhale at the UT School of Social Work for wraparound service models for low-income seniors. And the list goes on. But that tells you what we have been doing the last few years. So community goals that came out of the task force were to focus on healthy living, creating a transitions coalition, developing a health outreach program into low-income neighborhoods, and working on food availability, trying to limit the food deserts for older adults. As far as independence goes, Caregiver U is a great program that's offered. Home-based support services, home modification and repair services, making it easier for our older folks to find those people and get assistance. And then focusing on an informed community, ensuring that information is available, whether it's via website, via phone, or print material, that is a central clearinghouse for information about senior services and activities, what activities are available to them that they would be comfortable attending, and developing public awareness campaign for a lot of issues. There are several listed here, but also business continuity planning around our older population. The second vehicle of implementation recommended by the task force was an advocacy and planning organization for seniors, as well as creating a robust aging and disability resource center. From that, we developed Austin Up. It is a nonprofit that is helping. And Teresa Ferguson, who is here with me today, is the ED of that. She graciously volunteered her time for a number of months. And Austin Up is actually to the point now where they can pay her a nominal amount of money. But it is progressing. We're very excited about it. And with that, I'm going to turn the rest of the presentation over to Teresa. Thank you, Sally. So I'm Teresa Ferguson. I, back in the early 2000s, I served on the Music Commission as its chair. And so, in 2003, we moved my husband's parents here. And so, here I was supporting live music and promoting music and musicians. And then, I saw my city, my cool city, through the eyes of a couple octogenarians with some health challenges. And so, that changed my opinion a little bit. Still a cool city, but I really think that we need to just pivot just a little bit to view urban planning through a different lens. And so, that's why I'm so excited to be here. Thank you. So, Austin Up, we are raising the profile of our senior population. And we're preparing the next generation for the future of aging. This is not a front-line service provider. We truly are an organization that connects the dots between the nonprofits, the state agencies, seniors, boomers, caregivers, just kind of moving Austin forward. We're also working with our technologists, our entrepreneurs, people who are in their garages, maybe developing wearable devices, apps, and services for the aging space, but maybe don't have a voice. What I found from talking to these folks is that when they went to talk to VCs for venture capital, aging's not sexy. So, we're putting a spotlight on those folks, too, to give them some recognition in our community for the good work that they're doing. Our motto at Austin Up is, aging, everyone's doing it. So, we have early sponsors. The nonprofit was formed in 2014. Lots of great community advocates, wonderful people supporting our work. And one of the key areas that we're working in is livability, and thus the Age-Friendly Austin Five-Year Plan. Just a little bit of background. The Network of Age-Friendly Communities is something that the World Health Organization and AARP have devised and have nurtured. Since 2012, the network has grown to 102 communities representing more than 51 million constituents. In Texas, and this is very important, Mayor and City Council members, Austin, is leading the way toward becoming age-friendly. So, we're very, very proud of that. The process is outlined in this next slide. We talk about entering the network. I think someone mentioned earlier that back in 2012 and 2013, when the Mayor's Task Force was doing its wonderful work and they issued its report, we earned the recognition of an age-friendly city. However, since then, nothing's been done. And so, we are at risk of losing that designation. So, this is the process, and it is a process. And I'm happy to say that AARP, especially AARP Texas, has provided the tools and the best practices to help us along the way. So, what we did is we worked on our Age-Friendly Austin Plan. And we used a little bit of a framework devised by the World Health Organization, the eight domains of livability. So, things like housing and transportation, things you've talked about so much, it's like looking at those areas through the eyes of an older community member. So today's presentation, just the overview is we'll go into some background, talk about the proposed project, our staff recommendation, and recommended next steps. So most of you that have been on the board for a while know that the Oak Cliff Gateway District was originally created in 1992. It was substantially amended a few times. We've got three sub-districts, Oak Cliff Gateway, which is the original area, the Bishop Jefferson, and the Clarendon Beckley Keys, which is the newest sub-district. Altogether, the district has seen over $1.5 billion in new taxable value over its base year. This project is located at the southeast corner of Jefferson Bulletin Boulevard and Ewing Avenue. The property collectively is on the tax roll for a little over $4 million currently. We've estimated that the proposed project at completion will have a taxable value somewhere around $60 million based on some comparables. It has PD zoning. It's in Council District 4. It's in the Bishop Jefferson sub-district of Oak Cliff Gateway. Here's some photos of existing conditions. It's an assemblage of six parcels and an abandoned alley. Currently, there's storage warehouse structures that have reached the end of their useful life. The property was acquired between 2019 and 2022. So, just kind of going through the project summary. So, the project developers, BMH Oak Cliff LLC, and they are looking to design, fund, and construct what we're calling the North Oak Cliff Mixed Use and Mixed Income Development Project. The proposed scope would include a five-story mixed-use, mixed-income development with approximately 265 units and about 11,643 square feet of leaseable ground floor retail non-residential space. Streetscape improvements along with other amenities such as a dog play area are proposed. Total project cost is a little over $92 million. Here's the site plan of the site there. You can see. And then project renderings. You can see the, you know, the full illustrated vision for the project. And it's a walking distance to the new Halpern Park, Deck Park. The other part of the project is proposed is to do some off-site public infrastructure improvements, water, wastewater, stormwater. The estimated cost of those off-site improvements are about $1.5 to $2 million. The wastewater improvements will have the benefit of adding capacity to an entire sewer shed, which is about 11 acres of property in the surrounding area. The project went through the Urban Design Peer Review Panel in March of 2025. There are a number of recommendations. Hopefully, if you had a chance to go through those in advance, I won't read all of those. So, there were several rounds of response and comments from the developer. And then there was a substantial update on the design that was presented in August of 2026. So, they have satisfied the staff and panel recommendations for the project. Sorry. You're saying these have been satisfied? Yes. The Urban Design Peer Review comments. Yeah. So, here we have sources and uses. These are permanent sources, the permanent loan, developer equity, and the TIF subsidy. So, the developer or the TIF subsidy is about 31%, which is relatively common for a project like this in our TIF districts these days with a medium density, affordable housing, the kind of amenities that we've got planned for the project. There's a table with the proposed uses. The developer fee is below average. The costs have all been reviewed by our outside underwriter and deemed to be appropriate. So, the staff recommendation, we had a letter of intent signed with the developer October 19th. Based on the staff recommendation of $29 million, we have an approximate budget breakdown that includes environmental remediation, demolition, public infrastructure improvements, and an economic development grant to make the project feasible. We're proposing that the TIF subsidy would be paid in about two payments. The first installment would be $2 million for off-site infrastructure, and that would be based on actual costs at the time that those improvements are completed and accepted by the city. And then future installments would be the balance up to $27 million, based on, you know, substantial completion, verification of information, compliance with all other terms of the agreement. Some other conditions, fairly common, we want to make sure that the developer has all of their financing in place before we execute the agreement. Required project components are at least 250 new multifamily units, at least 10,000 square feet of rentable ground floor space, and site improvements, public and private, necessary to deliver the project, including a minimum of 150 structured parking spaces. Minimum investment, we're acquiring $60 million, that does not include land acquisition, because the property was purchased a few years ago, so it requires a lot of our typical tangible things like site work, hard construction costs, and professional fees, such as architecture and engineering, for that to be invested by December 31st, 2030. Building permit deadline would be December 2027, again, substantial completion, by December 31st, 2030, should we need to have public access to any infrastructure not owned by the city, we would ask for an easement, or some type of instrument. Again, we talked about the design review, that's been satisfied, we just need to make sure that their final permit drawings conform with that. The approved designs affordability component, we would require that 20% of the total units are affordable to 80% area median family income, and they would be de-restricted for 15 years. Is the 15 years common? Yes, that's our standard de-restriction bonus. And then, by city ordinance, all projects receiving any kind of subsidy from the city, also have to make a good faith effort when it comes to vouchers, you know, allowing at least 10% of units to be available for voucher holders, should there be folks coming with vouchers. We're also asking for a minimum of 40% of the ground floor space to be occupied, property management review, small business inclusion. This replaced the city's previous minority women-owned business program because of federal directives. The city's revamped its focus now to be on small businesses, so the goal is 33% participation for certified small business enterprises. And so, the developer will work with our Office of Procurement Services to identify potential vendors and provide opportunities, or at least give them an opportunity to bid on those scopes of work. Quarterly reporting, operating and maintenance agreement for non-standard improvements, this is a common requirement. Quarterly reporting, local hiring, local hiring, again, for any jobs created by the project, we would want a local hiring plan. Minor modifications, this is fairly standard, you know, if they do need a deadline extension with concurrence from the TIF board or minor modifications to the project would come before the board. And if the board recommends those modifications, then the director would approve those. A post-construction audit and possible reduction of TIF subsidies. So, if their actual costs fall below $82.6 million, we could look at deducting our TIF subsidy by a commensurate $24,000 for every $100 or $100,000 below that. So, this is something that we started doing a few years ago with projects as a way to, you know, a lot of times developers have to work with the budget, but then if their costs are actually less, we want to make sure that we're not overpaying the subsidy. So, this is a provision that allows us to take, you know, a review of the actual costs once the project's built. Minimum, ongoing minimum occupancy requirements. So, we want to see that for at least a five-year period that the ground floor space continues to have that minimum 40% occupancy. So, we have active ground floor spaces. Assignment until the project's complete. We won't allow an assignment to anything but a direct affiliate of the project. Any proceeds can be assigned to a lender. So, that's a fairly standard provision. Force majeure. Again, this is a standard provision. Default to recapture. Again, if there's an uncured default, we have the ability to potentially recapture funds. So, if the board is favorable today, we would look at going to the council's economic development committee December 1st and then council December 9th. We'll just kind of quickly go through the appendix, which has the development team, project team there. We've got project underwriting. Again, we had an outside underwriter review the project. The developer initially asked for $39 million. We went through a rigorous process with our outside underwriter and have recommended a subsidy of $29 million. They've assessed all aspects of the project, that the development team is unqualified, that there's adequate debt and financing information, cost reasonableness, and that the proposed subsidy does not unduly enrich the developer. Here's a tip budget chart, so you'll see that if this project were approved, that there would still be capacity, budget capacity, in the Bishop Jefferson sub-district of about $18 million. Other sub-districts of the tip have their own budgets, and so there's still a lot of budget capacity overall to do projects in the tip district. We'll follow our increment allocation policy. That's a pretty straightforward condition, and based on our current estimates, we would anticipate that this project, upon completion, would be paid over several years with a full payoff made

tags.definition: Street trees and green infrastructure: Street trees, canopy, rain gardens, bioswales, and living infrastructure.
Debt, bonds, TIF, and subsidies: Public debt, bonds, tax increment financing, incentives, and development subsidies.
Public art and culture: Public art, cultural facilities, local cultural programming, or creative districts.
Form-based codes: Form-based zoning, regulating physical form and public-realm relationships.

Rezoning (individual case): An individual property or site-specific zoning action: rezoning a specific parcel, a planned development (PD) zoning case, a specific/special use permit, a replat, or a variance request tied to one property or a small set of parcels. Do not use this for a citywide or district-wide change to the zoning code text; use the "zoning-reform" tag for those instead.
Infill and redevelopment: Reuse or intensification of already-served land within a city.
Walk, bike, and transit access: Walking, cycling, transit access, or multimodal connectivity.
Third places and public life: Informal social gathering places and the everyday public life of a community.
Parks and recreation: Parks, trails, recreation facilities, and access to everyday outdoor space.
Annexation and outward expansion: Annexation, greenfield growth, outward expansion, or its fiscal consequences.
Street safety and Vision Zero: Traffic safety, serious-injury reduction, or Vision Zero programs.
Parking mandates: Minimum parking requirements and their effect on development or public space.

tags.definition: Zoning reform: A citywide or district-wide change to the zoning code text itself -- a text amendment, a code rewrite, a unified development code update, or a comprehensive rezoning that applies broadly across many properties. Do not use this for an individual property's rezoning, platting, variance, or planned-development case; use the "rezoning" tag for those instead.
Infrastructure maintenance and liability: Maintenance backlogs, lifecycle costs, liabilities, and service obligations.
Traffic calming and road diets: Street redesigns that slow traffic or reclaim excess roadway space.
Accessory dwelling units: ADUs, backyard cottages, garage apartments, and similar secondary homes.
Historic preservation: Historic districts, landmark protection, preservation incentives, or reuse of historic fabric.

Rezoning (individual case): An individual property or site-specific zoning action: rezoning a specific parcel, a planned development (PD) zoning case, a specific/special use permit, a replat, or a variance request tied to one property or a small set of parcels. Do not use this for a citywide or district-wide change to the zoning code text; use the "zoning-reform" tag for those instead.
Incremental development: Small, phased, locally-scaled development anywhere in the city.
Community wealth and local ownership: Local ownership, community wealth building, cooperatives, and resident benefit.
Adaptive reuse: Converting existing buildings to new uses rather than replacing them.
Infill and redevelopment: Reuse or intensification of already-served land within a city.
Parks and recreation: Parks, trails, recreation facilities, and access to everyday outdoor space.
Walk, bike, and transit access: Walking, cycling, transit access, or multimodal connectivity.

chapters.title: 2:00 PM - Zoning and Neighborhood Plan Amendments (Public Hearings and Possible Action)
chapters.text: Members, the item before us is the 2 o'clock time-certain matter related to zoning, and I'm going to ask staff to make a presentation. Thank you, Mayor. Mayor and Council, Joy Harden with the Planning Department. Your zoning agenda begins with item number 36, C14H, 2022-0176, and there's a staff postponement request to your May 18th Council meeting. Item 37 is NPA-2022-0009.01, staff postponement request to your May 18th Council meeting. The related rezoning item is number 38, C14-2022-0149. This item has been withdrawn from this agenda only. It will be placed on your May 18th Council meeting to be considered with a notice, and so no action is required on this item. Item 39 is C14-2022-0168. This item is being offered for consent second and third reading with the following motion sheet that I will now read. Add the following conditional overlay to part two to read, except for side yard and rear yard setbacks of the property, development of the property must comply with neighborhood commercial LR site development regulations. And with that, again, a staff is offering this item for consent second and third readings. Item 40 is C14-2023-0006. This will be a discussion item to speak to the merits of the postponement request that was made by the neighborhood to your May 18th Council meeting. Moving on to the addendum items, item 46 is C14-2022-0203. This item is being offered for consent third reading. Council supported this item on second reading last week and to continue discussions, and there has been an agreement with some of the neighbors in the applicant. So with that, again, this item is being offered for consent third reading. Although I do think we do have a few speakers on this. Item 48 is C14-2022-0076. Again, this was an item passed last week on first reading only for continued discussions. And although this item has a ballot petition, we did receive an email from the neighborhood representative withdrawing their opposition, and there is a signed agreement. And so, again, we can offer this for consent second and third readings. And lastly, item 49 is C14-2022-0040. And there is an applicant postponement request to your May 18th Council meeting. Members, does anybody have any questions of staff? All right. We will go to the consent items. The consent items are item 39 on second and third reading with the amendment as read by Ms. Hardin. Item number 46 on third reading. Item number 48 on second and third reading. Item number 40 has been pulled. We will hear first from those speakers that wish to speak on the consent items. Then we will call up. I'll call up item number 40, and we will hear from speakers on item number 40. So with that, I'll ask the city clerk if we can start the speakers on the consent agenda. At this time, we have no remote speakers, so we will take up in person. Thank you. Mohamed Arami on item 39. Hello again. Hello. How are you? Been here last time and raised my position to CS1 zoning. And I wrote to every one of you, sent you an email. I spoke to one of the staffers and explained to him why I'm against it. And he told me that I have an option of stay opposed or apply for rezoning for my property and pay the fee again. And I told him I already paid the fee. I don't want to pay the fee. So I stay opposed. And my opposition is to the fact that there is a rules in the book. It prevents such a jump from LO to CS1. And I couldn't get that. It was just last year. And they told me there is a rules in there to prevent that. I comply with that. And then six months later, there is an application and they're asking the same thing and getting approved. And I really don't understand this. This is like double standard here. Why can't I get it? And then the other party can get it. The rules in the book. You guys or your predecessors created the rules. The other side is telling me that the rule is old, needs to be changed. I have no problem with that. Somebody needs to do that within your old department of zoning or whatever, not on individual basis. I come and ask you, somebody else come and ask you, you cannot do one at a time. You change the rule, we all, you know, abide with it. That's all I have to say as far as my opposition. If you want to give these things to this applicant, I have no problem with it. Apply that same to me. I already pay my fee of $12,500. We are next door neighbor. Thank you very much, sir. Thank you, sir. Appreciate your comments. Anna Aguirre, on item 46, on deck, Frances Acuna. Frances Acuna, on deck, Mario Cantu. Mario Cantu. Monica Guzman. Item 46. Good afternoon, Mayor and Council. I'm Monica Guzman, Policy Director at Go Austin, Vamos Austin, speaking on item 46. Montopolis is not in the GABA zip codes of focus, but we stand in solidarity with adjacent Eastern Crescent communities experiencing rapid gentrification and displacement of deeply rooted residents. This morning, we received the news they successfully negotiated an increase in three-bedroom units from five to 20. The developers added 10% of the units, 60% MFI, bringing it to 30. Building height is capped at 75 feet. And they'll make a lump sum contribution of $75,000 to the community benefit. But it is still a less than optimal deal because it shouldn't, oops, because the community didn't get everything they wanted or needed. We are aware work has been done for several weeks. And it is fortunate they were able to further improve the agreement. But it shouldn't and doesn't need to be finalized at the proverbial 11th hour. Going forward, we are urging Council to slow down the process. Instead of rushing by consent with no discussion, you must protect and respect the public process. Encourage developers to take time for authentic community engagement, especially in Districts 1 through 4 in the Eastern Crescent. A rushed process lacking community participation in the public process is a recipe for disaster. Can and will set dangerous precedents leading to gentrification and displacement. Last week, Council approved the Project Connect Anti-Displacement Fund's roadmap. Such roadmaps are dangerous when lacking a public process led by vulnerable and impacted community members. It included reduced funding to community-based organizations and moved it to land acquisition. That's disappointing since CBOs can provide direct support to vulnerable residents. We encourage Council to consider using the land acquisition funds in public-private partnerships to ensure truly, deeply affordable housing, especially in the Eastern Crescent and other vulnerable communities. Also, you've already heard a few names, they and others, who registered as opposed or neutral to this development but may not or will not be able to make it at all. It needs to be stated clearly, lack of physical presence does not equate lack of concern. Thank you, Speaker. Thank you. Tanya Payne, item 46, with Carolyn Kroom on deck. Carolyn Kroom, item 46, with Barbara MacArthur on deck. Barbara MacArthur, Roy Whaley, Ms. A.L. Ramos. Cynthia Vasquez, Tona Vasquez, Kalu James, Ann Tech, Erica Reyes, David King, Betsy Greenberg, Jill Parrish, Helen Plevik, Bill Bunch. Jolene Kielbasa, Jonathan Kinney, Zenobia Joseph, item 49. I think 49 is postponed, Mayor. It has been. So your comments would be on the merits of the postponement alone. Thank you, Mayor, Council. I'm Zenobia Joseph, speaking on the merits of the loan to item 49, which is 1-0-0-1-7-1-1-2. That's our road. Specifically, I would just ask you, as I have in the past, to look at transportation when the item comes back before Council. And I gave you written testimony that gives you some background information on the transportation. But I appreciate the postponement. Thank you. If you have any questions, I'll gladly answer them at this time. Thank you. Appreciate your testimony. Thank you. You're welcome. The only remaining speaker is on item 40. Very good. Thank you. Members, we will take up, as I indicated, the consent agenda. And let me start by asking if there's anyone who wishes to discuss or speak on one of the consent agenda items. That being the case, is there any? Yes. Councilmember Codry. Yeah, I just want to quickly touch on item number 48. I just want to say I'm very pleased with the outcome of the case. I'm very thankful for the neighborhood and the neighbors and their involvement. Everything they brought up were legitimate concerns about the applicant's proposal. But I know that a lot of good faith conversations occurred involving all those negotiations from the neighborhood association to the applicant to our own staff in the D9 office. And Melissa and Natalie, effort was put in and work was done. And so I'm glad we were able to get to an agreement that satisfies everyone's interest. It's a great example of how collaboration in the city can lead to, you know, great productive solutions that will make Austin a more livable and lively city. So I just want to thank the applicant again, the Neighborhood Association, and for Natalie and Melissa on our team for their hard work and engagement. And that's why we have the positive results we do. Good deal. Thank you very much, Councilmember. Does anybody else want to be heard on any of the consent agenda items? Is there anyone that wishes to be shown abstaining on any of the consent agenda items? Anyone wishing to be shown as recusing themselves from an item? Is there anyone wishing to be shown voting no on any of the consent agenda items? That being the case, is there a motion to approve the consent agenda as it was identified and read? Councilmember Velasquez moves to adopt the consent agenda. The Mayor Pro Tem seconds that motion. Councilmember Harper-Madison, I see you and I appreciate that. Is there any objection to the adoption of the consent agenda as read? Hearing none, the consent agenda is adopted. We'll now go to item number 40, which was a pulled item that was pulled for discussion on the postponement.

chapters.text: So, as I stated earlier, we're going to jump back into item one on the agenda for this evening and go through the agenda items. I just want to let the record show that Commissioner Pernetta and Commissioner Sanchez have joined us. Commissioner Cole is still absent. First item on the agenda is the minutes. And we had an update that was distributed in terms of who's absent and who's present. Is there any other updates that need to happen to the minutes? Great. So I do want Haley to update us on the new draft we got. Yeah, just one quick cleanup item on the plat. There was a reference to actually an older plat that this company had done, and they realized that was an error being left on this plat, so they just removed that and sent over a new draft. I don't know if any of you noticed it. It was a note referencing cross-access to an adjoining property to the north that doesn't actually exist. So they cleaned that up and provided this new copy for you all this evening. Great. Any questions about this item or really item 3B while Haley's up here? Great. Thank you, Haley. I'm here before you tonight with a request for an alternate development plan, ADP number 18-0006. The applicant is requesting to deviate from Sections 35, 13, 13, 4, non-residential and mixed-use buildings, and Section 35, 13, 10, access, parking, and circulation requirements. I should note that 35, 13, whoops, 10, staff worked with the applicant, and that issue was resolved, so that is not part of this request tonight. The site consists of 3.42 acres located in the NRMU district, and the applicant is proposing professional office park. The future land use designation of the site is neighborhood mixed-use, which does correspond with the NRMU district. This is applied to neighborhoods or districts where the predominant use is residential. However, they want to have a neighborhood service office-type component in it. And one of the requirements in this is to ensure that buildings are of appropriate scale and intensity to complement the surrounding neighborhood. The proposed deviations as listed, Section 35, I can read all of these different section numbers if you want, or I can just go through the deviations. I think going through deviations will be adequate. Okay. Thanks. Thank you. And that also applies to the next deviation, which requires at least 60% of the street frontage to have buildings within 10 feet of the front property line. Again, that 20-foot required easement along Teasley Lane prevents the buildings from getting that close to the property line. Developments shall have a minimum floor area of 0.4. Plazas and pedestrian areas shall count as floor area for the purpose of meeting the minimum FAR. The site, as shown, has an FAR of 0.23, excluding the pedestrian areas and plazas. If you add them in, they have an FAR of 0.27. The purpose for the deviation, as you'll see in my next exhibit, is the easements that are on the property. There are so many easements on the property, it would be difficult to bring the site up to the full FAR without going very tall. The next one is parking areas shall be located behind buildings or on one or both sides. The way the applicant has designed the site design is that we have one row of parking in front of each building. And this also will provide pedestrian access into the area. The site, as you can see, the site is pretty deep. It's deeper than it is wide. And with having the one row of parking along the front of the buildings, it also provides sidewalk access from Teasley all the way back to the back of the site, enabling the pedestrian. Yes, sir. Thank you, Chair. Could you show us where the walkways are? The walkways are right here and here and here. You'll see it better on another slide that doesn't have all the easements, John. Okay. And while I'm on it, too, we talk about this being a pedestrian-oriented bill. So can we address the – is there a sidewalk out front on Teasley? There are sidewalks all along here. Along Teasley? Along Teasley? Oh, yes, definitely. Okay. Okay. Couldn't quite pull that out myself. Thank you. And the final deviation is the building shall be set back not more than 15 feet of the right-of-way, and we already talked about that. This is an exhibit showing all the easements that encumber the site. There is the 20-foot utility easement, which I spoke of. There is a TPNL easement along the front portion of the site. This is a court-ordered access easement to this site, this lot right over here. This is a 30-foot access easement, and this is a 35-foot drainage easement. So there are a lot of easements on the site, which the applicant had to work around in order to develop the site. Kinsher Smith, what exactly is a court-ordered access easement? Well, from my understanding is the former property owner of this site would not give access to the property owner here, and this is a landlocked lot. The southern lot is a landlocked lot? Yes, yes, it is. The southwestern lot. And from my understanding is the court-ordered the previous property owner to provide access.
