chapters.title: Item 1 (Part 2 of 3)
chapters.text: All right. Thank you all for coming back relatively close to when I asked you to be here. We'll give you a half a little start. We'll share it with you in the future, so. So I've heard a number of comments about related metrics or context in terms of other data sets. So ways that you're typically used to seeing performance measure information is in the budget document, there's a list of measures and then there's numbers next to them for a number of years. Those days are going away. We have a number of tools available to us where we're able to post information. You can literally have a main metric that you start out with, but you can dig down into the data behind it with a simple click. We also, on that same page, we can include all related metrics and other data sets. So you may not, there may be something that you don't want to set a particular target for, but there's a particular data set that provides additional context and insights that relate to a particular metric. And all of this would be online, available at any time, from anywhere, to anyone. So that is, that's one of my big goals, is to make performance measure information far more accessible, far more consumable, regardless of if you work for the city, you're elected to the city, or you just live in the city, or you live not in the city. We want to just make it more accessible and make it more understandable. So I wish I had something just on the fly that I could show you, but we have some really great tool sets. That's the open data portal that y'all are familiar with, that the city has, and the vendor that provides that, as well as various other tool sets. It's opening far more doors for us than we've had available to us in the past to be able to present performance information, and pretty frankly, any information. Right, and I think Leslie or Ann, somebody had mentioned the idea of, and geographic, you know, can I see it from a visual, a geographic thing? For data that is that way, it's easy to, you know, I say it's easy. Somebody has to do the work, but it's relatively straightforward now to do that. Where before, we're like, we'll get back to you in three months, and it'll be a hard copy map, and you'll only get one copy of it. Yeah, you're able to embed maps. We're also in a partnership with Esri, that is the company that does all of our GIS software, so we're working actively with them. The segmentation aspect of all of these measures and all of this information is incredibly important, so these tools, whether it's through Esri or through Chicago, are incredibly important for us on how we can present this information and make it so you can break it down and dig down into it anyway and have a better understanding of how things are happening, and you're not limited to just citywide. You can be looking at things in a particular zip code or a particular demographic, whatever the case may be. Great. Without further ado, turn it over to Culture and Lifelong Learning. All right. Thank you, Steve. Good morning, Mayor and Council, Ray Bray, City Manager's Office. I'm also the Outcome Champion for Culture and Lifelong Learning. Just a reminder that we used to be called Culture and Learning Opportunities, but we have had a name change because part of our outcome has now shifted over to Jackie's team, economic opportunity and affordability. It's that educational component, educational attainment, which is now part of their workforce development category. So just to kind of the distribution part is that they're pretty much handling everything involving more formal learning, academic, K-12, and post-secondary, and we are handling the portion involving lifelong learning, which we define as personal growth and development, personal enrichment. So with that, I'm going to go ahead, and I know in the interest of time to move forward, I'm going to hand it over to my project manager, Laura Foss, who's just done an incredible job. I want to recognize her, as well as the wonderful efforts of our subject matter expert, Megan Wells from Economic Development. I've had a very, very strong team, and I'm very, very happy to engage in this conversation with you this morning, to see about our metrics that we've come up with, and to see what you think, and to take your feedback and engage in the conversation. So, Laura, over to you. Thanks, Ray. Good morning. Laura Foss, project manager for the Culture and Lifelong Learning Outcome. My intro is very, very short in the interest of time. I'm just going to go through each of the indicator categories to kind of set the table and get your frame of mind in the culture and learning area. The first indicator category, quality, accessibility, and diversity of venues, civic and cultural events, programs, and resources. We're really interested in accessibility of the resources, venues, programs, and events in the city of Austin. That gives us a sense of the stability of our culture and lifelong learning opportunities and the quality of the programs that we provide and venues that we provide. B, vibrancy and stability of the creative industry ecosystem. This is really a short and long-term ways to increase prosperity of organizations and individuals. We really want our creatives to be able to do the work that they want to do and to do it in Austin. We want to keep it in Austin. I'd like to say that our creative industry creates a $4.35 billion industry and generates $71 million in city tax revenue. However, my colleague has reminded me that that is data from 2012 and that I shouldn't repeat those numbers, however, I'm happy that I have committed just those two to memory. Unlike my hero, Ed Vaino, who has committed every number in the city to memory, I've just managed to memorize those two. But she also let me know that we are currently underway, there's a study underway right now to get current numbers for that. And I imagine you, like myself, are really interested to know if those have gone up or down in the past 15 years. C, five years. Five years. Math, also not my strong suit. Committing numbers to memory, not so great. C, appreciation and respect and welcoming of all people and cultures, even those who are math-averse. We see ourselves as being a really progressive and accepting city. However, that's really not the case. There are a number of our constituents who don't feel welcome here and are moving out because of that. And I think that we would like to become who we see ourselves as we are, as we'd like to be. And the last one, and then we can dive right in, is honoring and preserving of historical and ethnic heritage. There are many culture and cultural markers and traditions that are leaving Austin. They've been here for generations and they're disappearing. And we want to harness those and make sure we capture them and create a welcoming place for them to stay. And the last one is a new one that you'll see. This is replacing educational attainment is lifelong learning. And many, many studies show that rich culture makes cities attractive. And people who experience a variety of cultures are more accepting, they're more respectful, and they're even better at conflict resolution. And so with that, I invite you to dive in. Great. Thanks, Laura. Thanks, Greg. So let's take indicator category A. So feedback for the team about ways that you'd like to see them strengthen and improve, maybe add, I don't know, things here about trying to measure the quality accessibility and diversity of the venues and programs. Laura. Eighty-five. Eighty-five, okay. Eighty-five. I was just wondering, because I want to talk about it. Seriously, they haven't been, but this is one measure not to a sense exactly like it is, and that's why this is written this way, because you need to do a pre, sort of what is their true goal to do that, and then in a post, which would be, did we meet their expectations? So no, and that's why it's a new metric. I remember how, when we were trying to get people to have a card to swipe in, how people were resistant to that. How would we do that with the resistance we got with that exercise? It's still going to be difficult. We're actually coming back to a work session very soon to talk about the card card, but we'll do that through two mechanisms. One is through the opportunity through the card, but the other one is through the surveys that we would do pre and post. They're working on that now, and that's why this is a metric to find out really if we're meeting their goals when it comes to programs and their satisfaction. And I think the issue on the monthly was just that you're running programs all the time, so that when you're in a position to collect that data on an ongoing basis, you could look at every month what's going to happen. It doesn't have to happen at that frequency, but it's one that the cycle would actually happen at that frequency. Other, Anne? On A3, I would suggest some drill down, and I see this as a new metric, so I'm sure that's the intention, but I want to make sure that we're talking about real access and the ability, access to affordable places to artists, for example, for creative space. And so this is a survey. I also want to understand their ability to maintain their access to that service and a number of other details that we would have to know to actually really understand the extent to which they really have access. I just want to find out, certainly, how this, or maybe for Laura, how the piece on quality and accessibility embraces, for example, our aquatics and the master plan that we have for them, and also community centers and the conditions of the various facilities. Does this contemplate facilities? I think we've found that in A2 also. So were you talking about A5 or A2? I see facilities older than A2. Okay. And I think also you're going to see recreational facilities. I think there's going to come up in the health one and two. So I think this was focused more on the cultural and reshoring facilities, so libraries and other

chapters.title: 2. Presentation and discussion on Austin Light Rail Update – Austin Transit Partnership staff
chapters.text: Next up, we have discussion items. Presentation and discussion on Austin Light Rail update. Austin Transit Partnership staff. And I believe we have a presentation. Thank you. I think for the camera, don't they need to be up at the front? Are you good? Okay. Okay. Great. Thank you. All right. Thank you for having us. And we'll do quick introductions and then jump into our update. I'm Lindsay Wood with Austin Transit Partnership. Lisa Storr, Austin Transit Partnership. Daryl Lozano with Austin Transit Partnership. Yannis Banks with Austin Transit Partnership. All right. And before we jump into the update, I want to talk a little bit about just who we are and why we are here. So Austin Transit Partnership was created as a requirement out of the referendum to bring light rail to Austin. And we're here today to share an update that light rail is underway. And we are seeking input and feedback on this critical milestone in the federal process to bring federal dollars to Austin to help fund this project. Uh, we've recently hosted four open house meetings to share some updates on the project. And we're making our way through various venues across the community like this one to gather that critical input, uh, both in terms of, uh, feedback on our draft environmental impact statement, as well as our preliminary designs to help us inform what will be the final environmental impact statement. And to guide how we carry the design forward from here. So next slide, please. And because this is Austin's first light rail, I want to highlight a few of the unique characteristics that it will bring here. Uh, light rail is frequent and, you know, more frequent than some of the rail modes you might be familiar with, like commuter rail. Uh, whereas light rail operates every five to 10 minutes. So you don't really need to look up the schedule and when the next train is going to be there, but you can just go to the station at your convenience and know that a train is coming soon. Uh, light rail is reliable because it's in its own dedicated space. So it's not sharing a lane with traffic, but actually has its own, uh, right away and transit way. And it's accessible. It has stations that are located frequently along the alignment. Uh, so it's not far to get from one station, uh, to the next. It's also fully electrically powered. And next slide. Thank you. Uh, so this first phase of light rail extends from 38th and Guadalupe and comes down Guadalupe in a street running alignment running in the middle of the street down through, uh, the west side of the UT campus into downtown where it then turns right or turns east on third street. And comes over to Trinity turning South again and, and passing alongside the convention center crossing over ladybird Lake on a new light rail bridge that will also have bicycle and pedestrian connectivity to split into two separate branches. South of the river, uh, one going south along South Congress to old Torf and one going east along East riverside drive out to what we call the yellow jacket station or just shy of 71. The project also includes priority extensions that were informed by community input and hearing what people wanted most as the next phase of the project. Uh, because we are designing this to be an expandable system to grow with Austin and our preferred priority extension being the one to the airport, uh, from that yellow jacket, East end of line, extending into the airport and connecting into our soon to be, uh, expanded Austin airport. Uh, and there's also an extension planned from 38 street going north to connect to crest view. Uh, part of this update that we're here to share today and is published with our draft environmental impact statement, our recommendations on a series of design options. And those options are generally categorized as thinking about where stations are located, how many of them are there, how are they spaced, uh, multimodal integration and how the light rail will interact with all modes of travel and including vehicular traffic, buses, bicycles, and pedestrians. And also how we cross Lady Bird Lake, uh, and, and how we bring that bridge structure down to the ground. So we are recommending to add a station downtown near Wooldridge square. We're recommending to keep, uh, the East Riverside stations at Montopolis, but relocate or shift really one of the stations, um, to grove. In order to help connect with the planned, uh, affordable housing developments at that location, as well as provide a connection to ACC, uh, Riverside campus. We are recommending to extend that bridge over Lady Bird Lake that I mentioned and keep that elevated through the waterfront station and through the junction of bringing the South and East branches of the line together. Uh, and then tying the bridge back down when it comes into the natural hills in that area, as opposed to coming to ground first, and then going right back up those hills. Uh, and we are recommending improvements along East Riverside Drive, where we have a, a wider right of way and some really great opportunities to help move people in a comfortable and safe way, connecting them not only to the light rail system, uh, but really all through the neighborhoods in this area, which I think Lisa, you're going to talk a little bit about that. Next slide, please. So here is a conceptual visualization of what we are calling the greenway. One of our staff recommendations that Lindsay just went through this option brings both a pedestrian and bicycle path nearby adjacent to the light rail in sort of the median of East Riverside drive in between the two, uh, vehicular travel lanes, this new greenway would stretch from Lakeshore station all the way to Yellow Jacket station. So through five stations, long East Riverside drive and would form a new way to connect sort of to the hike and bike trail and all the way out along this corridor. We are also including, um, additional shared use paths on the outside of the curb edges here. But we think that the opportunity for a shaded tree lined area in this space could be really phenomenal. Um, we think there's a lot more opportunity for tree planting here, uh, as opposed to on the back of curb because of overhead and underground utility conflicts, as well as driveways that intersect a lot of locations there. Next slide. Another location that we're really, uh, excited to show off is a more pedestrian oriented drag. So this is a rendering showing what the UT station could look like, um, near 22nd street, where we really only have trains at the light rail. We have buses, bikes, and pedestrians in this area. So we are removing, um, personal vehicles from this section of this, of the alignment, which is very exciting. Next slide. And then the last rendering we have here to show you is at Old Torf. So this is the south end of line, uh, for phase one. And this is really imagining, you know, this is the new HEB there, but really imagining what it could be like to hop on and hop off at a destination near you. I'll turn it over to Darren. All right. Thank you, Lisa. Uh, next slide, please. So one thing to note, and we wanted to provide an update on tonight, is the actual process that we're going through. Um, right now we're going through a federal process. We're working with the federal government as a partner in the investment of light rail. And so, of course, we have to work through their process. We're working through right now what's called project development. And what project development requires is completion of an environmental impact statement, as, uh, Lindsay mentioned at the beginning of the presentation. But we also want to share what we're looking ahead toward. Um, this next year, we're going to actually work to bring a contractor on board to advance design and construction as we line up for those future phases, what construction anticipated to start in 2027, uh, what light rail operation anticipated in 2033. Next slide. So, as I mentioned, as part of the, um, federal process, we completed this draft environmental impact statement. And this is really an opportunity for us to share our work. And this graphic really signifies all the various elements that we looked at in terms of the, um, environmental impact statement itself. Anything that you can really think of is assumed or included in the document. One thing to note as well is that we worked very closely with our partners at the city of Austin and at CAP Metro as we developed this document. So, what the document actually entails is a summary of what's there today, uh, what the potential of effects could be as a result of light rail. And, and really important is what are proposed mitigation measures. That's all encompassed as part of this, um, actual environmental impact statement. Um, one thing to note as well is, as part of the process, we, obviously, we very, very much value community input. And so, as part of this, um, document itself, this was released to the public on January 10th. And the comment period extends through March 11th. Uh, that's a 60-day comment period, which is more than is required. And additionally, we had four public meetings, as you heard about, again, exceeding what is requirement per, uh, the environment, National Environmental Policy Act. Uh, next slide, please. So, you may have heard that, uh, the environmental impact statement is quite a lengthy document. And so, what we provided here is kind of a snapshot, and I know you all have this in your packet, of what does each and every discipline take a look at? At a very quick, uh, one to do in summary. Well, one thing that we did to make the document a little more, uh, reader-friendly is you don't have to dive through the entire document. We have put together an executive summary, which is about a 20-page, exactly what it is, a summary. And you can find the high-level findings that are in the document. The actual document itself, what we, we call the chapters, or chapters 1 through 7, are a couple hundred pages, providing a little more detail. And if you want to dive deeper into any specific item, we have technical reports that are part of the appendices. So, again, yes, it is a

Adaptive reuse: Converting existing buildings to new uses rather than replacing them.
Placemaking and public space: Public-space design, programming, and place-led improvement.

chapters.title: Items A \u0026 D.1 (Part 1 of 2)
chapters.text: All right, I think we have a quorum here. We'll go ahead and begin. Today is October 17th, Tuesday, 2017. It is 9.20. We're in the Boards and Commission room here at City Hall. We have our work session today. On our work session today, I think we have three items that have been pulled. We also have a briefing on the mobility initiatives. We have a presentation on two Code Next items, which we indicated will probably happen after lunch. I think that's when staff's ready to do those after lunch. And then, so I would think that what we'll do is we'll do the pulled items. Then we'll discuss the mobility initiatives, and then we'll go back into executive session to handle the executive session items. And then we'll come back after lunch to do the two Code Next items. Okay? So let's begin with the pulled items, item number 18. Council Member Pohl, you pulled that. So as we had directed staff, the anti-lobbing ordinance portion of the Waste Management Task Force working group went to the Ethics Review Commission, and I made a presentation about it, and some of the stakeholders were there representing two kind of different interpretations or preferences or desires for the elements of the anti-lobbing ordinance that were still kind of in flux. As anticipated, the Ethics Review Commission asked some really good questions and then assigned it to their working group. So they will be working on their assessment of it and taking input from the stakeholders who were there, and I think we will have a good outcome. We just need to give them a little bit of time to do their work. I think that we should have this back on our agenda probably November 9. The working group is having a special called meeting to deal with this officially on November 1. Okay. So you're going to be moving to postpone this to the 9th? Right, to November 9. Thank you. Okay. Thanks. Next poll item, Mr. Flanagan, you pulled item number 23. Yes, I wanted to ask the sponsor and the co-sponsors what the substantive outcome of this is. I'm in support of fixing the across I-35 thing. Like, I'm on board with all that. It's not the question. But I want to make sure that if there's a problem with cure zoning that we're actually solving it and that I don't – it's my understanding that we're not removing sites that already had cure zoning. We're just preventing new cure zoning. This is my question. I just want to make sure I understood the resolution because the be it resolved was one sentence, and I hadn't seen one that short before. So I've got to know more about this. Well, we're going to amend that last be it resolved because Council Member Renteria wants to keep 5th, 6th, and 7th, is that correct, Council Member Renteria, to have the ability to do the cure zoning. I really wanted some staff more info on exactly what is going to happen this morning, and that's why I signed up also. So I just wanted to know how it's going to affect what we already – it seemed like we already have done to South Diller and 6th Street. Right. And that's why we're going to be amending it. But just generally, it's to remove the cure zoning from East 11th, that strip. Because since 1996, I think, times have really changed, and I think those additional entitlements are a negative impact on the community that's still there. And I'm with you, but I'm still confused because I'm hearing conflicting either it will change sites that already have this right or that we're just preventing new sites from getting this. And I think I'm going to have to ask staff to answer that. Greg Guernsey, Planning and Zoning. I think the cure zoning will probably be treated like other properties that we have that have certain entitlements. We already have buildings built under cure, and certainly downtown. So those buildings would be grandfathered under the previous regulations. I understood the resolution was removing some of the fingers from East Austin. And when I think it was Council Member Eric Mitchell brought this forward back in the 90s, there wasn't a whole lot happening on the east side, and he was trying to incent development to occur in East Austin, and that's certainly happening now. So if Council passes a resolution, we can move forward in Code Next to remove those fingers that are part of this resolution and leave the remainder in play. Wait, so this is about Code Next? No, we could do that through Code Next. So we should also do that through Code Next. But I guess my concern was, are we passing a resolution that is directing staff to do something in Code Next when we have decided not to do that on anything else? And that being one question, and then the second question is, if we're just removing cure between now and at the point we adopt Code Next, is that actually substantively doing anything? So the way the resolution reads right now is, does Council initiate the following Code Amendments? And that really would address, I think, those fingers that go to East Austin. We could do this as a separate amendment now, or we could fold it into Code Next. So what I've heard from the Code Next consultant, when we've talked about that, they said you need to go ahead and do it as a part of Code Next while we're in the process, so instead of waiting until Code Next gets adopted. And so that's why we brought this forward. There are parts of Lower East Austin in Councilmember Pio's district, Smyteria's district, where this would, he wants to keep those options open. For the people on 11th and 12th Street, they're saying no. And I'm completely on board. So I'm not trying to undo the intent. I'm trying to better understand it. Because if we're hearing from staff consultants that in order to get something in Code Next, I should pass a resolution now, I could go home and start writing a bunch of resolutions. And I don't think that's what we're trying to do either. No, but how is this different from having it go through the Code Next process? I mean, with this direction, we would just move forward. And those 11th, 12th, and I think MLK, too, those would be the three fingers that would be removed from the Code as it comes forward. And you still have 5th, 6th, and 7th would remain as they exist currently. Yes, I understand that part. Can I speak maybe? Please, please. Because you're right. This is part of the concern with Code Next. And partially what I spoke to last week was that we have all these districts and overlays that we have been told Code Next is not touching. And so that's part of the problem. If CURE was something implemented that we need to take another look at, we need to take a look at all of it. We should, we're not supposed to be looking at, you know, there's serious concerns about how it has affected East Austin. But it hasn't been used a lot near Lamar. And so maybe it needs to be taken away near Lamar. Or maybe it needs to be taken away in certain areas. So now we're just going to pick little areas. Instead of looking at the whole thing in the Code Next process and determining, is this appropriate, period. And that's my biggest concern with this Code Next process. If we're looking at parking regulations, we're going to look at all parking regulations. Not, you know, where they're not allowed. We can't look at it in this neighborhood, and we can't look at it over there. And this neighborhood's excluded. It just defeats the whole purpose of what Code Next was supposed to be about, I think, is the point here. I mean, that's what I've been discussing about ADUs. And there were concerns, rightfully so. We'll have to agree to disagree, saying, no, we're not changing ADU regulations at all. But I do plan to bring an ADU resolution before, you know, this Code Next process is done, hoping that we take another look at those and how they're implemented. So that being said, I don't disagree with what you're trying to do here, Councilman Houston. I just, maybe it needs to be meant to say, let's look at all of Cure, and if it's right. It seems like a compatibility issue is the problem. It's not all the Cures. The Cure from downtown was eliminated in 2013, so they've taken care of the downtown. Was it 2013 or not? Yes. It was in 2013. And so now the only cures that are still in place are in those areas that we just outlined. So does your resolution mean that there's no more cure except for where Councilmember Ben-Anthony wants to keep it? Correct. Okay. So I have a similar concern, just because, and I need to think this through more, because it does feel like something that should be part of Code Next at some level. And I certainly don't want us to be bringing in a series of resolutions between now and March to create a parallel process. From a substantive standpoint, I know that Cure allows for greater density and height without an exchange for affordability or anything else. So in that regard, it seems to me that where we're trying to move forward to in Code Next, if we can, I think, is to try to say, in areas where we're going to lose any measure of affordable housing, like I think immediately on the other side, east of I-35, because the market's going to push the value of those single-family homes to a place where only the richest in our community can afford them. If we're going to actually preserve some opportunities for mixed-income opportunities in that area, it's going to be because we create tools that operate outside the market or use market incentives to get people to build those units. The Saltillo, Todd, is an opportunity to create affordability where the market's not going to create it by itself. So I think that it's, one, I also agree that letting the density or height with Cure without that corresponding benefit to the community is not good. And when the resolution was passed in 2013 with respect to downtown that moved Cure out of downtown, it did two things. It said, we're not going to just give extra height or

chapters.title: Items 85 \u0026 86 (Part 2 of 3)
chapters.text: We are out of recess, and we will take up, as previously advertised, items 85 and 86. We'll hear the presentation and conduct the public hearing for both 85 and 86 together. And when that's done, we'll vote on the two items separately, one being the flum and the other, the zoning case for the same property. Mr. Guernsey. Thank you, Mayor and Council. Greg Guernsey, Planning and Development Review Department. Item number 85 is a neighborhood plan amendment in Montopolis neighborhood planning area located at 1700 and 1 half Frontier Valley Road. This is a change to a future land use map from a commercial land use to multifamily. The related zoning case is item number 86, case C14-2012-00-67 to zone the property in at 1700 and 1 half Frontier Valley Road to a multifamily residence medium density neighbor plan or MF3 MP combined district zoning. The property that we're talking about is just over 9 and 1 half acres in size. It's undeveloped currently at this time. The surrounding properties in the area are zoned MF3 to the north, MF3 CO, CS, and GRMU MP to the east, about SF3 to the west, and CSMU MP to the south. The proposal is to develop the property with an affordable housing project of approximately 252 units. It is located in the Montopolis neighborhood planning area, and the contact team has voted to recommend the request. As it comes before you, both the staff and the commission have recommended the change. There are some differences to the recommendation by the planning commission, and just kind of let me say that the staff recommendation on the neighborhood planning plan amendment was to grant the multifamily residential. The planning commission, in moving forward to recommend that on a 9-0 vote, also recommended the zoning change. The zoning change to MF3 MP would have a conditional overlay added to it that would limit the vehicle trips to 2,000 per day. They did not impose a cap on the number of units, although the TIA would probably limit the property to about 311 units because of the TIA limitation. If they generate more than 2,000 trips, they'd have to do a TIA. The commission also included in their motion that the buildings adjacent to the proposed right-of-way reserve, which would be through the property or on the edge of the property, face that reserve area. Surface parking would be the interiors of the site, sidewalks we provided along Frontier Drive. On the dais, you have a copy of the ordinance and a restricted covenant. There is, I'll say, some variations of the restricted covenant. The owner has agreed to reserve 70 feet of right-of-way perpendicular to Frontier Valley Drive and would also propose an alignment that's different than the staff alignment. On the dais, you have, in yellow, on Exhibit B to the restricted covenant. Again, this is on item number 86, an alignment that takes it through about the bottom third of the property. That is an alignment that would mirror the regulating plan for the East Riverside Corridor that is also staff is recommending and will come before your planning commission next week. So that is our recommendation to bring it forward. I believe the applicant would prefer that the right-of-way alignment be along the south property line of the area being rezoned and an adjacent property owner would like it along the northern boundary of the area being rezoned. And I think you'll hear from a speaker and from the applicant to explain their reasonings why for that tonight. Mayor, I know you have numerous speakers. I think about 20-plus speakers have signed up on this. So I'll pause if you have any questions, and we can go to the applicant's presentation. Okay. Any questions for staff? I'll hear from the applicant. Amelia Lopez is here to speak on behalf of the applicant. So, Ms. Lopez, you're entitled to five minutes as applicant, and you have a bunch of people donating time. Steve Helm. Is Steve Helm here? All right. Frank Del Castillo. All right. George Colley. George Colley. Randy Marino. So, that means you've got 11 minutes. We have some materials we'd like to distribute to the council. Pass them to her pro tem, and she'll pass them down. Okay. Great. If you can be ready. Okay. What I will do, hopefully I won't take up that much time. What I'd like to do is begin with reading a letter that's being distributed to you that basically lines out the process we've gone through, where we've ended up starting in April and where we are today. So, if you don't mind, I will be reading for this so I don't leave anything out. We began this process as any development would begin in the City of Austin. After our internal review due diligence, we met with staff from the City of Austin Planning and Development Review Department to determine the feasibility of the project and the applicable ordinances and requirements. As outlined in the City's process, we initiated the public process by scheduling a meeting with the Montopolis Neighborhood Plan Contact Team on May 21st. We met with the members of the Contact Team Executive Committee to introduce the project, received input from the committee, and to request an out-of-cycle submittal. The Executive Committee provided input and positive responses, but requested that we return to the Contact Team to meet with the entire Contact Team. That meeting occurred on June 14th, 2012. The contact team voted to approve the out-of-cycle submittal and provided support for the Neighborhood Plan Amendment requested and the zoning change requested. Following the June 14th, we met, we prepared our application and submitted to the City of Austin on June 25th. Per the City of Austin Neighborhood Plan process, public notice was mailed to invite interested persons to attend a public meeting on our application for July 30th. This meeting was sponsored and led by the Neighborhood Planning staff members, Maureen, Meredith, and Jason. And on that same night following this meeting, a meeting of the Planning Contact Team was held and again voted in support of the Neighborhood Plan and the zoning request change. For the next three weeks, we received input from City staff and neighboring residences, which we incorporated many of the suggestions and requests into our plan. A number of residents in opposition to our project requested a meeting, a separate meeting, which we had, and we met with them on August 24th. And this was primarily at the Arbor's Condominium Complex, where we discussed connectivity, primarily connectivity, street parking, and how our plan fit into the neighborhood, among other things that they had mentioned to us and asked questions about. On August 28th, the staff provided a positive recommendation to the Planning Commission. The opposing residents requested a 30-day postponement and received a 14-day postponement, which we did not oppose. During that postponement period, City staff, residents, and our team met on September 4th to discuss the project further. Additional input was provided, and we made a couple of additional modifications to our plan. So one thing that's constant is we kept modifying our plan through every meeting. Zoning and neighborhood planning staff provided their recommendations on September 7th prior to the Planning Commission for September 11th, and prior to the commission meeting, we met and discussed all these changes that have been occurring through the process with some of the commission members to try to get some input and any questions they may have. After the presentations from staff, our team, and supporting opposing and supporting residences, and a general discussion by the Planning Commission members, the commission supported our project of the 6-1-1 vote, and we were scheduled for discussion for action by council on September 24th. Based on the input we received at that meeting and afterwards from various parties, we requested a postponement at the September 27th City Council meeting to allow us to voluntarily meet with the contact team and the Planning Commission to present our modifications that we had made based on a lot of the input we received in requests and considerations. The residences in opposition again requested a postponement. The commission denied the postponement and heard our case. They provided the staff still supported our project, and the commission voted in favor of our project with a 9-0 vote. Our cases have already been delayed at least twice as a result of our client wishing to continue to work with the residences in opposition and our offer to voluntary return to the contact team and the Planning Commission to provide them the most updated information before this case came before you. Our voluntary action was in an effort to provide council with a comfort level that all parties were able to review, comment, and act on our most recent and updated modifications. In addition, we did not shortcut or expedite the process to allow more buffer time for potential postponement requests, such as today's request. City Council understood our deadlines of the October 18th, and you all have supported the October 18th hearing, 11th hearing. Unfortunately, because of the notification process, it brings us today to October 18th. This brings us to today, and after all of these meetings, all these discussions, and all these modifications, we've met with supporting and opposing residences, the representative of the adjoining properties, Mr. Ron Thrower on behalf of his client, the zoning staff, the neighborhood planning staff, long-term planning staff, and the planning commissioners and council offices to get as much input as we could. We've incorporated many of the ideas and suggestions into our plan. We've explained why we did not incorporate certain ideas and suggestions into our plan at the same time. Our project has changed no less than 10 times because of all the community involvement that we've had and we have encouraged. We've had as many changes as we can do, subject to the project and market feasibility. The residents in opposition, again, are requesting, as you heard earlier, we're requesting a postponement. We feel this plan presented to you today is the best plan for the nearby residences, the Montopolis community, the City of Austin, and our client. We respectfully ask for your support on our project, which will provide 252 units for workable, affordable housing units as provided, and ask for your approval on the neighborhood plan and zoning requests. A point of clarification, even though it's not a conditional overlay to max out the units, because of the way this application has gone through with the state for the tax credits, we are limited to 252 units. So I just wanted to make sure you knew that we wouldn't

chapters.episode_title: Work Session and Regular Meeting – Feb 27, 2024
chapters.text: Moving on to item 5, items for individual consideration. Item 5A, present, discuss, and consider action on a resolution approving an agreement with OJB, Landscape Architecture, for the Addison Circle Park Vision Plan, in an amount not to exceed $188,000, and providing an effective date. Jana. Mayor and Council, Jana Tidwell, Director of Parks and Recreation. The item I'm bringing before you this evening is to consider a contract for a professional services agreement with OJB, Landscape Architecture. Before we, and I do have the OJB team here, Tara Green and Katie Martin, who will make a presentation to you. But before we do that, I'd like to share a little background with you about this project. This project was first recommended in the Park, Recreation, and Open Space Master Plan, which was adopted by Council in 2019. At that time, the master plan identified the need to plan for development of Addison Circle Park in the conference center in theater area in conjunction with the TOD development. The plan included the following recommendations. To design and promote the park as Addison's central hub. Considering new frontages, circulation patterns, and connections to the Dart Station and Cotton Belt Trail. Improve the park's southern edge in relationship to the TOD and create a new gateway into the park. Discuss impacts to special events and preserve lands and opportunities integral to Addison's signature seasonal events. Priorities, prioritize creating a gathering space along Festival Way that allows for park and light rail access to regular occurring programs and activities. Evaluate opportunities to connect the Northwest Plaza to the conference center patio. Improving the pavilion, plaza, and grounds to support various public and private events. And then bolster outdoor programming and create daily activation opportunities that attract visitors to the park, such as programs implemented at Clyde Warren, Discovery Green, and Bryant Park. So that was a lot. That's a big task. And because of that, staff actually brought a council item or a budget item to Council for consideration in the FY23-24 budget. And at that time, Council awarded $205,000 for or included in the budget, $205,000 to develop a vision plan for the activation of Addison Circle Park. And so to begin to implement that vision, in November of 2024, staff issued an RFQ soliciting responses from qualified project teams to submit their qualifications. And the RFQ identified the following metrics for the project and asked the respondents to provide experience around the following. We asked for consultants to provide a track record for proven and successful public engagement strategies. We understand that this park is surrounded by an existing community. It has very different density than Clyde Warren, although we heard in our master plan that our residents wanted that. And so there will need to be a public engagement process that identifies what's the right fit for Addison, what's appropriate for our residents and visitors. We have heard from people that preserving open space is very important. And so those are important conversations that we need to have in order to determine what this park needs to look like and what it needs to be. We also asked the teams to provide their track record for creating visions for dynamic, multifunctional urban parks that serve as amenity to residents and attracts visitors of all ages. We were looking for substantial experience developing programming bubble diagrams that include spatial analysis of uses and creating park programming activity plans, which includes daily, weekly, monthly, seasonal, and annual events. We were also looking for substantial experience developing park operation plans that identify management, programming, maintenance, and security needs. And then finally, we were looking for a track record with revenue generation for parks, understanding that to implement the vision plan, we also need to look at how this can be sustainable. So as we issued that RFP, the selection committee had eight, we had eight, I cannot speak this evening. We had eight, I'll slow down. We had eight consultant teams that responded to the RFQ. We identified four consultant teams to make additional presentations to the selection committee. And the selection committee selected OJB Landscape Architecture as the most qualified team. Their submittal and presentation showcased an experience developing, operating, and maintaining highly activated parks. They have experience developing successful park programming strategies. They had a track record for showing quality of similar urban design projects. They have experience with philanthropic and external funding sources for activated parks. And they had engagement strategies for gathering input and building consensus. So with that said, I have representatives from OJB here. They are going to make a presentation to introduce their firm to council and share some of their relevant project experience with council. And so I'm going to turn the podium over to Tara Green and Katie Martin. And so you can just hit that. Okay. All right. It's great to be here tonight. We appreciate you taking the time to listen to our presentation. I'm Katie Martin, and this is Tara Green. We're both principals in the Dallas office of OJB. Tara has a specialty in public realm strategies and community engagement, and I'm a landscape designer. OJB has six offices throughout the country, and so with that, we have a really deep bench of expertise that we can reach out to. But the Dallas office really likes to work locally, and we have great relationships throughout the Metroplex. One of the things that's really important to us is that we call it our three-legged stool. So we have our public realm strategies component of our work. We have OJB Lab, which does research, you know, within landscape architecture and project-specific research. And then we have construction and continuing care team. And at the heart of all of that is design. So in terms of project management, some of the things that are very important to us are communication, collaboration, planning, resource management, risk management, quality control, feedback, and leadership. And that's a lot. But I think what we find is our projects are so much richer when we're able to really collaborate with our clients and when we're really able to listen to a community. We also believe in equitable spaces. We think it's really important. That's part of the community engagement process is being able to identify how people feel welcome, how they feel engaged with the space. One of the things we wanted to go through in our interview process was our approach. And we feel it's really important to do discovery in the beginning. So how do we get started? What is the fact finding? What is the site analysis? We've already been to the site. We're watching tonight. It's amazing to see how many people are out this great weather walking their dogs, enjoying the park, running through the park. But how do we improve that experience? How do we build on what you have already built out there to enhance what's coming? We have eyes on the park. And that's going to grow. That's going to grow with the foot traffic that's coming in and out of this building. It's going to grow with the transit-oriented development. And then we look at the benchmarking. I'm Tara Green. I am the principal of Public Realm Strategies, as Katie said. And before I joined OJB, I was the president of Clyde Warren Park. So I was the first president of Clyde Warren for the first five years of the park's operation. And our firm, OJB, designed Clyde Warren Park. So our firm has been attached to that project since it was just an idea, long before it even began construction in 2009. And so my role at Clyde Warren as the president of the 501c3 that ran that park was to put a business plan in place. So Jana was talking earlier about our experience in operations, maintenance, programming, design. Katie leads design. I'm your operations, maintenance, boots on the streets, been there, managed a public space, and figured out the business model to make it sustainable. So that two-pronged approach permeates everything we do throughout this process. Yes, and Tara and I sit next to each other, so it is a great dialogue for us to kind of bounce off of each other and really get the best out of a project. Yes, so she looks at it from a designer's perspective. I look at it from an operations maintenance. How are you going to pay for it? Who's going to do it? How does it look great 10 years down the road? So we want to make sure that we're delivering economies of scale, efficiencies, great material choices that are beautifully designed. You do not have to sacrifice design to get something that's efficient and will stand the test of time. Part of our approach and one of the foundational things that was explained in the RFQ was community engagement. We truly believe equitable spaces are a result of the community's input. How do we listen to all voices? How do we invite them in? How do we meet people where they are? Not everybody likes an online option. So how do we go where people are? How do we pull their voices and iterate? How do we show them that their voices are being heard throughout the process? And so we also know that creating connections and amplifying opportunities are an important part of this vision planning process. And one of the case studies we thought was important to show you was our new parks in Omaha, Nebraska. Three existing parks that have been sub-optimized for years. Gene Leahy Mall, Heartland of America, Lewis and Clark Landing. Our job was to come in and renovate these parks to connect downtown Omaha to the riverfront. Each park in and of itself is about the size of Addison Circle Park. But created together, they now have a unified experience. You would not have walked from one park to the other in the past. Now the pedestrian experience matters. We worked with them to master plan these parks, then to design and build them. So my job in all of that was to help the new management entity that was identified as part of the process. The city of Omaha partnered with local philanthropists to create a public-private partnership to build it. But they didn't know how the parks department wasn't able to take it on. So we worked with them to find the right business model that made sense to operate. We put an activation plan together. We put a budget forecast together. What would it cost them to activate these spaces? And then we created three parks unlike anything that had been seen in the state

chapters.title: Item 6
chapters.text: So, slowly making our way through here. Next is Code Next Draft Land Development Code Diagnosis. Mr. George Napolak. And thank you and everybody else for hanging in there. You're welcome. Good evening, commissioners. Thank you for the opportunity to be here. Here tonight to talk about Code Next, which is the name that we've given to the project to revise the city's land development code. And in particular, I want to talk about the code diagnosis report, which was just released on May the 5th. But I want to give you a little context just to explain a little bit about how this project fits into the overall, how this report fits into the overall project. So, essentially, we are revising the code in order to respond to one of the priority programs in Imagine Austin, which is to update the city's development regulations. The last comprehensive revision we had of Land Development Code was in 1984, although it's been amended hundreds of times since then. It's become very complex, and the approval process has become very difficult. Meanwhile, Austin's growing by 140 people a day, and we need better tools for helping to implement the vision of Imagine Austin. Imagine Austin does, of course, include the growth concept map, which encourages the trying to accommodate much of the growth in a series of centers and corridors along major arterial streets. The work has been divided into a four-step process. We began last summer with a listening and understanding phase. That is wrapping up now, and we're in the second phase, the diagnosis and approach alternatives. That will be concluding in the fall when we go to City Council for some direction on which general approach to proceed. And only at that time will we actually begin writing the draft of the new code. So that will start around the end of this year. We'll be going through an extensive review and approval process, revisions, and so on. And the target date for final adoption of the code is the fall of 2016 by City Council. We have a number of products that are coming out. Some of them already released. Others will be coming out shortly. The first one was the listing to the community report, which came out on April the 4th. The second, the code diagnosis, as I mentioned, came out on May the 5th. The third is the community character manual. We will be releasing that this week, at least the first edition of it. This is something that is a work in progress, and we will be adding to it throughout the remainder of the year. The next report will be the code approach alternatives coming out in the fall, and that will be accompanied by an annotated outline. I'll talk a bit more about those in the future. So in terms of listing and understanding, we've conducted interviews with over 100 stakeholders. We've held a number of listing sessions, workshops, and small group meetings. We've involved over 800 people in the process to this point, and have received thousands of comments, literally. The first report, listing to the community, summarized all those comments, and what we identified were six major themes, as indicated here. Affordability, environment and open space, neighborhood characteristics, design of development, transportation, and general code issues. Code diagnosis was prepared by our lead consultant, Opticoast Design, and there are copies of it on the dais in front of you, and I apologize. I think I miscounted on the number of members, and I have enough for everyone, but I'll be glad to get additional copies for those that don't have them. The diagnosis summarizes the major issues, which have been identified by the public, the staff, and the consulting team, and it defines the basis for revising the code. It identifies the problems with the code and the major issues that we should address in doing the revision, but it does not recommend a specific direction for the code. That will be the next step in the process. So there were ten major issues identified as the top issues, and this is not all the many details. There were many, many comments we received, some of them very specific and things that we need to address. But these are sort of the top ten things that, the overriding issues that we need to look at in revising the code. The first is just ineffective based zoning districts. The existing districts that we have don't recognize appropriate form or different types of places. We have most of the city, over half of it is regulated by some sort of overlay district or combining district or a special district like a planned unit development. And this is a sign that the base districts themselves are not working very well. What our consulting team is suggesting is that we look at different types of base districts for different types of neighborhoods within our community. One set of regulations for what we would call walkable urban areas, more the core and the older parts of town. Another set of regulations for the transitional areas, somewhat beyond the core but not quite suburban yet. And then finally, the more suburban parts of the community which have been designed around the automobile and will probably continue to be largely dependent on the automobile. The second major issue that identified is competing layers of regulations. The base districts, 33 base districts in combination with the 19 combining districts in our code would lead to over 600 possible combinations. And we actually identified at least 400 that are currently in use in the city. Basically, it goes back to the same problem that the base districts have are somewhat ineffective. So we've added many layers such as compatibility standards or design regulations. And we've never really addressed the problems with the base districts themselves. So we think that we could do a more effective job by coming up with some better base districts that differentiate the different parts of town without throwing out all the issues or concerns that led to the development of the overlay districts themselves. Third issue is the complicated opt-in opt-out system. In our neighborhood planning areas, there are many tools that are available that have been selected by different areas. But they're somewhat piecemeal. They're not really identified in the code. You have to go to a different document to find out what they are. And again, it makes it hard to figure out what types of regulations apply to specific properties. Fourth major issue is that a lack of household affordability and housing choice. The regulations, the code itself cannot fix the affordability problems in the city. It's going to take many different efforts to address the high cost of living. But there are things that the code can do to affect construction development costs, to improve efficiency in the permitting and approval process, to look at some of the restrictive limits on density that we have in certain areas. The consulting team also felt that we have few mechanisms in place to preserve or enhance existing affordable housing, and that some of our density bonus programs are not yielding the results that we would like to achieve. One of the important tools that they think we should try to address is finding ways to accommodate a variety of housing types that are not often considered in our current code. Things somewhat between single-family development and mid-rise apartments, such as duplexes, townhomes, bungalow courts, and other similar housing types. Our code makes it difficult to develop many of these housing types under the present situation. The fifth major issue is an automobile-centric code, as I've already mentioned. This makes it difficult to encourage pedestrian transportation. The diagram you see on the left here is the intersection of Burnett Road and Anderson Lane, and the gray shaded areas are all land that's devoted to parking or driveways. In most commercial developments in suburban areas, the parking exceeds the amount of land that's devoted to buildings, and so it forces development farther apart and increases dependence upon the automobile. Issue number six is that the code is not always in line with Imagine Austin. There are concerns that if we really want to invest in a compact and connected city, we need to take a look at our regulations, and not just the code itself, but how we invest in our infrastructure. Many of our roadways are not the type that are amenable to pedestrian transportation, and even if we come up with better development types along the roads, we need to address the facilities themselves. Same with drainage, we need to look at various alternatives and a variety of approaches for different types of development. In more suburban areas, a stormwater detention facility, the types you see on the left might be more appropriate. In a more urban area, something that you see on the right is something that we should consider. Similarly, with tree protection, it's a very important value, but we need to consider how it's going to affect our ability to achieve the compact and connected goals we have. The seventh major issue is a lack of clarity and usability in the code. The format and layout are not user friendly in many cases. There are a few graphics. The numbering system is complicated, and it's very hard to find your way around and figure out what regulations might apply. The eighth major issue is the ineffective digital code. The online version of the code is not very user friendly. It doesn't have many searchable links or cross-references, and it's somewhat awkward to use. So this is a big area where we can make an improvement. Issue number nine is that code changes have adversely affected the departmental organization. The staff that reviews development permits covers many different departments. As the code has become more complicated, we've had to have more people to specialize in different aspects of it. And any time you involve multiple departments, then you have difficulties in maintaining a consistent mission and consistent interpretations. Just the sheer volume of applications, the amount of paper that we require strains our workspace and increases the potential for conflicting requirements. Climate resilience: Heat, flooding, extreme weather, resilience planning, and adaptation.
Walk, bike, and transit access: Walking, cycling, transit access, or multimodal connectivity.
Infill and redevelopment: Reuse or intensification of already-served land within a city.
